en: Śrīḥ.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
The Viṣṇu-saṃhitā
Now begins the first chapter.
Having prostrated before the perfected one seated on the peak of Śrīśaila, who had mastered the tantras and possessed an exceedingly radiant form, Aupamanyava questioned him. (1.1)
"O Blessed One! Having as it were conquered the sun, you stand here with your radiance;
never before have I seen such a form belonging to anyone. (1.2)
"Are you the sole lord among the gods, or among the sages, or perhaps among men?
I wish to ask you this, for I am struck with wonder by your splendor."
The origin of this exceedingly brilliant splendor is praiseworthy.
From where have you come here, for what purpose, and from which family was your birth? (1.4)
You have accomplished all that was to be done, you are free from desire, and your greatness is certainly incomparable;
[yet you do not know] your lineage, name, deeds, and so forth, in their entirety and according to reality.
"There is great curiosity to hear this, yet it is incomprehensible to me.
Thus questioned, the Siddha, having meditated upon Hari with palms joined in reverence, spoke.
With a voice faltering with joy, his hair standing on end and his eyes filled with tears, he said:
"Listen, I shall tell you everything; for this is indeed the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu. 1.7.

"I am Sumati, the son of the seer Idhmavāha, belonging to the lineage of Bida; she [the goddess] deludes embodied beings through the manifold diversity of the senses, their objects, and the intellect. (1.8)
Having exerted myself in the three Vedas with their auxiliary branches and in the Tantras during my youth, I lived here on this mountain of pure waters in the practice of celibacy.
I lived for a long time as an attendant near Raibhya while he was engaged in silent recitation, desiring to see this former benefactor whom I had not seen for a long time. (1.10)
I have come here from the world of Viṣṇu through the air; may it be well with you.
O Teacher, what mantra did you not obtain while chanting here in this city?

Or what else [is needed], since through such practice this transformation occurs; for even when he had vanished by means of the perfection of mantra without having given any instruction, [this result followed]. (1.12)
Weeping, I heard a faint voice in the sky crying out loudly, "What is my refuge?"—a cry rendered difficult to understand by this [response]: "My refuge is Tāranātha. (1.13)
Having recited the Śiva-mantra as it was remembered, I beheld the Lord through its perfection;
he said to me, "Recite the Brahma-mantra," and then I recited it.
Then Brahmā, the bestower of boons and creator of the worlds, appeared;
addressed by him, I bowed down and was told, "Let the mantra of Viṣṇu be recited."
Then, seeing both of them wearing matted hair, rosaries, and other marks of asceticism,
he considered them to be insufficient [to defeat him], while regarding Viṣṇu alone as sufficient.
Reciting the six-syllabled mantra day and night without distraction,
I have beheld Him who is the form of the universe, yet formless, appearing now in embodied form.
[He is distinguished] by the conch, discus, mace, lotus, Śārṅga bow, sword, arrow, and shield;
by the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem, the yellow silk garment, and the forest garland.
The supreme among gods, whose noble limbs were adorned with ornaments such as crowns, necklaces, armlets, and earrings, was immeasurable.
Possessing a divine form, mounted upon a bird, anointed with divine perfumes,
he resembled a thousand suns and was difficult for even the gods and asuras to behold.
Having propitiated him with mantras from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as with various hymns of praise,
I then addressed him once more with devotion.
O Blessed One! O Lord of the gods of gods! O Vāsudeva! O Lord of the universe!
Grant me that knowledge by which I may have fulfilled my purpose. 1.22
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, being pleased, spoke with a profound voice:
"By good fortune, my child, your intellect is pure; your name 'Sumati' (Good-minded) is not in vain. (1.23)
I am well-pleased; may prosperity be yours. Therefore, I shall speak for your benefit.
Listen, having first become initiated into the *Īśvarasaṃhitā*. (1.24)
After [hearing it] from the Lord Brahmā,
and likewise having heard the *Brahmasaṃhitā* and my own *Viṣṇusaṃhitā*, you will then attain knowledge.
"Three mantras—of Śiva, of Brahmā, and mine—have been recited by you;
therefore, by way of grace, you shall attain the three [goals] in succession."
When the god had vanished after saying this, Śiva appeared as soon as he was remembered;
pleased, he said to me as I bowed before him, "Let that which was spoken by Viṣṇu be done."
Then, having performed the rite of initiation, he obtained from him the Īśvarasaṃhitā consisting of twelve chapters, which prescribes the method of worship without seed-syllables (nirbījārcā).

Then, having heard from the god Brahmā— who had arrived as soon as he was remembered— the *Brahmasaṃhitā* consisting of thirty-two chapters, which is based upon the worship of both the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and the non-seed-syllables (*abīja*).
Then, having prostrated as before, I addressed this once more to the eight-armed Adhokṣaja, the god who had appeared through my recollection: || 1.30 ||
O God of gods, salutations be unto you, O Vāsudeva, O best of deities!
I have heard this from Lord Brahmā for your sake.
O Lord of all worlds, since this *Viṣṇusaṃhitā* has been compiled according to the rules by your command, may you therefore graciously favor it as it truly is.
Thus entreated with devotion, the imperishable Lord Viṣṇu expounded the extensive Viṣṇusaṃhitā, which serves the purpose of all spiritual perfections.
It consists of one hundred and eight chapters and bestows the supernatural powers of the eightfold sovereignty and others;
it possesses four auspicious feet consisting of knowledge, conduct, ritual action, and yoga.
Then, through the practice of the ritual of worship involving the seed-syllable, the non-seed-syllable, and that which possesses the seed-syllable,
delusion was destroyed in an instant, and desire for sensual pleasures ceased.
All my doubts have been severed and my mind has become serene;
that supreme abode of Viṣṇu has become manifest before my very eyes.
The sound of celestial instruments arose, and a beautiful rain of flowers fell;
on all sides, the wind was pleasant to the touch and fragrant.
Then, after that Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of All, had vanished, I dwelt here for some time, devoted to the recitation of mantras, worship, and other such practices.
While I was reciting, there occurred at one time a rain of flowers and other such signs as before; accompanied by auspicious omens, all the quarters of the sky were stirred.
Then Tārkṣya, having swiftly approached me at the command of Hari,
took me up and conveyed me to the world of Viṣṇu by means of his divine motion.
There, having again beheld Mahāviṣṇu in his divine form, who was being praised by Brahmā and the other gods, I bowed down and stood before him. (1.41)
Being pleased, the granter of boons said, "May you dwell near me.
Having lived very happily in his presence for many years, [I remained there].
Having attained through his grace this eightfold sovereignty that is free from calamity,
and having obtained such splendor here, I have reached these worlds by my own will.
But you are devoted and humble, and indeed everything must be heard by you;
yet that Viṣṇusaṃhitā cannot be heard in a short time.
I shall extract the essence for you and speak it so that there may be nothing here unheard by you,
just as the Blessed One, when questioned by me, summarized [the teaching] out of a desire to condense it.
He spoke to me this essential and concise Viṣṇusaṃhitā, which consists of:
the summary of the Tantra, its commentary, the majesty [of the Lord], and the determination of the sacred fields (kṣetra).
The extraction of mantras, worship, mudrās, the consecration of the fire, the mandala, initiation,
consecration, the ground, the temple, and the characteristics of the image.
The fivefold consecration, as well as the sequence for the purification of the image,
the preliminary rite (adhivāsa), the consecration itself, and the rites following the consecration.
Likewise, there are festivals and processions, offerings and the universal worship, the restoration of dilapidated structures, the pacification of great portents, and ritual ablutions.
The sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), the remainder of the ritual (karmaśeṣa), the compendium of conventional conduct (samayācārasaṅgraha),
and the yoga pertaining to the Lord (bhāgavata)— thus there are exactly thirty chapters.
This is a compendium of all the subjects taught therein in the extensive Viṣṇu-saṃhitā, which consists of one hundred and eight chapters.
This most secret and meritorious Viṣṇu-saṃhitā, which provides both worldly enjoyment and liberation, should be known as having its meaning made clear, as it was spoken by Viṣṇu himself.
Thus ends the first chapter of the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the second chapter.
Now, I shall explain the exposition of the tantra from the beginning in brief, by which, when properly performed here, eternal accomplishment is attained. (2.1)

A devotee who has received initiation and consecration, a Brāhmaṇa established in his observances, compassionate toward others, eloquent, perfected, and one who has reached the further shore of the Siddhānta. (2.2)
He defeated the systems of others through formal debate, informal discussion, and destructive criticism;
he was endowed with all auspicious marks, a speaker of truth, and firm in his vows. (2.3)

Free from fault, a knower of yoga, self-controlled, skilled in ritual action, and most proficient in the knowledge of time—he should explain [the teachings] to those who have approached him, especially to his own disciples. (2.4)
[He gave] with great effort to those who were initiated, disciplined, and devoted,
to the twice-born who had studied the Vedas, and indeed to those who possessed faith.
Having saluted the teacher, the disciple, sitting comfortably and being diligent, should recite [the text] preceded by the syllable Om, and listen again from the teacher. 2.6.
And he should practice together with such twice-born initiates;
having thus understood this and being consecrated, he should impart it to others.
Then he should initiate the disciples and perform the installation and other rites;
even though initiated, a Śūdra may neither recite nor listen [to these texts]. (2.8)
He should mutter the mantra given by his guru and perform worship upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
however, he has no authority over the worship of deities installed in a temple or over fire-offerings (homa). || 2.9 ||
Even for one who has been initiated, he may nevertheless have this performed by Brahmins;
for it is by him that all goals are extended and people are protected from fear. (2.10)
Thus, those who know the tantras explain the "tantra-nature" of a tantra, either because it is rooted in the Veda or because it possesses an authoritative source. (2.11)
It would be authoritative like the Purāṇas and likewise like the words of Manu and others;
it is fivefold: through perception, inference, comparison, verbal testimony, and presumptive implication. (2.12)
If there were no appearance of error, all objects would be cognized;
for cognition arising from the senses is seen to be a mental state whose objects are sound and the like. (2.13)
The appearance of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) as fallacious is known to arise from defects in the object, the sense organs, and so forth.
Consequently, inference is threefold: the "prior" (pūrvavat), the "residual" (śeṣavat), and the "generally observed" (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa). 2.14.
Inference would be the means for knowing objects that are yet to come or have already passed;
analogy is that wherein there is the perception of the object to be compared through its similarity [to something known]. (2.15)
That which is established by implication is accepted here as presumption (arthāpatti);
however, verbal testimony (śābda) is recorded as being manifold, through divisions such as the Vedas and the Tantras. (2.16)
For some, the self is self-luminous; for others, it is inferred by means of its transformations, as well as through both scriptural traditions and various logical arguments. (2.17)
The creator, though partless, is inferred through all the created entities;
knowing that "everything is thus created," he is indeed omniscient. (2.18)

Those who know that the Tantra is authoritative because it was spoken by a trustworthy person (āpta) also assert that the authority of the Veda rests solely upon its having a trustworthy source. (2.19)
That Tantra is divided into five types— Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, Saura, and Kaumāra— and is further distinguished according to its specific speakers.
Because Viṣṇu is the proclaimer of dharma, that which he spoke is like the words of Manu;
for Brahmā and Viṣṇu are traditionally remembered by the wise as the proclaimers of dharmas. (2.21)
Just as there are numerous divisions of branches for the tree of the Veda, so too have the divisions of the Pañcarātra been proclaimed by the wise. 2.22.
They are distinguished individually by specific recitations of ritual acts; and from those [recitations] as their source, the Tantras were composed by sages, gods, and humans. (2.23)
Because it was composed in many ways by him, this is remembered as manifold;
likewise, even within this Pañcarātra which is so extensive and of many varieties.
Reality, however, exists as one alone without distinction and not otherwise;
it is called the "Kula" object of experience by virtue of its specific mode of practice. (2.25)
That itself is the proof of their status as teachers; of this there is no doubt.
The Vaikhānasas and Sāttvatas are renowned as being rooted in Ekāntika devotion.
The spheres of perception (gocara) are declared to have their basis in Vāsudeva and the other [vyūhas];
yet these ultimate spheres are divided fivefold. (2.27)
One should perform the worship of the God of gods constantly at all times,
and support one's family with what is obtained unasked.
Where the Vaikhānasa lineage exists, characterized by specific modes of conduct and ritual action,
the worship of Viṣṇu is clearly performed once or twice a day.
The maintenance of one's family through the occupation of a kshatriya, not retreating in battle, and proficiency in all the sciences. (2.30)
Those endowed with these characteristics are proclaimed as Sāttvatas:
agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing, as well as the worship of Viṣṇu twice a day.
And this is observed where those who possess the tuft of hair (śikhins) are proclaimed:
the service of the twice-born and subsistence by means of the mendicant's way of life. (2.32)
Those who perform worship even once are known as *tataikāntikas*;
[those who worship] once a day, twice a day, or again three times a day. (2.33)
The worship of the God of gods through the actions of mind, speech, and body, and the practice of subsisting on what is obtained unasked—these are seen among them. (2.34)
Or even subsistence from one's own disciple—these are to be known as the categories termed "roots.
Each of these consists of five subdivisions, making twenty-five in total. (2.35)
Furthermore, the tantras concerning these are of infinite extent;
and there are devotees of the Blessed One, as well as servants and attendants.
Thus, another division ending with the Bhāgavatas has been proclaimed here:
those devotees who are attached to their social classes, who are peaceful, and who are Vaiṣṇavas though not initiated by you.
Initiated devotees of the Blessed One are indeed known as lifelong servants;
they are the attendants who find their sole purpose in his service and subsist on what is offered to him. (2.38)
Those Brahmins who are perpetual performers of instrumental music for worship and who observe celibacy are to be known as Bhāgavatas; indeed, they are the most excellent of all.

"The initiate (samayin), the spiritual son (putraka), the practitioner (sādhaka), the preceptor (deśika), and the teacher (guru)—thus another classification of those initiated has been ordained here by Viṣṇu. (2.40)
Having drawn the mandala according to the ritual procedure and having displayed the form together with its limbs according to the rule,
the teacher who shows it here is known by the name Samayin.
Having worshipped the deity together with the complete form in the mandala according to the rule, the preceptor himself should reveal it; he is known as a *putraka*. (2.42)
Having displayed the mandala and offered oblations into the fire according to the rule, the preceptor should initiate that disciple; he is then a practitioner who possesses the mantra.

The teacher who initiates a disciple through all the procedures for the worship of the mandala and the fire sacrifice (homa) in their proper sequence is indeed a preceptor (deśika) who knows the tantras. || 2.44 ||

One who has been initiated, who follows the traditional conduct and possesses virtuous character, who is learned in all tantras, and who performs meditation, worship, and other rites—such a person should be known as a guru. (2.45)
Among the castes, the Brahmins; among the Brahmins, the Vaiṣṇavas; among them, those who are initiated;
among them, those who know the mantras; among them, those who know the tantras; and among them, the worshippers. (2.46)

Among them, those who possess the texts are superior; among them, those who can recite them; among them, those who understand their meaning; among them, those who have attained mastery; and among these, one who has been sprinkled with the water of initiation is distinguished.
Therefore, Hari himself is the bestower of grace and the expounder of this;
thus have I explained to you the scope of the Tantras by way of summary.
Those who desire to attain that supreme state of Viṣṇu should constantly serve the five nights, which have as their range the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest. (2.49)
Or rather, this Pañcarātra consists of the great elements (mahābhūta);
for it is by attaining that supreme splendor that these five nights [of ritual] exist.
That which destroys all ignorance perishes in five nights;
therefore, it should be studied and listened to with devotion for the sake of putting its meaning into practice. 2.51
Such is this Tantra called Pañcarātra, the most excellent of authoritative scriptures;
it is distinct from these [other] five nights (Pañcarātras) and is stainless (nirañjana).
When one perceives that supreme reality, then one is liberated, and not otherwise;
he alone is to be known as the true teacher, the one who ferries others across the ocean of saṃsāra. (2.53)
That very Lord Viṣṇu is not without fruit; such is His grace.
Thus ends the second chapter of the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the third chapter.
Now, I shall briefly describe the supreme majesty of Viṣṇu, by knowing which the pure-souled one attains the station of Viṣṇu. (3.1)
O Goddess, here the supreme light is the one and only Supreme Person;
he alone is divided manifold in the world by his own māyā. (3.2)
Having manifested the primordial nature (prakṛti), which is called Māyā, that one known as Puruṣa exists in two ways;
and he is perceived in three ways according to the distinction of the qualities (guṇas) such as sattva and the rest. || 3.3 ||
He is considered to be known as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva, performing the functions of maintenance, creation, and destruction;
his forms are Vāsudeva and the others, distinguished by dharma, jñāna, and so forth. (3.4)
His four [states] are to be known as resting upon the Vedas, the castes, and the ages:
Parameṣṭhin, Puruṣa, Viśva, and Nivṛtti, who is Sarva. 3.5.
Through the fivefold distinction of its subtle causes (upaniṣad), it has attained the state of the great elements;
and through the six limbs, namely the mind, the ear, and so forth, as well as the heart and so forth. (3.6)
Consisting of six syllables, it is eternally divided by the seasons, as well as by the seven vyāhṛtis, the worlds, the meters, and the sacrifices. (3.7)
This [Self], when divided sevenfold, is to be understood by the wise as consisting of eight constituent natures (prakṛtis) and likewise of eight forms (mūrtis).
Consisting eternally of eight syllables, he is divided eightfold:
Nārāyaṇa, Nṛsiṃha, Varāha, and likewise Vāmana; (3.9)
Rāma, Brahmā, Indra, and Sūrya, along with Candra—by them he is established in nine ways;
likewise Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and Varuṇa. (3.10)
Vāyu, Soma, Īśāna, Brahmā, and Ananta—these ten, differentiated by the eleven sense organs as well as by the lords of the twelve months, [constitute the manifestations]. (3.11)
It is recorded as being thirteenfold through the Viśvedevas and others;
it is divided fourteenfold by the Manus, beginning with Cākṣuṣa.
It should be known as existing in fifteen ways by means of the lunar days (tithis);
it is divided into sixteen ways by the vowels, and likewise by the cardinal directions, the intermediate corners, and the sub-directions.
The expansion of his [nature] is to be understood through various other forms;
he possesses faces on all sides, appearing as one, two, three, four, five, six, and so forth. (3.14)
The various divisions of the faces of that Viśvātman Hari have been fully described;
likewise, the divisions of the arms of him whose hands are on all sides are recorded as being two and so forth. (3.15)
They were adorned with various ornaments, tall, and wielded diverse weapons;
their heads, it was said, were graced with glittering crowns and earrings.
In the Pauruṣa Sūkta, there are a thousand feet and many eyes;
he is Hiraṇyagarbha, the manifold self, stainless, and indeed dark-complexioned.
He is proclaimed to be blue, yellow, red, and of various colors;
the moon and the sun are remembered as his left and right eyes.
They say that Brahmā is his head and the trees are his hair;
likewise, Rudra is situated between his eyebrows, and Soma resides in his mind.
The eleven Rudras are to be known as residing in his throat;
the lunar mansions, planets, and stars are proclaimed to be his eyes. (3.20)
Likewise, dharma and adharma reside in the cavity formed by his upper and lower lips;
Indra and Agni are in his palate, and Sarasvatī is in his tongue. (3.21)
The cardinal and intermediate directions are situated within the two ears;
Vāyu is to be known as residing in the vital breaths (prāṇas), and the Maruts are remembered as being the fingers. 3.22.
The sages reside in his pores; the oceans are within the range of his bladder;
the rivers, the earth, and the nāgas are situated in his shanks.
The two Aśvin deities are established in his knees, the mountains reside in his thighs;
the Guhyakas are to be known as being in his private parts, and the Vasus are situated in his chest.
And it should be known that divine medicinal herbs reside in the tips of the nails;
the two nostrils are to be understood as the southern and northern solstices.
The seasons were situated at his armpits, and the months were upon his hands;
the Siddhas were located on the tip of his forehead, and the clouds with lightning were between his eyebrows.
Yakṣas, kinnaras, gandharvas, daityas, dānavas,
as well as rākṣasas and cāraṇas, have taken refuge within his belly.
The Pitṛs, Pretas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Vetālas, and Pramathas,
as well as those who dwell in the netherworld, stood at his pair of feet.
On its two sides should be known the sacrifices, the Vedic and Tantric rituals, the rites such as the Agnihotra, and those pertaining to the castes and stages of life. (3.29)
The utterances of Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭ—all reside within his heart;
indeed, those who are celebrated as the thousand names of Viṣṇu abide there. (3.30)
Those thousand forms are situated here according to their respective functions;
for even the number "thousand" is proclaimed as a designation for a great multitude.
All his forms are indeed beyond numbering and manifold;
for the forms of all the gods and others are proclaimed right here. (3.32)
Therefore, Viṣṇu, being of a thousand forms, is considered the soul of all;
yet, just as unity is not perceived when there is a multiplicity of mirrors, [so it is with his manifestations]. (3.33)
In that same way, those of small intellect consider Viṣṇu to be manifold,
just as the reflections of the moon's orb and echoes appear in various ways within water.
"Even though the Self is one, it appears as many in this way," so say the seers of truth;
but the deluded, ignorant of the ultimate reality, are bewildered by their lack of knowledge. (3.35)
For they say here that the knowers of the field (kṣetrajña) are many, and they take delight [in this view]:
"The Brāhmaṇas are from his mouth; the Kṣatriyas are from his arms. (3.36)
From whose thighs the Vaiśyas were born—that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
such is that Great Viṣṇu, immeasurable and free from all ailment.
Without his grace, it is impossible to speak of or even to know [him].
Viṣṇu is the refuge of all gods; all gods have him as their very self. (3.38)
This entire body of speech, as well as the world with its light and darkness and all that is moving and stationary,
is eternally pervaded by the body of Viṣṇu, just as the sky is pervaded by the wind.
All the gods are proclaimed in all the scriptures to be devoted to Viṣṇu;
from him the entire creation was born, and into him it finds its dissolution.
Who else besides the lotus-eyed one remains pervading the universe?
Janārdana exists in two ways, through the relationship of the container and the contained.
Established for the welfare of all beings, he exists both with parts and without parts;
thus should Viṣṇu, who is higher than the highest, be known as possessing this dual nature. (3.42)
The Lord exists in three ways according to his gross, subtle, and supreme aspects;
he is remembered as Prabhaviṣṇu, Mahāviṣṇu, and Sadāviṣṇu. (3.43)

For he is remembered as the Self (ātman), the inner Self (antarātman), and the supreme Self (paramātman); he is the Vairāja, the Laiṅgika, and the Īśa, existing externally, internally, and everywhere.
Sound and the rest are the form consisting of consciousness, pervading the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
the wise man should seek this triad within the mantra, the resonance (anusvāra), and the primordial sound (nāda). 3.45.
In the Vedas, in Sāṃkhya, in Yoga, in the pure Pañcarātra, in the Dharmaśāstras, and in the Purāṇas—by sages, gods, and humans alike. (3.46)
It is recited by all that this entire universe is pervaded by Viṣṇu—whatever exists in the past, the future, and the present. (3.47)
The sense organs and the objects of the senses, the elements and the internal organ, the unmanifest, the three qualities, Māyā, Vidyā, and likewise dharma and the other [qualities]. (3.48)
Necessity, limited agency, time, and everything else is composed of that;
Viṣṇu alone is the supreme deity, abiding within all beings. (3.49)
And he is indeed all beings; there is nothing here that he is not—gods, asuras, and the like, mortals, beasts, and reptiles. (3.50)
Trees, creepers, grasses, and herbs; great clouds, lightning, and thunderbolts; mountains, oceans, rivers, gardens, cities, and lakes. (3.51)

And the worlds—consisting of the infinite fire at the end of time, the abode of pretas, and the lair of serpents—as well as the seven worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, are designated as Brāhma, Śaiva, and Vaiṣṇava. (3.52)
And understand that all these were pervaded by Viṣṇu alone:
Varāha, Bhārgava, Siṃha, Rāma, Śrīdhara, and Vāmana. (3.53)
Aśva and Kṛṣṇa are among their [directional] quarters; with these, the entire mundane egg is encompassed.
And whatever has not been mentioned in its entirety—all these are the manifestations (vibhūtis) of Viṣṇu.
By virtue of his all-pervasiveness, this Lord attained the state of Viṣṇu;
and by dwelling within all beings, he likewise attained the state of Vāsudeva.
He is known as Saṅkarṣaṇa because he draws forth from the Primordial Form;
he is Pradyumna because of his abundance of splendor (dyumna); and he is Aniruddha because he is unobstructed.

He is Acyuta because he does not fall from his yoga; he is Tridhāman because of his three abodes; and he is known as Antaryāmin and Adhokṣaja because he is to be perceived by the senses in a manner contrary to their ordinary functioning. 3.57.
Because his complexion is as pure as Vaikuṇṭha, he is called Vaikuṇṭha;
and because he has hair (keśau) at the beginning and end of creation, he is Keśava.

He is Nārāyaṇa because he is the creator of men and women, because he is the refuge (ayana) of men (nara), because he arises from the primordial waters (nārāḥ), and because those waters are his place of rest (ayana). (3.59)
Mādhava is so called because he was born among the Madhus, or because he supports (dhavatvāt) Śrī;
Govinda is so named because he finds (vindati) the earth (gām); and Hari is so called because of his taking away (haraṇāt) all sufferings. (3.60)
He is called Madhusūdana because of his slaying of the demon named Madhu;
he is to be known as Trivikrama because he pervaded [the three worlds] with his three strides. (3.61)
He is Vāmana because of his association with shortness; he is Śrīdhara because he bears the goddess Śrī;
and he is called Hṛṣīkeśa because he is the lord of the senses known as the hṛṣīkas. (3.62)
Because a lotus (*padma*) arose from his navel, he is remembered as Padmanābha;
and because a rope (*dāman*) hung from his belly (*udara*), he is called Dāmodara.
He is Rudra because he was born from weeping; he is Brahmā by virtue of his act of expansion;
he is Indra due to supreme sovereignty; and he is called Vahni because of carrying [the oblations]. (3.64)
He is Yama because he restrains men; likewise, he is Varuṇa because he encompasses them. He is Vāyu because he blows, Soma because he bestows, and Īśa because he is desired among people. (3.65)

He is called Āditya because he is the son of Aditi, and Candra because he delights (candayati); thus, although he is one, he is designated in many ways by words that grasp his various qualities. (3.66)
The moon is perceived as if in water, yet its multiplicity does not thereby exist;
just as the all-pervading wind, being extremely subtle, is not seen. (3.67)
Likewise, Viṣṇu is omnipresent; he is not perceived by the ignorant, but is seen by those who know him.
Indeed, his powers are threefold, distinguished as will, knowledge, and action. (3.68)
That power which is divided twelvefold as his four forms is the supreme, subtle Śakti, known as Will (icchā), whose form is desire (kāmarūpiṇī).
That by which all this, including the moving and the unmoving, is seen as woven across and through—dividing itself twofold, it sets in motion both action and knowledge. (3.70)

By virtue of that [power], Viṣṇu, as another [aspect], creates the entire universe as if it were independent through his power of action (kriyā-śakti); while the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) [acts] through his power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti). (3.71)
They call him the Sacrificial Being (Yajñapuruṣa), the sky-farer composed of austerity and the Vedic meters;
yet he who is the supreme, imperishable Puruṣa is to be known through the power of will (icchā-śakti).
An agent should engage in action preceded by knowledge; therefore, action is to be understood as having knowledge as its support, and it does not proceed alone. (3.73)
The single power of the Supreme Person, through the distinction of action and knowledge, remains pervading the entire world of moving and non-moving beings in two ways. (3.74)
Since there is no mutual difference between power and the possessor of power, the wise should understand that the dyad of action and knowledge is non-different. (3.75)
The One alone exists in a threefold form, established through this differentiation;
for the triad of action, knowledge, and will is indeed one and the same.
The distinction between Khaga, Upendra, and Śiva is known as a mere figurative designation (upacāra) of the one Great Self alone; therefore, they are proclaimed to be non-different from Him.
The sense organs and the objects of the senses are merely manifestations of the intellect;
the transformations of the ego are considered to be like bubbles upon water. (3.78)
Just as milk has a single color even when the cows are of many colors, so too should one perceive a single form even when the substrata are diverse. (3.79)
Know that this entire world, including all things moving and unmoving, is subject to momentary destruction;
yet that which is not subject to destruction here is the one, supreme state of Viṣṇu.
And from the sovereignty of that Lord, all this proceeds;
for the entire world possesses a Lord, and it cannot be without a Lord. (3.81)
Those deluded by ignorance speak of a multiplicity of the Knower of the Field;
however, a plurality of Knowers of the Field is not accepted by those who possess knowledge of reality. (3.82)
But those fools who, on account of the difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi), say that the Supreme Self is manifold—they indeed wander in saṃsāra and do not attain the supreme state. 3.83.
Those for whom even the Creator of the universe does not desire omniscience for this [Lord] have not determined the relationship between the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge. (3.84)

That which is considered the birth of the world through the production of those possessing form is brought about by the Lord; indeed, there is no need for any other impelling cause than primordial nature (prakṛti). 3.85.
Therefore, let it be understood that the universe is created by the Lord, supported by Him, composed of Him, protected by Him, for His sake, and belongs to Him. (3.86)
Surely the power of such a god is not difficult to understand;
he himself knows it, or at least so it is heard from sacred tradition.
Who knows that Supreme One from whom this entire creation was born?
For even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, are but embodied forms created by Him and are themselves limited.
Nevertheless, the description of the greatness of that one whose form is inconceivable declares that your infinity of greatness does not exist in Viṣṇu; such is the Śruti. (3.89)
Thus ends the third chapter of the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

Now I shall explain in brief the determination of the field and the knower of the field, as well as the yoga of creation and dissolution, together with the relationship between the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment. 4.1
Nature is to be known as the field (kṣetra), and its knower is the Lord, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). Both of these remain as if absolutely non-different from one another. (4.2)
The unmanifest, the intellect, the ego, and here the five subtle elements, together with the eleven organs and the gross elements—thus is the field proclaimed. (4.3)
The field exists in two ways through the division of gross and subtle:
the sixteen effects are gross, while the subtle is born solely from the intellect and the rest. (4.4)
The body of all embodied beings is both impermanent and eternal;
the enjoyer who dwells within this city is called the Puruṣa. (4.5)
The Puruṣa is pure consciousness and all-pervasive; the city [of nature] is composed of the three qualities and is insentient.
By his direction, it produces and also withdraws all states of being as if it were independent. 4.6

Prakṛti is for the sake of another, insentient, subtle, composed of the three guṇas, and eternally changing; however, due to the differentiation of the guṇas, it undergoes threefold transformations beginning with the intellect (buddhi). 4.7.
Sattva is happiness, rajas is suffering, and tamas is delusion; these are their qualities. They function by mutually suppressing, manifesting, pairing with, and supporting one another. (4.8)
Sattva is light and illuminating; rajas causes persistence in action; tamas is heavy and obstructive. They are known as white, red, and black respectively.
All these states of being—whether superior, middling, or inferior—arise when endowed with these very three qualities residing in primordial nature. 4.10.

Though he is one and devoid of qualities, the person appears as manifold through the various distinctions of association with the qualities of *prakṛti*, just as a crystal appears endowed with other colors. 4.11.

One should worship with *sāttvika* dispositions for liberation, with *rājasa* dispositions for enjoyment, with *tāmasa* dispositions such as those involving the infliction of pain on others for the sake of harming others, and with mixed dispositions for the attainment of mixed results. (4.12)
Therefore, attending upon that [Self] with vigilance, one should perform all actions as purely sattvic states alone, without suppressing other states. (4.13)
The intellect, known as the Great One, arises from the unmanifest through the three qualities; having four, one, and three divisions, that intellect is traditionally said to be of eight kinds. (4.14)

Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty are the qualities of the intellect when characterized by sattva; lack of dispassion, passion, and unrighteousness and so forth belong to that which is dominated by tamas. (4.15)
Restraint (yama) and observance (niyama) constitute dharma, consisting of actions born of mind, speech, and body;
these must be practiced by those desiring liberation in order to propitiate the gods. 4.16.
Faith, fortitude, and that supreme mental quality called serenity—these are declared here as the dharma of the mind;
while speaking what is true, pleasant, and beneficial is proclaimed here as the dharma of speech. (4.17)
The bodily [dharma] consists of three types: service, purity, and favor;
these are the duties to be performed by those belonging to the various castes and stages of life. 4.18.
Whether one follows the Vedic or Tantric path, success in this [practice] occurs, and not otherwise.
Knowledge, moreover, is fourfold because it serves as a limb for liberation, dharma, artha, and kāma. 4.19.
Detachment is held to be twofold, produced by seclusion and by world-weariness;
the former is internal for the sake of liberation, while the other is external and leads to bondage. (4.20)
From the intellect (buddhi) is born the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which is threefold and composed of the three qualities (guṇas);
by means of this, a living being regards what is not the self as if it were the self. (4.21)
The Vaikṛta pride is of the nature of sattva; that called Taijasa is of the nature of rajas; and the Bhūtādi is of the nature of tamas—these are remembered as the different types of pride. (4.22)
From the *vaikārika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the five sense organs of cognition have arisen, by means of which knowledge regarding objects is produced for a person. (4.23)
From Taijasa arise the five organs of action for the sake of action;
from that [Taijasa] is born the mind, which is twofold and serves as the instrument of volition. (4.24)
The mind (manas) is to be known among the sense organs such as hearing, and consciousness (citta) is remembered among those such as speech;
from the source of the elements (bhūtādi), the five subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi) are born in their respective order. 4.25.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these are to be known as the five powers of Viṣṇu, beginning with Parameṣṭhin. (4.26)
By means of those [powers] by which this supreme deity abides in the highest heaven—
this very Supreme Lord is the power of consciousness (cicchakti), the immutable foundation of all effects and so forth.
The second is its power, which consists of transformations such as the person (puruṣa) and the syllable (akṣara);
the third is called the universe, appearing in various forms, and consists of the instruments of action. 4.28.
The fourth [power], having reached its object, abides again as that called "withdrawal" (nivṛtti);
his fifth is called "all-pervasive" (sarva) due to the fullness of the powers of knowledge and action. (4.29)
Endowed with these powers, the stainless Supreme Self becomes the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction, even though it remains inactive. 4.30
The Lord also effects the restraint and favor of the world through fivefold powers, distinguished by the predominance of each one individually. (4.31)
These fivefold selves are indeed remembered as being established in subtle form; they transcend the objects of worldly existence, are accessible through yoga, and are eternal. (4.32)
This subtle body is said to be the cause of material form; indeed, from the subtle elements (tanmātras), the five gross elements are born in succession. (4.33)
Space, air, fire, water, and earth as the fifth—this gross body arises as the support of all. (4.34)

The ear, the skin, the eyes, the tongue, and the nose are the organs of perception; while speech, the hands, the organ of generation, the anus, and the feet are recorded as the organs of action. (4.35)
Thus, the process of creation, ending with the body and distinguished by its gross and subtle aspects, has been described to you by me; the sequence of dissolution is the reverse of this creation.
Just as a single embodied being, though possessing only one subtle body, assumes multiplicity through various bodies in birth after birth,
so too does the Lord manifest through manifold forms.
The powers of that very Supreme Person are millions of others, appearing as if distinct due to the differences in their classes, names, and essential natures. (4.38)
Having obtained a body composed of the elements through their own accumulated actions, those people who wander in saṃsāra indeed roam for a long time within the cycle of existence. 4.39.

By means of auspicious action, they go to an auspicious destination with its face turned upward; by means of inauspicious action, they go to an inauspicious destination with its face turned downward. (4.40)

Men, though their nature is consciousness by its very essence, are submerged in the differentiated world; deluded by the darkness of attachment, they are incapable of knowing themselves or the Supreme. 4.41.
Attachment, aversion, and the like are their defects arising from nature;
they produce for him manifold latent impressions of saṃsāra. (4.42)
When the quality of goodness (sattva) predominates in them, their destination is held to be divinity;
humanity is said to arise from passion (rajas), and likewise, the state of being an animal from darkness (tamas).
In this way, all embodied beings go to various destinies;
mounted upon the wheel of time, they revolve through the illusion of ignorance.
He in whom the sattvic qualities such as dharma exist, either individually or collectively, is dear to Him; he in whom adharma and the like reside is His opposite, the one who is not dear.
When the end of the dissolution has arrived, the Supreme Person,
free from activity and consisting of a mass of pure consciousness, abides in the supreme ether.
Since this is so, therefore, having obtained this body which is the means for all [attainments], men should perform only auspicious action for its purification. (4.47)
When this [path] has been clarified for all through the duties of their respective castes and stages of life,
all desires come within reach, and liberation is not difficult to attain at the end.
His embodied forms exist for the sake of his work, as means to favor the world;
therefore, by worshipping him with form through devotion, all perfections are to be attained.
Satisfied by that supreme devotion alone, the God of gods, who is the goal of yogins,
first assumed a four-armed form in order to bestow grace through worship and other such means.
Therefore, he should always be meditated upon and worshipped by the wise in that very form.
Worship, praise, or even meditation performed toward this image [yields great fruit]. (4.51)

According to the procedure prescribed by the scriptures, he becomes truly a god; one is to be worshipped for the sake of worldly emergence, while the Supreme Person is to be worshipped for the sake of Nirvāṇa. 4.52.
Worship of these two is recommended in both the forenoon and the afternoon;
one should visualize the dark-hued, eight-armed deity together with his vehicle.
One who desires prosperity should worship him, together with his weapons and his retinue—
he who resembles pure crystal and who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
One should worship with devotion the four-armed Lord residing in Ananta for the sake of liberation;
they know the lotus to be the seed of creation and the discus to be the basis of preservation.
The mace and the conch are always remembered as being for the purpose of withdrawal and liberation;
the worship of that which is endowed with all the principles (tattvas) is indeed performed by way of withdrawal.
Meditation is the state of being indifferent to fruits; this is the sequence for those seeking liberation:
the performance of action, speech, intellect, and worship becomes increasingly abundant at each successive stage.
It may be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), passion (rājasa), or goodness (sāttvika). First comes the agreement, then the conduct, the study of the scriptures, and the collection of materials.
Intellect, sacrifice, stability, and meditation—thus the rule is eightfold.
The person is of two kinds: the initiated devotee and likewise the uninitiated. (4.59)

The initiated one is the performer of all [rites], whereas the other merely partakes in the worship of the observance (samaya). The observance consists of ritual worship, devotion, faith, and reverence for the act of worship. (4.60)

Listening to sacred stories, tranquility, a livelihood not based on worldly gain, and the eightfold observances—[with these] one should worship [the deity] with flowers produced in one's own garden, or with wild ones, or even with those purchased. (4.61)
Since the fruit belongs only to the giver, one should not accept [the offerings] for the sake of worship;
even in the absence of incense and flowers, one should perform the worship with flowers alone. 4.62.
But in the absence of flowers, one should offer water; and in the absence of water, one should offer them with the mind.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Now I shall explain, in brief, the supreme method for extracting mantras, by the proper performance of which mantras become potent and grant one's desired goals. (5.1)
In a secluded, level, pure, moist, and delightful place,
strewn with heaps of flowers, one should perform the extraction of the mantra.

Having bathed, sipped water for purification, performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), and adorned himself with perfumes, flowers, and other ornaments, the practitioner, self-restrained and accompanied by his attendants, should perform the laying out of the ritual lines.
Having prepared a sixty-four-square grid with fragrant sandalwood paste,
one should inscribe the eighty-fold Mātṛkā alphabet, beginning from the first letter to the end.
One should recollect the arising of the eight groups from the all-pervading *nāda*: in pairs in the first row, and then by groups one after another until the end.
The primordial sound (nāda) is the letter 'A', which is self-born and has Vāsudeva as its essence;
the letter 'Ā' is known by the name Saṃkarṣaṇa, and the letter 'I' is known by the name Śiva.
From that, the vowel *ī* was born, and those two [the letters *i* and *u*] are of the nature of Saṃkarṣaṇa;
the syllable *o* is Brahmā, and those two [the letters *o* and *m*] are known as Pradyumna. (5.7)
From this [letter A] arose the letter *ṛ*, known as Haṃsa; from it arose the letter *ṛ*, which is Aniruddha.
O Unborn One, from that was born the letter *lṛ*, called Mahat, and then the letter *lṝ*.
Then follows the letter *e*, called Rudra, and immediately after it the letter *ai*;
then the letter *o*, called Prajāpati, and the letter *au*, which has that as its essence. (5.9)
From that [A] comes Bindu, whose essence is Hara and Īśa; from this [Bindu] come the vowels (visarga).
From that Hara-Īśa, there are sevenfold divisions through the distinction of the Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī.
The *ka*-group and the letters beginning with *ya* should be placed in the other rows;
thus one should worship the auspicious Goddess Sarasvatī, who consists of eight groups. (5.11)
One should worship with perfumes and flowers, using the names of the deities of the colors in their proper sequence;
then [one worships] the Gāruḍa [mantra], which was extracted by the Aśvins and removes the loss of color.
Having performed the ritual with the two known as Yamaka, one should extract the mantras from them;
in the extraction of the eight syllables of the Praṇava, Vāsudeva himself becomes manifest.
In the Ṣaṭka, Saṃkarṣaṇa is Brahmā; in the Gāyatrī and the Cakra, Hara;
in the Ajita and Uddhāra, Pradyumna; and in the Nārasiṃha, Aniruddhaka. (5.14)
The seed-mantras and weapons of Vāsudeva and the others should each be raised by their respective [mantras], while the five Upaniṣads and so forth are to be raised by Āditya alone. (5.15)

One should first extract the very first letter; then, in that same place, one should join together three letters—the fifth, the end of the sixth, and the first of the first group—placing them all in one spot. (5.16)
This is that supreme reality, the imperishable, the highest state;
by this alone is the worship of Viṣṇu performed, and its recitation and fire-offering bestow liberation.
Having himself become the tenfold state consisting of the three gods, the qualities, the Vedas, the fires, and the twilights,
he attained the status of being the source of all mantras through his pervasion of the imperishable syllable that begins the Vedas.
The fifth vowel is the end of the first word, starting from the syllable *tā*; the sixth vowel is the end of the second word, together with the thirteenth consonant;
and the name of the deity ends in the fourth case—this is the characteristic of the mantra.
Thus, the six-syllabled mantra is seedless, and likewise the eight-syllabled one;
in the twelve-syllabled [mantra], the word "Bhagavat" should follow after the salutation.

The seed-syllable, beginning with *tāra* (oṃ) and ending with *natyanta* (namaḥ), is used everywhere; however, if there is no such designation, then where the name ends in the dative case, the word *namaskāraḥ* is placed at the end. (5.21)

The fourth [vowel] with the eighth [consonant], marked by the bindu at the end of the first sixth [vowel], is the heart-mantra of that seed-syllable, which they know as the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu. (5.22)
One should fashion its first head from the second [letter] ending with the bindu;
the seed-syllable of the crest (śikhā) is the first of the eighth [group], differentiated by the third vowel.
The fourth is the armor-mantra (kavaca), ending with the fifteenth vowel (au) and the bindu;
that same mantra becomes the weapon-mantra (astra) when conjoined with the sixteenth vowel (visarga).
This is declared to be the five-limbed [mantra] of the six-fold seedless [form];
when joined with the names and castes [of the deities], the wise know it to be the bestower of all desires. (5.25)

They say that the heart-seed, the root-mantra, and the limbs—six in total—are formed by joining pairs, fours, and sixes, ending with the twelfth, the final (sixteenth), and the fourteenth vowels respectively. (5.26)
The nameless [mantras] end with "namas," while those with names end with "svāhā" when they possess a seed-syllable;
however, if there is no seed-syllable, the word "ananta" follows the *praṇava*, provided it is accompanied by "namas. (5.27)

This has been taught as the characteristic of the root mantra together with its seed-syllables: [it consists] of letters preceded by the syllable *tāra* (oṃ), accompanied by the nasal bindu, and containing seed-syllables differentiated by vowels. (5.28)
One should assign the six limbs up to the eyes with the names beginning with "namaḥ":
the heart, resembling a kunda flower; the head, with the luster of crushed collyrium. (5.29)
The crest (śikhā) should be known as piṅgalā; the armor (kavaca) is like gold;
the weapon (astra) should have the form of lightning; and the eye (netra) is like a blazing fire. 5.30.
Endowed with the qualities of the heart and others—namely, knowledge, contentment, permanence, sovereignty, and unimpeded majesty—the Sakala [deity] performs acts such as bestowing grace. (5.31)
The utterances *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ* are used in the fire-oblation (*homa*) for rites of pacification and nourishment;
*namas* is used in recitation (*japa*), worship (*arcā*), and so forth; and the *praṇava* (oṃ) is placed at the end for rites of mastery (*aiśvarya*). (5.32)
First, the letters ṣa, ya, ra, va, and la, ending with the bindu (ṃ), are placed between the *tāra* (oṃ) and *namaḥ*;
[the mantra] "parāya" is used in the place of "bhagavate" in the five Upaniṣads and other texts. (5.33)

The first is the Self of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), and the next is the Self of the Person (Puruṣa); then the Universal Self (Viśvātman), the Self of Cessation (Nivṛttyātman), and the All-Self (Sarvātman)—these five are traditionally taught. (5.34)
These five [mantras] are to be employed in invocation and dismissal, both in direct and reverse order;
they are proclaimed for use in sprinkling, in the propitiatory oblation, and in the purification of ritual substances. (5.35)

Both the Puruṣa and Prakṛti are designated as Jīva and Prāṇa; likewise are the intellect (buddhi), the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), volition (saṅkalpa), the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi), and the sense organs (indriyāṇi). 5.36.
And the elements— these twenty-five principles (tattvas) are to be understood by the teachers in their proper order, ending with the letter *ma* and preceded by the nasal bindu.
The eighth vowel and the final vowel [are used] for Kāla and Diṅ respectively;
the syllable *kha* is for Vainateya, and after that, for Vighneśa. 5.38.
The seed-syllable of Kāla is that of Ananta; its six long limbs are the seed-syllable of Akṣa, which is the final letter of the alphabet, for the visualization of the wheel-mandala.
The syllable *praṇava* is the lotus; its parts are the petals, filaments, and pericarp.
The short vowels are the seeds located in the navel during the three libations.
One should apply the unvoiced consonants during the months of Kārttika, Āśvina, and Mārgaśīrṣa;
and the initial vowels without the visarga to the left and right sides respectively. (5.41)
By means of those [calculations] beginning with the visarga, the lunar days (tithis) for the zodiacal signs (rāśis) are also to be inferred in two ways;
and within these, the asterisms (nakṣatras) starting from Aśvayuj follow in their proper order.

The nine planets—beginning with the Sun—are represented by the vowels ending in the nasal bindu (aṃ), the consonants from ha to ma, and the two letters ya and ra; they are situated in their own respective signs, as are Rāhu and Ketu. (5.43)
The letter *sa* and the letter *ṣa* are on the inner and outer rims [of the wheels];
here, the principles beginning with *prakṛti* are to be joined separately in their respective order. (5.44)
Viṣṇu and the other deities residing in the spokes should be joined with the twelve-syllable seed-mantras;
likewise, the seasons beginning with spring should be joined with the root-mantras in their proper order. (5.45)
In the sacrifice of the wheel-mandala, however, this specific distinction is declared here:
in the worship of auspicious sacrificial altars, the mantras do not depend upon the [specific] time.
One should arrange the eight names and the two sets of six, accompanied by "vidmahe" and "dhīmahi," in their proper order; "tanno viṣṇuḥ" should come at the end, followed by "pracodayāt. (5.47)
This Gāyatrī, belonging to Viṣṇu, should be known as the remover of all sins;
for by her, the King of the Gods accepts everything that is given. (5.48)
It should be employed during the ritual service, at the cooked offering, and at the final oblation;
having proclaimed "Sahasrāra," one should join the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*.
This six-syllabled [mantra] is to be known as the Sudarśana, unbroken;
it wards off minor spirits, piśācas, and the like, and destroys disease. (5.50)
The fourteenth vowel (au) with the final bindu (ṃ), and likewise the Nārasiṃha mantra,
[are formed] by the letters of the eighth consonant class in reverse order, preceded by the Tāra (oṃ) and the bindu.

The forms beginning with Vāsudeva, ending with "namaḥ," are to be applied in the cardinal directions; likewise, with those same [names] in their long forms, Śānti, Śrī, and Sarasvatī are placed in the corners.
And *rati*—these four form-powers (*mūrti-śakti*) are to be applied in sequence;
and the first seed-syllable of the eighth [form] is joined with the end of the twice-seventh [syllable]. (5.53)
The second and likewise the third [syllables] of the seventh [letter] shall be so;
and the third of the second [letter], in sequence, in the third enclosure. (5.54)

The long vowel at the beginning of the last [syllable], ending with a bindu, is joined with the second letter of the second [group] and a bindu; that same final letter, together with a bindu, is conjoined with the eleventh bindu. (5.55)
And the eight seed-syllables have been declared in sequence for the cardinal and intermediate directions;
by means of these seed-syllables, beginning with the [consonant] classes, Indra and the other deities are traditionally remembered as being situated all around.
The weapon-mantras beginning with Vajra are [formed] with their second letters accompanied by the bindu; Viṣvaksena is proclaimed to end with the syllable *vaṃ* and to conclude with *namaḥ*. (5.57)
A wise man, proficient in the Pañcarātra, should fashion the seed-syllables (bījas) by combining the qualities and powers of all the deities. 5.58.
Speech is said to consist of syllables, and it is indeed imperishable;
therefore, even when a letter has been grasped, the cavity [of speech] is not called empty. (5.59)
In this [system], one should take the consonants separately from the vowels;
having taken each one that is grasped and joined it [with the vowel], one should extract the next. (5.60)
The supreme consecration by means of mantras is called sakalīkaraṇa;
therefore, having worshipped the Mātṛkā within the compartments, one should perform its extraction.
One should worship the extracted mantra within the squares that are without syllables.
Thus, the mantras are extracted with their syllables illuminated by the Praṇava.
They shall become possessed of vigor, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having gone to a solitary and pure place, bathed, sipped water for purification, and having subdued the senses... (5.63)
Having worshipped the deity together with the limbs and the retinue in the maṇḍala in due order,
one who observes the vow with an undistracted mind should recite [the mantra] twenty-six hundred thousand times.
One should offer a thousand oblations of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter;
then the mantra becomes perfected and it also becomes a granter of boons.
Whatever is desired in the seven worlds as a means for one’s own happiness, that becomes an object of enjoyment for him immediately through the practice of meditation. (5.66)
This divine power of mine is unfailing; it is never thwarted among gods, dānavas, or yakṣas—how much less so among the race of humans? (5.67)
A yakṣiṇī, a kinnarī, a celestial woman, or even a human woman shall become his servant within six, five, seven, or one month respectively. (5.68)
Having pronounced the name of the person to be accomplished, one should add "vaśam etu" at the end of the seed-syllable;
and at the very end, the seed-syllable should be joined, emitting sparks of blazing fire. (5.69)
One should accomplish [the goal] quickly and by force against an angry [opponent] through the application of the *pluta* (protracted) utterance;
likewise, in malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), one should employ the mantra ending with the syllable *phaṭ*.
"May this specific distinction also come to an end at the conclusion of the name;
having spoken thus at the end of the name, one should then contemplate the seed-syllable. (5.71)
In the rites of attraction and subjugation, this specific distinction is taught here:
one should clearly visualize the subject as being unconscious, agitated, and approaching.
One should meditate upon a water-pot, rich with gold and jewels, held by her and pouring forth incessantly before one's eyes an immeasurable stream of wealth. (5.73)
"This yoga for one desiring prosperity belongs indeed to Vaiśravaṇa; at the end of the name, let it bestow the name 'Vasu,' which shares its name. (5.74)
By practicing for a long time, one obtains a supreme maiden through the rite of subjugation;
at the end of her name, one should utter the words "may she be obtained. (5.75)
For expulsion, one should practice with "gacchatu"; for summoning, "āyātu"; for affection, "āvahatu prītim"; and for inciting hatred, "dveṣam ṛcchatu. (5.76)
Whatever a wise person desires to accomplish, if he recites this [mantra] once it has been mastered, that will be swiftly accomplished; however, it may fail due to a lack of faith. (5.77)
One should contemplate the seed-syllable of the heart as protracted (pluta), situated within one's own body blazing with light;
by means of this very [syllable], one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon one's own body.
"By whatever tone this [mantra] is joined and to whatever purpose it is applied, it accomplishes that quickly; it is not in vain—thus it is called 'The Shatterer' (Dāraṇā). (5.79)
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Viṣṇu-saṃhitā.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Now I shall explain in brief the ritual of bathing, sipping water, and so forth, by the proper performance of which the practitioner may attain accomplishment in this world. (6.1)
Having gone to a sacred ford, a river, or a pond, the wise man, provided with kuśa grass and other requisites,
should take earth free from all defects while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Having established the bathing place purified by the Astra-mantra, one should divide it into three parts;
having sprinkled those portions with the Astra and Hṛdaya mantras, one should protect them with the Kavaca-mantra.
Having circumambulated [the water] clockwise and paid homage, one should perform the cleansing bath with the eastern portion of that water and immerse oneself while reciting "tri-roma. (6.4)
With the second [mantra], he should offer it afterwards, having sipped water according to the prescribed rule;
with the third, he should scatter it in all directions for the pacification of obstacles.
Having meditated upon the Vaiṣṇava tīrtha, he should dive back [into the water] against the current;
then, having reached the tīrtha again, he should sip water according to the rule, remaining silent.
Having performed the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa) in sequence and likewise sprinkled [the body] with the root mantra and others,
one should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and carry out three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) in order.
Then, being well-composed, he performed the *adhamarṣaṇa* rite with water not drawn up from a vessel, using the root mantra along with its limbs, both individually and collectively.
Having performed the ablution which, as previously described in its entirety, removes all sins,
and having emerged from the water and put on white garments.
Having sipped water, performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), and sprinkled himself with the tips of kuśa grass in the same sequence as before,
he should sit in a clean place and perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having thus performed [the ritual] by means of the Supreme Reality (paratattva) and having offered salutation, one should perform the purification;
thereafter, the teacher should perform the rite of attendance (upasthāna) by means of the Supreme Reality.
Having meditated upon Viṣṇu, who consists of light and resides within the maṇḍala, the giver of water-offerings (arghya) stands firm while reciting the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having sat down in a clean place with the Gāyatrī and the Vaiṣṇavī mantras enclosed by the Praṇava at the beginning and the end, one should then commence the libation (tarpaṇa).
One should satiate Viṣṇu and the other deities, as well as the ṛṣis, humans, and the ancestors; having satisfied them all without exception, one should thereafter withdraw the sacred water (tīrtha).
Chanting the root mantra, he should proceed with his speech restrained, meditating on Hari;
having washed his feet up to the ankles and his hands up to the elbows once more. (6.15)
One should drink three times from the Brahma-tīrtha, wipe the mouth twice, and then,
having sprinkled the left hand and the feet, touch the limbs once again.
The three Vedas, the fathers, and the grandfathers attain satisfaction in due order through the three drinks; likewise do the great-grandfathers.
In the first sprinkling, Brahmā is satisfied; in the second, Dakṣa;
and there, the Atharva-veda and the Itihāsas also attain satisfaction when remembered. (6.18)
The moon and the sun shall attain satisfaction when their eyes are touched; Pavana placed his ring finger on his thumb and his index finger at his nostrils. (6.19)
The two Aśvins are satisfied by the little fingers at the ears; Śakra and the mountains by the thumbs at the arms; and Viṣṇu by the middle finger at the navel.
"Mahāviṣṇu is always Viṣṇu; [one should meditate on him] with all four [mantras] in the heart.
This is declared to be the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), especially for one who is initiated. (6.21)
Having reached the place of sacrifice, recollecting the deity while remaining silent,
he should inspect the house with the Astra-mantra, as well as the altar and the sacrificial mound.
Then, having circumambulated and paid homage with a concentrated mind,
the pure one, facing eastward, placed his upper garment over his left shoulder like a sacred thread.
Having performed the binding of the directions with the Nārasiṃha mantra, seated in the lotus posture,
and having uttered the Supreme Reality (paratattva), he formed the auspicious Brahmāñjali gesture.
One should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) conjoined with three concentrations (dhāraṇā).
In the center of the navel-circle is the syllable Yaṃ, smoky in color, whose nature is fierce wind.
One should dispel from the body that sin which withers all the limbs, and one should maintain within the heart the fire brought forth from the sun by means of the *tāra* (the syllable Om). 6.26.

With great concentration, having joined the vital breath (jīva) at the tip of the crest-lock with the seed-syllable, one should burn the body like wood with flames spreading sideways, upwards, and downwards.
Having gone through the aperture of the *suṣumnā*,
he then brought nectar from the moon situated above the sun, [to revive] his own body which had been reduced to ashes.
Having washed away the new body composed of earthly atoms,
one should fashion the body pertaining to Prajāpati as being situated within a water bubble.
Having united oneself here with the Omniscient One who is free from all taint,
one should place the pervasive [seed-syllable] at the base of the two hands purified by the weapon-mantra.
Beginning with the right thumb, one should place the seed-syllables in sequence;
they should be preceded and followed by the *tāra* (oṃ) on the left as well, extending to the palm in both cases.
Having assigned the limbs of those two, one should assign the pervasive [mantra] over all the limbs;
first having placed the first on the head, and the second on the forehead.
One should place the third [syllable] in the heart, the fourth in the region of the navel,
the fifth on the thighs, and the sixth situated on the feet.
This Sṛṣṭinyāsa (creation-assignment) should be performed while seated for the sake of attaining desired results;
while standing, one should perform the Sthitinyāsa (stability-assignment), starting from the navel up to the heart.
The placement for lying down is the "withdrawal" (saṃhṛti), starting from the feet and proceeding in reverse order;
the placement for the householder is "stability" (sthiti), while that of the student is called "creation" (sṛṣṭi).
For one desiring liberation, the *saṃhṛtinyāsa* is thus prescribed; in this way, the ritual of placement (*nyāsa*) is said to be threefold.
Having performed the ritual of placement in this manner with the six-syllable mantra preceded and followed by the *tāra*, || 6.36 ||
One should assign the limbs, such as the heart and others, to their respective locations;
then, having recited the mantra and pierced [the object] with the weapon-mantra (astra), one should discard the fragment.
Having cast [the offerings] with the Flower Weapon (puṣpāstra),
one should prepare the ritual requisites in water that has been purified by the Weapon [mantra], placed in a vessel, and mixed with perfumes and flowers.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra eight times, one should consecrate it with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Then, one should perform a sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) on all sides using the weapon-mantra (astramantra).
Then the wise one, ending with the syllable *phaṭ*, should prepare the seat;
the learned one should worship it in the mandala, on the sacrificial mound, in the image, or within the heart. (6.40)

Having attained perfection through worship on a sacrificial mound and other such sites, one should worship with the mind within the heart-lotus the seat consisting of Ananta, whose feet are dharma, adharma, and the rest. (6.41)

Having worshipped, in due order, with perfumes and flowers, the vast sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) which is composed of the three qualities (triguṇa), and whose surface is dark and white through Māyā and Vidyā; 6.42.
Above that, being composed, he should likewise [visualize] a lotus with the syllable Om (praṇava);
then, by means of its parts, the triad of spheres consisting of the sun, moon, and fire.
Having visualized, one above the other, the petals, filaments, and pericarp, [the six stages] are Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Yogā in their proper order. (6.44)
Prahvī, Satyā, and Īśā—these eight Śaktis are on the filaments;
Anugrahā is in the center; they should be worshipped at the end for the accomplishment of all goals.
Having thus meditated upon Viṣṇu seated on the yoga-pīṭha within his own heart,
the vigilant practitioner [should place] water mixed with fragrance and flowers in a cleansed metallic vessel.
With the syllable *praṇava*, one should remember Viṣṇu situated above the unmanifest;
then, having meditated upon the form of Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Lord who consists of every splendor.

Having meditated upon [the deity] seated upon the pericarp and having restrained [the breath], one who has performed the ritual integration (sakalīkṛta) should worship Acyuta, along with his limbs, with devotion and without distraction, using the arghya and other offerings. 6.48.
Having placed the heart with the eastern [syllable], likewise the head with the southern;
the crest with the western, and the armor with the northern.
In the [four] openings beginning with the southeast (āgneya), one should worship the supreme weapon;
having assigned Vāsudeva and the others to the cardinal directions, and the Śaktis to the intermediate corners.
Outside of that, one should place the conch, discus, lotus, and mace in the cardinal directions;
then, in the corners, one should set down the Śārṅga bow, shield, sword, and arrow.
One should install Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna in their respective directions in due order. (6.52)
One should arrange outside of them their weapons: the vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, the banner, as well as the mace and the trident. (6.53)
Vainateya is in front, outside the third enclosure;
likewise, Viṣvaksena is in the northeast, outside the second enclosure.
The wise man should also, with devotion, prepare a lotus seat for each of these [deities] individually and offer it to the God according to their names. (6.55)
Water for the feet, water for sipping, as well as bathing water, ointment, clothing, ornaments, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
All of that should be given in due order with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī;
having given [the offerings] up to the ornaments to the deity, one should arrange the bathing and other items upon the limbs.
Then, with the Gāyatrī mantra, he offered a flower to the God and to the others as well,
using both the root-mantra individually and together with all of them combined.
This sacrifice is to be understood as belonging to Him; always other [deities] are to be honored by their own names.
Having finally pervaded them with the Supreme Reality (paratattva), one should worship that Eternal One.
Having offered incense, a lamp, and an oblation to him according to the prescribed rite,
one should likewise prepare an oblation for the others as far as possible.
And one should conceive [the deity] in the fire, radiant and seated upon the yoga-pīṭha together with its limbs,
performing whatever is required such as the strewing of grass, the sprinkling of water, and the preparation of the purifiers.
Having performed all that with the *praṇava* alone, one should then offer oblations of clarified butter;
for the limbs and the forms, one-tenth of the total, and for the others, one by one in sequence.
One should offer the bali-oblation in the eight directions with the mantra "namaḥ pariṣadebhyaśca.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), having performed the sakalīkaraṇa, and having recited the mantra, praised, and prostrated, [one should proceed].
Having offered the *arghya* and said, "Forgive me," one should withdraw [the deity] and join [him] within the heart;
one should meditate upon the Lord consisting of light, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Vāsudeva has four arms, wears yellow garments, possesses noble limbs, is adorned with all ornaments, and resembles pure crystal.
One should likewise meditate upon Saṅkarṣaṇa, who holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and possesses a radiance equal to molten gold.
One should likewise meditate upon Pradyumna, who resembles the emerald-colored durvā grass,
and likewise upon Aniruddha, who has the appearance of a dark blue cloud.
One should contemplate Śrī, who resembles a tranquil crystal and possesses the luster of lotus pollen;
likewise, one should contemplate Sarasvatī in that same form, and Rati as dark-complexioned.
Likewise, he saw a white conch, a discus with a radiance like fire,
a mace the color of turmeric, and a lotus with the luster of gold.
One should meditate upon the mace, endowed with feminine characteristics and capable of destroying all things,
and upon the sword, which resembles the sky and has the form of a discus.
The *śārṅga* is yellow and similar to that [the *cakra*], with its lower part like a mace (*gadā*);
the arrow is shaped like a bow, and the shield resembles a sword. (6.71)
A fierce wheel with many spokes, a hub, a wide rim, and a felly—licking, difficult to behold, with its mouth of whirling sparks of fire. (6.72)
He may have four arms or two, possessing fangs and tawny hair;
likewise, he may have a protruding belly, or a conch-like neck, with short and curly hair.
Indra is dark-blue, Yama is yellow, and Varuṇa is indeed dark-blue;
Soma has the pure luster of a conch shell, while Vahni is proclaimed to be crimson.
Sadaṃṣṭra and Nirṛti are dark blue, Vāyu is praised as smoke-colored, and Īśāna should be red; thus one should meditate upon these in sequence. (6.75)
The vajra should be made in the form of Indra, or as described in various treatises;
in this same manner, one should fashion the weapons of the guardians of the directions and others as well.
Agnivarma, Caturbāhu, Tārkṣya, and Lūnāgranāsika—these of great wings and great strength should be meditated upon as if devouring with their very gaze. 6.77.
Viṣvaksena, cloud-colored, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
five-headed and four-armed, was Ananta behind Hari.
The other attendants of his are to be known from other scriptures;
the devoted man who worships Viṣṇu according to this rite [attains success]. (6.79)
For that yogin, all objects of desire are already within his grasp, both in this world and the next.
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the seventh chapter.

Now I shall explain in brief the supreme characteristics of the mudrās, those mudrās which are employed in the rites of ritual placement (nyāsa) and so forth, and which have been well-guarded in secrecy. 7.1.
The first mudrā is the añjali; it quickly propitiates the gods. The vandanī is placed at the heart and slightly inclined toward the right. (7.2)
The left hand is a fist with the thumb pointing upward, while the right hand binds the thumb;
the thumb of that left hand remains positioned facing upward. (7.3)
Three common mudrās of the deities are proclaimed here:
seated in the lotus posture, one should form the añjali gesture at the crown of the head. (7.4)
The mudrā known as Brahmāñjali brings about the presence of the gods; by binding it, the deities are constantly pleased. (7.5)
Therefore, one should display this mudrā to all the gods: having brought the two hands together with palms facing each other, slightly curling the fingers. (7.6)
One should draw [the lines] within with the two thumbs; this is known as the *āvāhinī* mudrā.
Having bent the fingers of both hands, one should move the two thumbs upward.
The *sānnidhya-mudrā* is to be known as that which is to be placed as if already installed;
one should form two fists with the thumbs tucked inside for the *nirodhinī*.
Having joined the two hands together, one should press the two thumbs in the middle;
extending all the fingers, this is the mudrā of Parameṣṭhin.
One should sequentially join the other fingers one by one;
in this very order, beginning with the male [fingers], one should fashion all the mudrās.
The sin committed over seven lifetimes, as well as the five great transgressions, are undoubtedly destroyed through the realization of the five mudrās. (7.11)
Having formed a fist with the left hand and raised the thumb, one should place it against the heart while grasping it with the other fist. (7.12)
This is declared to be the Yonimudrā, belonging to Viṣṇu, which bestows both enjoyment and liberation;
having first assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), one should display it before the God of gods.
Upon seeing her thus revealed, the gods immediately prostrate themselves;
and the yakṣas, vidyādharas, and others wander about, bewildered by fear.
Then, having turned the left hand upward and the right hand upward as well,
one should rotate them while holding them together, and subsequently interlace the fingers in sequence.
This is declared to be the Koṭimudrā, beloved of the God of gods:
having placed the extended thumb between the ring finger and the middle finger. (7.16)
This mudrā is prescribed for the right hand at the heart:
having formed a fist, one should strike the index finger with the tip of the thumb. (7.17)
One should place it at the edge of the forehead; this is known as the mudrā on the head. Having formed a firm fist, one should raise the thumb upward. (7.18)
