One should place it at the region of the crest; this is proclaimed as the Śikhā-mudrā.
Having inserted the two thumbs within and having encircled [the fingers] all around, || 7.19 ||
One should bring together the two index fingers; this mudrā is known as the armor (kavaca).
Having turned the forehands over and bound them like a nārāca-fist, [this is the arrow mudrā]. 7.20.
One should release [the breath] while stretching it sideways; this is declared to be the mudrā of the weapon (astramudrā).
Having bound the śikhāmudrā facing downwards, one should place it between the eyebrows.
This is declared to be the Netra-mudrā; these six are the mudrās of the limbs.
By means of these, practitioners must always perform self-protection.
Having placed the two thumbs upright and together, and having joined the hands with one another, this is the Yoga-sampuṭa mudrā; it is employed everywhere during meditation.
Having likewise rendered it flawless, one should place it at the crown of the head facing downwards; this supreme purifying mudrā is to be employed during the consecration.
The two hands, level with the wrists, with the fingers extended upward and the thumbs drawn inside, are known as the lotus posture (padmamudrāsana). (7.25)
Holding the hands level with the wrists and whirling them crosswise like a wheel, one should perform in succession the mudrā of the wheel, which brings great prosperity. (7.26)
Having formed a fist with both hands and bent both thumbs, joining them and whirling [them], the two released [mudrās] called *gadā* destroy obstacles. (7.27)
Having grasped the right thumb within the fist held in the left hand,
one should join the thumb and forefinger, extending them equally.
One should bind three others on the right, with the fist held upward;
this is designated as the Śaṅkhamudrā, supreme for the placement of ritual substances.
The grip on the bow, the grip on the arrow, the drawing of the sword from its scabbard, the seal of the shield, and the circle [of the sword-blade]. (7.30)
Having joined both little fingers and likewise both index fingers, with both hands turned over, the two thumbs are placed together below. (7.31)
Joining the middle and ring fingers, one should move them like a pair of wings;
this is the bound Garuḍa mudrā, which brings strength when used for mounting vehicles and the like.

Having formed the hand with the fingers pointing upward and viralized, one should display it with an outstretched palm; this is to be known as the mudrā of Ananta, employed at the beginning of his reclining and other rites. 7.33.

Having placed both hands palms upward with the fingertips joined and extended, one should always perform the mudrā of prayer during the rites for invoking the presence [of the deity] and other such occasions. (7.34)
The Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha mudrās are formed by touching the chest with the fingers extending toward both sides. First, one should perform the Ūrdhva mudrā, and then turn it upward again. (7.35)
One should release [the mudrās] in the four forms in sequence, beginning with the left little finger;
having slowly joined the fingers, their tips slightly curved. (7.36)
The wise one, having joined the two index fingers on the backs of the middle fingers, should draw within with the two thumbs that which is known as the womb of the Śaktis. (7.37)
Grasping with the left hand the hand extended crosswise, one should move it together;
this is proclaimed as the Dhvaja-mudrā.
When the thumb is extended from between the middle and ring fingers while the middle finger is bent,
this mudrā, formed with the right hand in a fist, is known as the Vaināyakī.
The fist with the thumb pointing upward is known as the liṅga-mudrā in the case of Śiva.
One should threaten the world with the left index finger held near the tip of the nose. (7.40)
That mudrā of Viṣvaksena is prescribed for the restoration of dilapidated temples and similar rites;
for those seeking liberation, the mental visualization of forms is known as mudrā.
For others, however, the wise recommend the application [of mudrās] with both hands;
one should not form a mudrā while looking at another, nor should one bind one without a specific purpose. (7.42)
For this is indeed a secret within the tantras; therefore, one should apply it in solitude. It brings joy to the gods and puts the rākṣasas to flight. (7.43)
Thus, the tantric adepts know the nature of all mudrās as being "seals" (mudrātva).
A wise person should bind the mudrā at the edge of the cloth and should not speak of it.
From speaking of them, there arises a loss [of their power]; therefore, they must always be kept secret by the wise.
O Brahmin! Because of their infinity, it is not possible to describe all the mudrās. (7.45)
And because of the great number of deities, I have set forth this enumeration of mudrās;
these mudrās, such as salutation and prayer, belong to all the inhabitants of heaven.
Even for those who are ignorant, one should arrange these [mudrās] during the worship of Acyuta;
in the absence of all mudrās, one may use the añjali gesture at the heart or on the head.
The common mudrā should be known for all the inhabitants of heaven;
the mantra *praṇava* (Oṃ) should be employed, and in this way, success will be attained.
Having first performed the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa), the binding of the mudrās will be auspicious;
otherwise, all [the rites] will become fruitless, without a doubt. (7.49)
Furthermore, when employed for the purpose of seeing others in vain, they are likewise fruitless;
the deities become angry with him and swiftly take away his spiritual success.
He who displays the secret assembly of mudrās at the proper time achieves all his desires, and the deities become pleased with him. (7.51)
These mudrās are proclaimed to be of four kinds: those called general, those called specific, those called limb-related, and likewise those called retinue-related. (7.52)
The wise one should press the middle and ring fingers with the two thumbs;
the little and index fingers should be joined, and thus one should display the Śrīvatsa.
The ring finger is joined to the back of the right little finger;
then, having grasped the ring finger with the little finger and likewise the ring finger with the forefinger— (7.54)
Having grasped the ring finger and the middle finger, raise the thumb;
the index finger of the left hand should be joined to that thumb. (7.55)
Having placed the middle fingers in the middle and the thumbs at the wrists,
this is the Kaustubha mudrā, which should be displayed by practitioners.
Raising both hands before one's face, one should release them into the middle of the air;
joining the index fingers and thumbs together, one should display the garland mudrā.
Thus, these four kinds of mudrās should always be guarded with effort;
they should be employed at the proper time by practitioners who desire accomplishment. 7.58.
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Now I shall describe, in brief, the supreme consecration by fire (agnisaṃskāra):
one should prepare a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the east or the north, or, if that is impossible, a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila).
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be two cubits or one cubit in size, square in shape, and provided with three,
two, or even just a single girdle (mekhalā).
The depth of the pit for a single vessel should be half its measurement, and elsewhere it should be equal to that;
the height of the girdle (mekhalā) should be twelve, eight, or four finger-breadths.
In this context, the girdles are recorded as being of three types—sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa;
they are all four finger-breadths in width and one cubit in length.

It should be known that the dimensions double at each successive stage; the base (yoni) should be at the rear, measuring fourteen finger-breadths (aṅgula), while its stalk (nāla) is four finger-breadths.
It should be eight finger-breadths in circumference and six finger-breadths in width;
its shape should be like an elephant's lip or like the tip of a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha).
The vulva with the elephant's lip at its tip belongs to Prajāpati, while the other belongs to Viṣṇu;
the power (śakti) residing in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is that of Viṣṇu, which is primordial nature (prakṛti) consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa). 8.7.
That is the source of all beings and especially of all accomplishments;
its head is declared to be in the east, and its arms extend toward the south and the north.
The belly is said to be the *kuṇḍa*, and the womb and the two feet are at the rear.
There are forty-nine squares in the *kuṇḍa* when divided into seven parts.
One should arrange the letters from the beginning to the end in sequence within those sections;
having first designated the Praṇava, one should place the constituent parts upon the three girdles.
One should meditate upon the pervasive Puruṣa as sound (nāda) and the pervasive Mātṛkā;
and having visualized the Visarga, which consists of the drops of Agni and Soma, in the center of the Yoni.
This womb, however, is of the nature of a fetus; she is born from it as the mother.
One should worship her, who abides as a portion of the ancestors, mortals, and gods, by circumambulating her clockwise. (8.12)
The letter *ha* is the final one in the middle cell; likewise, Viṣṇu is the individual soul (*jīvātman*). This Prakṛti, whose belly has the shape of a pit, is the one who possesses the embryo.
Thus it should be understood by the practitioner who desires the supreme accomplishment:
this Gāyatrī, in the form of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), exists in twenty-four ways.
Viṣṇu, whose essence is Tārā, is proclaimed here as the presiding deity. One should know that the region between the navel and the private parts is the seat of fire for embodied beings. 8.15.
In that very place the embryo is placed, and there the fire-oblation is performed for the sake of success;
the sacrificial pit is recorded as being twenty-four finger-breadths in measure, according to the number of the Gāyatrī.
The twenty-four principles (tattvas) are two finger-breadths each across the two hands;
there are fifteen vowels below, and the womb (yoni) is fifteen finger-breadths [in height].
The sixteenth [vowel], accompanied by the visarga, is situated here at the end of the navel;
that indeed is the supreme Śakti of Viṣṇu, which carries the highest nectar.
Divine and consisting of Agni and Soma, she is that through which all that is to be known is composed;
she effects withdrawal by means of the form of Agni and manifestation by means of the form of Soma.
Abiding within the pair of drops, she eternally acts by my will;
having pierced through the world of Brahmā, she remains stationed there and has gone to my abode via the crown of the head.
The path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna) is on the left, and the path of the gods (devayāna) is on the right;
in the middle is the path of Brahman for liberation—thus it has been described. 8.21.
In the form of fire she ascends upwards; in the form of the moon she descends downwards.
Having abandoned the left and right [channels], she stands pervading the three worlds. (8.22)
The two channels, Iḍā and Piṅgalā, are on the left and right sides;
the Suṣumṇā channel, which extends upwards, is remembered as the path to liberation. 8.23.
Having concentrated the mind there, free from both dharma and adharma, one is liberated from all diseases and undoubtedly attains dissolution [into the Absolute]. (8.24)
In this way, the body of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be known as consisting of the Mātṛkās;
it is called a "pit" (kuṇḍa) because the entire universe dissolves within it through that universal dissolution.
Therefore, one should offer oblations here in this sacrificial pit according to the path prescribed by the rules;
just as a farmer obtains fruit from a well-prepared field. || 8.26 ||
And likewise, the fire-god should be known as one who, when consecrated, bestows fruits upon men;
just as a consecration must be performed for the clarified butter, so too must it be performed for the fire. 8.27.
Therefore, the wise should offer oblations into a consecrated fire, not into one that is unconsecrated;
for in this matter, the consecration belongs either to the disciple, the fire, or the clarified butter.
Therefore, in reality, fire is in every way desired for sacrifices;
it may be produced by friction, born from a jewel, or taken from the house of one learned in the Vedas.
Having brought the fire with a shallow bowl, one should purify it with the Astra-mantra;
then, by means of the Saṃhāra-mudrā, one should unite its vital essence (jīva) with one's own self.
First, he should contemplate his bed as being joined with merit and demerit and the like,
covered with excellent coverlets, and perfumed with the fragrance of incense.
One should meditate upon Lakṣmī, who is strewn with fragrant flowers, adorned with various substances, embodied as Speech, and graced with the bloom of fresh youth. (8.32)
One should always contemplate him as gentle, with a perpetually smiling face, desiring her who has bathed after her menses and holding a full-blown lotus. (8.33)
Having thus meditated upon both [deities] in this form— the one seeking pleasure with his gaze fixed intently on the lotus-face of the Goddess— one should worship them with perfumes and flowers.
One should contemplate the seed-syllable of Agni, white and situated in the center of the deity;
it has entered the womb and is united with the blood. (8.35)
After the rite of conception has been performed, one should dismiss the deity;
then, one should contemplate the Goddess as having become the sacrificial pit and that Fire as having become the deity. (8.36)

Having offered clarified butter eight times each with the *hṛdaya* and other [mantras], one should perform in sequence the rites of *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, naming (*nāma*), and the first feeding (*āśana*).
With the mantra ending in *vaiṣaṭ* and having a protracted (*pluta*) final syllable, according to the prescribed rule,
one should offer a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) separately and worship with perfumes and flowers.
The *praṇava* is to be known as the *sruva* ladle and the *mātṛkā* as the *sruc* ladle; these two are to be understood by the wise as being the Puruṣa and Prakṛti. (8.39)
One should make the *sruva* spoon one *ratni* in length and its mouth circular with a diameter of two *aṅgulas*;
it should be like a cow’s hoofprint sunk slightly into soft mud. (8.40)
The width of the knot immediately following the rounded section shall be one finger-breadth;
the staff, moreover, should be circular in shape and free from knots, curves, and the like. (8.41)
The tube should be four finger-breadths long, with its tip gradually tapered toward the bottom;
it should be one that has fallen of its own accord, or is dried, burnt, or broken by an elephant. (8.42)
One produced in a defiled place, crooked, cracked, hollow, scarred, infested with worms, grown from another tree, or facing in another direction—[such a tooth is unfit]. (8.43)
A *sruva* ladle is for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), whereas a *sruc* ladle is for that purpose; therefore, one should not employ them [for peaceful rites].
One made from a milk-tree is for pacification (*śānti*), while one made of *khadira* wood grants all desires. (8.44)
The ladle of Brahmā, which bestows spiritual luster, should always be of the nature of Brahmā;
the three Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, and the deities, beginning with Brahmā, [are likewise to be contemplated]. (8.45)
One should conceive of the fires beginning with Bhūḥ, the stages, the pressings, and the syllables,
according to the sequence of the parts of the Praṇava, within the staff, the knots, and the circles.

One should have a sacrificial ladle made measuring one cubit in length, with a width of seven, six, or five finger-breadths; it should be rounded at the middle and hollowed out by one-third [of its width].
One should clear away an equal portion of it horizontally and upwards, and half of that on the outside;
one-fourth of a finger-breadth at the remaining half, and likewise half of that at the very end.
One should cause a beautiful girdle for the pit to be made with half of the remaining [material];
the neck should be one and a half digits in length and one-third of that in width.
The opening should be four finger-breadths in width and likewise five finger-breadths in length;
it should be made auspicious, shaped like the face of a swan.
In the middle of that [tube], there should be a channel or a streamlet entering a circular pit;
one should fashion a small opening at its neck. (8.51)

The *dhārā* should be at its lower part and at the base of the staff (*daṇḍa*) according to the proper method; the remainder of the staff should be well-rounded, gradually tapering toward the tip. (8.52)
The sixteen vowels are to be placed inside the hole in clockwise order;
the other [consonants] are on the staff, while the semi-vowels (antaḥstha) are from the corners, and the remaining [sibilants and aspirate] go to the sides and the tip of the hole.
In this case, it should be offered full by her, protected within the cavity formed by the *sruva* ladle;
the oblation may be performed with the *sruva* alone or together with that [other vessel].
Whether with the *sruc* or the *sruva*, [the deity] is the grantor; for even alone, he bestows success.
This *sruva* is for the purpose of creation; therefore, one should perform the oblation while seated with it. 8.55.
For the sake of stability, one should cause the *sruk* ladle, when full, to be offered while standing;
the *juhū* ladle, belonging to Brahmā, should be twenty-four finger-breadths long. (8.56)
One should visualize the limbs beginning with the heart and ending with the eyes upon the tip of the staff, the tip of the face, the interior of the cheeks, and the path of the clarified butter.
One should always offer as an oblation that which has been cooked upon her, who is spread out with the *tāra* [syllable].
Both the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are said to be the very nature of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths. (8.58)
The two [nostrils] should not be pressed together; they know that to be the seat of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The smoke is to be known as the nose, and the ears and eyes are on the two sides. (8.59)
This region from the forehead to the mouth, extending front to back, is the station of fire;
having performed the ritual tracing and other rites with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should worship the consecrated fire while wearing the sacred thread.
Having meditated on the lotus as before, one should contemplate all the principles (tattvas) in their proper sequence;
in the center, one should meditate on Janārdana, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
One should satisfy him with a thousand oblations or with a hundred;
there, one should offer ten full oblations with the root mantra.
One should satisfy the others with a tenth part [of the offering], or indeed with cooked rice alone;
for this is the rule that must be observed by initiated twice-born men in their daily rites.
The abode of fire should always be purified by the conceptualizations of drying, burning, flooding with nectar, and hardening, each produced from its respective seed-syllable. 8.64.
That which is strewn with darbha grass, that which is placed as the praṇītā water,
and that which is appointed here as the brahmā— all this is for the pacification of obstacles.
When the fire is oily, turning to the right, well-kindled, smokeless,
and licking [the offerings], one should offer oblations for the successful accomplishment of the rite.
Fire that is of little brilliance, dry, white, or black; that which is devoid of fuel, emits sparks, or has a foul odor is not commended. (8.67)
Kālī, Karālī, and Manojavā, Lohitā, Ardhadhūmrā, Jvālā, and Sphuliṅginī—[these are distinguished] by their differences in form and other qualities. (8.68)
These seven tongues of the consumer of oblations are to be known as Viśvarūpā; his mouth is filled by them, and it is rent asunder with its seven tongues. (8.69)
One who desires to offer oblations should always meditate upon [the fire] as blazing and licking [the offering];
he should offer half a karṣa of clarified butter and a quantity of food equal to half a mouthful.
He offered oblations of curd, milk, and honey, each measuring a śukti; likewise, he offered a handful of barley, rice, and śāli grain, as well as a handful of flattened rice (pṛthuka).
A mere handful of parched grain, fruits according to one's own capacity, edible foods in the measure of an *abhayā* fruit, and three pieces of root—these are the portions. (8.72)
Three tips of dūrvā grass, one karṣa measure of barley meal,
and five each of sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and mung beans.
Each flower and likewise each fuel-stick should be offered individually;
having filled the large ladle with clarified butter using the dipping-spoon, [the offering is made]. (8.74)
The *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) should always be offered with an unbroken stream [of ghee];
likewise, a bundle of fuel-sticks (*samit*) known as the *idhma*, measuring one cubit (*aratni*) in length, should be soaked in clarified butter.
One should always offer oblations from a vessel made of *pālāśa* wood simultaneously and without wavering.
Having spread a base of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, one should place two portions of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) into the *juhū* ladle. (8.76)
That which is cooked and sprinkled with clarified butter is offered with a final oblation from the *sruva* ladle;
likewise, each individual *piṇḍa* is again sprinkled twice.
At the conclusion of the principal oblations, the Sviṣṭakṛt offering should be made;
all other [offerings] should be smeared with ghee using the right hand. (8.78)
One should always offer liquid substances such as curd and milk using the *devatīrtha*—the part of the ring finger located at its base—and with the *sruva* ladle itself. (8.79)
Everything must be offered according to the prescribed rite; otherwise, one incurs fault.
First, one should prepare the sacrificial oblation (caru) with three times-washed, pure śāli rice.

Having placed it on the fire by means of a mechanical device, he should cook it with the wind from a fan; having consecrated the clarified butter according to the rule and having wiped the sacrificial ladle with *darbha* grass. (8.81)
Having placed the enclosing sticks and sprinkled water around the fire, one should worship the fire;
once the fuel-sticks, the pouring of clarified butter, and the portions of ghee have been offered, one should invoke the deity.
Furthermore, other cooked offerings, such as the fuel-sticks and so forth, must be offered in their proper sequence;
for one who desires success, this procedure must be performed according to the rules of the *āghāra* oblation. (8.83)

Having established the fire, strewn it around, consecrated it, and worshipped it in due order, one should offer oblations with all the ritual substances; this is the procedure for the *āpūrvika* sacrifice.

Then, having completed the remainder of the fire-oblation (homa) and having ritually dismissed the deity according to the rules, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's capacity; in this way, the supernatural powers (siddhis) are accomplished.
This fire-rite has been described by me in general;
however, its specific performance in each particular case will be explained in those very places.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, on the fire-ritual, in the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Now I shall describe in brief the mandala that fulfills all desires, knowing which the sages have rightly attained supreme perfection from this [path]. 9.1
First, one should examine a sacrificial ground that is free from all defects, carefully cleared of stakes, level, and sloping toward the northeast. (9.2)
Having purified it according to the rule, one should have a pavilion constructed there—either square with four doors, or else with a single door. (9.3)
It was provided with archways and banners, adorned with canopies and the like,
and featured the eight auspicious signs, including auspicious sprouts, a mirror, parched grain, and a water-pot.

Having consecrated the sacrificial ground associated with the fire-altar, which possesses a mirror-like surface and a level altar, by means of sweeping, smearing, cow-products, perfumes, unbroken grains, and so forth; 9.5.
Then one should cast the lines according to the division of the directions;
the line extending from east to west has its midpoint at the center with loops on both sides.
Having made marks with those two [lines], one should mark two fish-shapes in the south and north;
then, having stretched a string between them, one should mark the directions according to the measurement.
Then, one should mark the corner-fish figures with pairs of numbers;
having struck the arm-threads, one should perfect the square.
Having divided it equally into sixteen parts and stretched the lines,
one should draw there a beautiful, auspicious, and perfectly square maṇḍala.
The white lotus with its pedestal has four doors and is adorned with five colors;
it consists of four groups of nine petals, while the pedestal outside is formed by a single row.
One should fashion the two streets as well as the gates and the location for the lotus by dividing [the area] into four parts,
each reduced by one-twelfth of that half.

One should visualize the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth within the pericarp and other parts, [placing them] in sequence upon the pericarp, the filaments, the joints, the petals, and their tips. 9.12.
Having struck the diagonal threads, one should fashion an eight-petaled [lotus] such that,
when the junction-threads have been cast, [the petals are formed] by means of the space between the joints of the petals.
One should fashion the petals and their tips according to the measurement, using both the side-measurement and the central one;
on the pedestal, one should arrange the legs and the body-parts with three and four [units] respectively.
One should sweep inside and outside; at each of the four gates, one should clear three [spaces] for the sake of beauty and one [space] for the sake of ornamentation, or otherwise.
The courtyard has six corners with canopies of creepers and leaves, and the pathway is radiant;
the auspicious [pavilion] measures one cubit, two cubits, or four cubits.
Beyond that, however, the lotus-diagram (cakrābja) is desired to extend up to eight cubits;
the altar (vedi) should be twelve aratnis or ten or eight aratnis.
One should fashion the axle from the twelfth part of that [diameter], and the nave (nābhi) should be of the same size;
the area for the spokes outside should be double that.
One should likewise designate the fields for the navel, the rim, and the path in succession;
having divided the axle-hole into three parts, one should arrange the pericarp and the rest in their proper order.
One should rotate the petals situated at the navel and arrange the tips;
that lotus-wheel has three navels, twelve spokes, and auspicious pathways.

One should imagine the intermediate directions as being situated upon the spokes, and the primary directions as having the spaces between the spokes as their domain; one should conceive the measurement of both to be exactly equal everywhere.
Having divided the hub into twelve parts, the threads extending upwards [are arranged];
the spokes at the base and the tip are thick, while they are circular in form in the middle.
The ant-bellies (pipīlikodara) should be made, and the barley-bellies (yavodara) in reverse;
having divided the area of the rim into two parts, the widths should be arranged from bottom to top.
It should be made twenty-fourfold, with its spokes and joints being distinct; here, one should fashion the outer enclosure according to the measurement of the rim.
There, the stations for the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) should be arranged in due order;
one should fashion all of them as quadrangular and measuring one tāla in height. 9.25.
The outer gate and so forth should be made square as previously described;
having thus drawn the mandala, one should fill it with colored powders in the proper sequence.
In this case, [the petals] are white, red, black, yellow, and dark green;
in all instances, the pericarp is yellow and the other lotus petals are white. 9.27.
One should fashion the filaments as being yellow in sequence, with broad and reddish centers, and bright, clear drops at their tips. 9.28.
The intervals between the petals are dark blue; the bases outside the sky are red.
Dharma and the others are white, while Adharma and the others are recorded as being dark blue.
One should arrange the doors in all four directions as white; those facing north and so forth are for the Brahmins and the other castes respectively, in due order.
The primary beauty is red, while the secondary ornamentation is yellow; the corner is blue.
In the Bhadraka [mandala], one should arrange everything according to what is beautiful, using all colors.
Likewise, one should likewise draw a lotus within the wheel-lotus; its three naves should be white, red, and black, while all the spokes are yellow and the junctions are white.
The stripes should be white and black, with yellow junctions due to their reversal;
the svastikas of the guardians of the directions, however, should be made of various colors. (9.33)
Outside of that, there are lines of yellow, clear, pale-red, dark-blue, and black;
in the Bhadraka [mandala], three lines of white, red, and black are prescribed in sequence. 9.34.

Whatever [features] such as the doors exist in the Bhadraka [mandala], they should likewise be diligently fashioned on the outside of the lotus-wheel by the most excellent preceptors during the initiation.
Whatever form is to be depicted according to rule in the maṇḍala,
that very color of powder is used here for its respective filling.
One should prepare these powders from gems, medicinal herbs, metals, fragrances, seeds, minerals, and leaves of trees used for sacrificial rites. (9.37)
For liberation, the ritual placement (nyāsa) should be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) using the deity-tīrtha;
for the sake of prosperity and the fulfillment of all desires, it should be performed with the fingers.

Many defects arise from knots, curves, thinness, thickness, depressions, elevations, and their various combinations; likewise, from fissures. A break in the lines is not desirable in any respect. (9.39)

If, due to negligence on the part of the disciples during the drawing of the mandala, there should be knots or other defects, the teacher, being untiring and skilled in the ritual procedure, [should rectify them]. (9.40)
One should employ the pericarp, filaments, and other parts gracefully,
by means of a single reflection alone, and not through repeated turnings.
One should make the pericarp elevated and draw petal-lines on all sides;
these lines, measured by the little finger, the middle finger, and the thumb, should be raised in three ways.
In the superior, middle, and inferior [levels], the destruction of that [impurity] should be inferred according to the sequence starting from the lotus and so forth;
in their respective centers, the placement of the *rajas* (dust) should be elevated by the measure of each corresponding foot.
Having avoided the knots and other such obstacles through diligent effort, the supreme teacher should gradually scatter lines of equal measure everywhere. 9.44.
This maṇḍala, drawn upon a wall or a cloth according to the rules of measurement, should be worshipped constantly in the home for the pacification of minor spirits and other such beings. (9.45)
But at the proper time, one should perceive this for oneself; it is not something accessible to ordinary people.
By the mere contemplation of it, all evil is shattered. (9.46)
Vetālas and Brahmarākṣasas do not remain in his presence;
mounted upon this discus is Viṣṇu, the Lord of the entire world. (9.47)

He should always be worshipped with effort by devotees for the sake of accomplishing all goals; even when such [a large image] is unavailable, worship and other rites may be performed using a measure of two cubits or more.
The wise man should fashion the lotus within the wheel, provided it is not too small when there is ample space;
even if there is no such space, he should not omit the positions ending at the rim.
The outer enclosure, however, may be conceived as small as desired; its colors are white, red, yellow, and variegated, corresponding to the deities of pacification and the other rites. (9.50)
These are to be applied respectively to the ages (yugas), the Vedas, and the social classes (varṇas);
however, the fifth form is dark-complexioned (śyāma) and corresponds to the intermediate age (yugāntara).
The universe consists of the five colors; through the differentiation of the subtle elements (tanmātras) and the distinction between objects and sense organs, it exists in fivefold form. (9.52)
That which is to be known in the form of sound is pervaded by the primordial syllable;
transcending the conceptualization of letters and so forth, that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu. 9.53
The supreme power, however, is all-pervading, formless, and facing in every direction;
the Lord, who is never separate from her, should always be beheld by practitioners. 9.54.
She is proclaimed by practitioners as being without armor (avarman) and yet possessing all colors;
she is that supreme Māyā, the primordial nature (prakṛti), whose essence consists of the qualities (guṇas). 9.55
That single, supreme, subtle [power] becomes threefold through the differentiation of the qualities (guṇas);
from that differentiation arises the distinction among the gods, consisting of Brahmā, Upendra, and Hara.
That [power] subsequently becomes fivefold, just as I have previously stated;
for it is seen in scripture that the Lord conforms to those divisions. (9.57)
The sages have conceived of innumerable divisions arising from its qualities;
one should know the person as the mandala, and the lotus as his heart. (9.58)
The middle part situated between the arms is the lotus stalk at the root of the navel;
the two feet are to be known as the southern and northern gates at the rear. 9.59.
The lotus stalk has nine openings and is the locus of the kalās beginning with Vimalā;
its root is the subtle Janārdana in the form of a seed.
One should know the lotus-root as the support of everything, established in its own majesty, from which the vowels beginning with 'a' arose. (9.61)

The Maruts are its thorns; the stalk consists of the great knot made of qualities (guṇas); the eight petals are the divisions of the intellect (buddhi), from which arise dharma, adharma, and the rest. (9.62)
At the tip of the stalk is the infinite Ego (ahaṃkṛta), which sustains the subtle elements, the senses, and the gross elements;
the lotus is the Unmanifest (avyakta), differentiated by the vowels beginning with 'a', and it contains the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire.

Others know the eight petals beginning with the south as being merely the pride of the intellect (buddhi-garva-manaḥ); still others understand them to be born from the eight powers beginning with Vimalā.
The lotus situated in the center of the egg is the great abode of Piśvā;
Vidyā is established above, residing in the lower shell of the egg of Māyā.
One should conceive of the pericardium as a protective wall for the heart-lotus; outside of that, the deity Vairāja is said to have the form of a city. (9.66)
The earth and the other elements are situated in the yellow, clear, reddish, black, and dark-blue [sections];
the Vasus are stationed on the tips of the lotus petals, while the Rudras and Ādityas are on the filaments.
The Maruts reside at the joints of the petals; the dust motes are the planets and stars;
and upon the lines at the edges of the spaces between the petals are the rivers and the oceans. (9.68)
Mount Meru is situated within the pericarp; the sages abide within the seed-syllables;
and Viṣṇu, having entered the sun, moon, and fire, stands beyond them with his splendor.
He who perceives that supreme, eternal nature of reality—perceiving it as the Self, the inner self, and even the supreme self—he truly sees. (9.70)
He alone who beholds its fourth, supreme form is that very [Brahman].
Yakṣas and other beings are the thorns on its stalk; the Apsarases are said to be its hairs. (9.71)
The Sūtra is Prajāpati; at the base of the petals are the vital airs, such as prāṇa and the rest;
situated in the center of the wheel-mandala is the Self, Hari, the Lord of All. (9.72)
He is declared to be partless (niṣkala), established in the supreme ether;
he who knows the God in this way as being likewise situated within the mandala—9.73.
Having abandoned the illusion of Viṣṇu, he shall attain the supreme state—
he who, even in the absence of formal ritual, worships the God stationed within the mandala.
Or by that [means], one shall certainly see the Lord of Gods directly;
here in this mandala, there shall be the eternal presence of Him who possesses all forms.
Therefore, worship within the maṇḍala is superior to the merits of sacred fords and other such places.
Thus ends the ninth chapter of the Viṣṇu-saṃhitā.
Now begins the tenth chapter.

Now I shall briefly explain the favor consisting of initiation, worship, and so forth, for the sake of accomplishing the qualification of the disciple and for the sake of liberation for yogins. (10.1)

All supernatural powers (siddhis) are bestowed, and even the knots [of the heart] are dissolved; such is initiation (dīkṣā), by which the self’s merit and demerit are removed from the heart through initiation. 10.2.

Initiation should be performed during the spring or summer, or in the months beginning with Kārttika; it is prescribed that the initiation of those born of the [four] castes may take place in autumn or Āṣāḍha. (10.3)
Having first personally and with care examined their birth, purity, and virtues, the teacher should recognize them as pure—especially in the case of women and Śūdras. (10.4)
Having then recognized their devotion toward the Supreme Lord, those who possess devotion for him should perform service to him for a long time, as if to a god. 10.5.
O Blessed One, through your grace we desire the crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra;
and especially, O one whose wealth is austerity, we desire worldly success in this life.
Having thus informed him and gratified him with gifts, favors, and consolations, they should, according to their means, collect the necessary provisions as directed by his wish. (10.7)
Having brought the ritual substances, purified them, and performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) on the preceding day,
he should initiate the disciples on the twelfth lunar day, having performed worship according to the rite for the deities.
Near a temple, a river, a sacred ford, a cow-pen, a grove, or similar places,
one should prepare a sacrificial ground according to the divisions of the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
However many Vaiṣṇavas there may be who desire initiation here, they should all strive together in this matter according to their own individual capacity. (10.10)
Whosoever possesses greater effort or greater wealth, his reward shall likewise be greater;
however, he who practices stinginess regarding his wealth will certainly fall into hell.
Permitted by the Vaiṣṇavas, together with those who were initiated and skilled, he bathed, sipped water for purification, became pure, performed his daily rites, and adorned himself well. (10.12)
The preceptor himself should enter the ground prepared for the sacrifice,
having meditated in his mind upon the deity as being complete and consisting of the mandala.
Having consecrated the altar according to the ritual rules, one should begin the placement of the water-jars (kalaśanyāsa);
then, having scattered white mustard seeds over which the Nṛsiṃha-mantra has been recited, ending with the syllable *phaṭ*.
Having recited the *mūlamantra* over the scattered offerings (*vikirān*), one should prepare the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*):
cow’s urine with the *praṇava* (OM) and cow dung with the *visarga* (HAḤ).
One should offer milk with the [mantra] ending in the bindu, curd with the long Viṣṇu [mantra], and ghee with the pure primordial Viṣṇu seed-syllable; thus one should worship.
From cow urine, one should take half as much cow dung; then eight times as much milk;
one should add seven times as much curd, and likewise four times as much clarified butter. (10.17)
Having sprinkled [the site] with kuśa grass while reciting the three seed-syllables,
he should scatter the *vikirāḥ* while standing facing east, reciting the root mantra three times and meditating upon Him with his palms turned upward.
Following the sequence of the deposition on the seats (pīṭhanyāsa), one should place the pitcher together with the water-jar (karkarī) in the northeast;
it should be made of metal, adorned with gems, free from blemishes, beautiful, and wrapped with thread.
Having filled it, the wise one should worship with perfumes and flowers in due order;
he should place within the jar a lotus situated upon a pedestal consisting of dharma, adharma, and so forth.
The root-tube of the plantain tree has a cavity like a thorn;
it is neuter because of its similarity to the two knots situated within the [four] principles, beginning with Dharma. (10.21)
It is endowed with three petals each beginning with the letter *ka*, extending as far as the pericarp.
It has the visarga and bindu as its radiant tips, and the vowels beginning with 'a' as its filaments.
Endowed with the three parts of Tārā through the sequence of the self, the vidyā, and the other,
and joined with Nāda and Śakti in the center, one should invoke and worship the Lord there.
When the *vardhanī* and the seat have been prepared, the invocation (*āvāhana*) should take place;
likewise for the clarified butter (*ājya*), the water of honor (*arghya*), the *praṇītā* vessel, and especially for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles. (10.24)

Having worshipped Keśava, together with his limbs (aṅgas), within the five products of the cow, the sacrificial porridge, the fire-pit, the mandala, and the hand of Viṣṇu, as well as [him] residing in the water-jar; 10.25.
In front of the sacrificial post (vardhanī) and around the pavilion on all sides,
one should cause an unbroken stream [of water] to fall, starting from the northeast and proceeding clockwise until the end.
Thereafter, the practitioner should lead the flask back along that very same path, having gathered up all the scattered grains along with those remaining in the vessels. (10.27)
One should worship the jar containing all kinds of grain as well as the *vardhanī* vessel;
one should wrap it with a pair of new white cloths.
One should likewise provide protection for one ghaṭikā with the Astra-mantra,
and scatter all kinds of grain consecrated with the Astra-mantra on all sides.
Having cleansed [the vessel] with the forms [of the deities], one should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) in the consecrated fire;
with the root mantra and the forms, one should cook the caru in the consecrated fire. || 10.30 ||
Having placed washed rice, smeared with clarified butter and mixed with milk, into the mouth of the vessel;
and having poured it out after first spreading a base [of ghee] over the washed grains and stirring them, [he should offer it]. 10.31.
Having spread [the sacrificial grass] and removed it toward the north, having washed and sprinkled [the vessel], one should worship it;
and one should apply the vertical mark of ashes (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on its side with the eight-syllable mantra. || 10.32 ||
Having spread [clarified butter] as a base in a beautiful vessel, having poured [the meat] over it,
and having again poured clarified butter over the wound and the first portion, one should set aside the share for the deity.
One should offer three oblations soaked in clarified butter with the root mantra: the second to the one residing in the jar, and the third to the one residing in the fire. 10.34.
Having drunk the *bali* offering with the remainder of that, he drank the fourth portion of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) with the *praṇava*,
having previously drunk the fourth portion of the *pañcagavya*.
The preceptor, together with his disciples, should consume a portion for the purification of the body;
[a substance] consecrated seven times, twelve finger-breadths in length, should be buried in the eastern direction.
They should examine an auspicious tooth-stick made from a milk-tree, free of blemishes and fit for consumption; by means of it, a propitiatory oblation is prescribed in the event of inauspiciousness.
Having sipped water and become pure in every way, the guru should pray to Acyuta, having circumambulated him, bowed down, and propitiated him. (10.38)
O Lord, you alone are the refuge for those bound souls submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra; you are ever compassionate toward your devotees. (10.39)
O God of gods, grant me your permission; by your grace, I shall liberate these bound souls who are fettered by the bonds of material nature.

Having received permission and having purified those who have fasted by means of meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās), he should sprinkle the sacrificial victims (paśus) stationed at the liṅga with the weapon-mantra (astra) and unite them with his own self. 10.41.
Having sprinkled that body again while it is held before him by the wind and fire,
and having meditated upon it as a heap of ashes, he should flood it entirely with water.
Having correctly meditated upon the single ocean-treasury of the circle of saṃsāra,
one should conceive of the earthly power as having the singular nature of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).

One should meditate upon the Person whose essence is the Praṇava, who is composed of the subtle elements (tanmātras), pure, spherical, and resembling a bubble, once he has been transferred into the liṅga. 10.44.

One should meditate upon this Prajāpati, whose faculties and form are distinct, who has split the cosmic egg with his intellect, and from whose two fragments the heaven and earth arose in the midst. 10.45.
Having sprinkled [the materials] again with the Praṇava and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa,
the preceptor should meditatively contemplate the entire maṇḍala and other elements with reverence upon his own hand.
That city has four gates in the sequence beginning with the Brahmatīrtha;
in its center is a lotus as previously described, and its petals are known to be the fingers.
The center of the pericarp is its joints, and the filaments are its nodes;
the locus of fire is here in the middle, and Keśava is situated within that.
Having meditated upon him within the three mandalas, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, one should worship him in the center with perfumes and flowers in due order.
With a well-composed mind, he should place that hand upon the head of the disciple;
since Viṣṇu resides in that hand, it is known as the "Hand of Viṣṇu. (10.50)
Whatever sin was accumulated in the past over thousands of previous births—all that undoubtedly goes to destruction by the mere touch [of this]. (10.51)
In this way, through the practice of meditative concentration, one may produce either one or many [bodies].
Thus, one should worship that person whose body has been completely purified with perfumes and flowers.
Having cleansed his hands with the root mantra and bound his eyes with a new garment using a fresh, unwashed cloth and the eye-mantra, the wise one [should proceed]. (10.53)
One should cause the disciple, holding a handful of flowers and facing east, to enter;
if many wish to enter, they should do so according to the order of the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
The southern door of the pavilion is the best for entering; the four doors beginning with the north are specifically for the Brahmins and the other [classes]. 10.55.
The entry into the city should be performed according to the desires of the disciple:
for progeny, strength, wealth, and good fortune; for jewels, food, victory, and women. (10.56)

Fortitude, liberation, long life, health, cattle, sons, happiness, and so forth shall result from entering through the eastern and other directions; having given a fee, one should cause [the person] to enter.
Having caused the disciple— who has performed circumambulations and successively saluted the guardians of the quarters—
to face the deity, he should then cause him to stand facing the east.
Instructed by his teacher to remain silent, he restrained his speech, body, and mind;
then, having first bowed down, he supported himself upon the ground with both knees.
Having meditated with devotion upon the god Hari, who possesses a splendor equal to ten million suns,
who is accompanied by Lakṣmī, who is gentle, and who is adorned with eight arms.
With a concentrated mind, he should cast the garland while awaiting the teacher’s instruction;
having removed that veil from his eyes, he should observe where the flower falls.
One should address him by the name of the deity's form according to the manner of the flower-fall;
there, among the forms of the deities, one should perform worship without mantras.
For a Brāhmaṇa, it is said that [the name] ends with "deva"; for a Kṣatriya, however, it ends with "varman";
for a Vaiśya, the name ends with "gupta"; and for a Śūdra, one should designate it as ending with "dāsa. (10.63)
For women, her name shall be Devī; she is his form that grants all desires.
Merely by being seen, the accumulations of sin within the maṇḍala are destroyed.
Having offered incense and a lamp in succession, one should here present the food offering (naivedya),
[visualizing] the sequence from primordial nature (prakṛti) down to earth, together with their respective elemental beings (adhibhūta) and presiding deities (adhidaivata).
Having seated him to the south, with darbha grass in hand and restrained in speech, one should gradually deposit everything withdrawn within oneself into the body of the disciple. (10.66)
The wise teacher, while being held by the student, should offer oblations into the fire according to the *sampāta* rite, one hundred times for each of the principles (*tattva*).
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should present everything to the Lord of the Jar (kumbheśa):
the ritual instruments (karaṇī) and the scissors (kartarī), as well as the colored powders (rajas) and the water-clock (ghaṭikā).
And whatever else may be required, all that, having been touched with the root mantra together with its ancillaries, one should consecrate within the domain of the wind.
Then he should lie down with those disciples, having spread out kusha grass and remembering Him;
through this, there shall be peace from bad dreams and the like, for otherwise there is no success in this world. (10.70)
Having bathed in the morning and dismissed the Lord from the mandala, one should worship Him again with coral,
pearl ornaments, and beautiful golden flowers.
Having gratified the fire with various offerings and having summoned them in due order,
he [beheld] those who had performed the worship of the deities as before, seated in the lotus posture before him.
Having sprinkled [the disciple] and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should touch him with the hand of Viṣṇu,
while meditating in due order upon the entire creation beginning with Prakṛti and ending with the Earth.
Having joined that [consciousness], which consists of the subtle elements and has attained equality with the individual soul within that body,
to the Self by means of the syllable *Tāra*, one should meditate upon it as having been made of a single flavor.
By bestowing the soul, that body, time, fire, power, and the womb, [the Lord grants] the embryo, birth, qualification, experience, and destruction through these five.
Having offered sixty-four oblations, he likewise purified [the soul] from hell,
and furthermore from the netherworld (pātāla) and the earth, [liberating it] from births such as those of immobile beings.
One should apply the sixteen rites, beginning with the *pākayajña* sacrifices, in reverse order for the status of Śūdra, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa, using the root mantra in sequence. (10.77)
Having purified [the soul] through rites ending with the horse sacrifice, one should prepare for the final stage of life;
having performed the funeral rite according to the eightfold division of wombs beginning with that of a Piśāca.
Having led [the breath] through the three suras in sequence, one should destroy the bondage of karma;
then, having sprinkled that body with a hundred oblations, one should [proceed].
One should conceive of the Lord of Creation as indifferent by means of the final oblation;
then, with white powder consecrated by the recitation of the root mantra, one should strike the heart.

One should separate [the deity] by means of the name ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, beginning with the syllables of the reality (*tattva*), and further consecrated by the seed-syllable preceded by *āyāhi* and ending with *hāṃ*. (10.81)
Having taken [the substance] and brought it to a state of equilibrium, join it with the sequence "huṃ phaṭ";
then, having performed the rite of creation (prakṛti) by that very same [mantra] ending with the rite of withdrawal (saṃhāra), one should perform the oblation (homayet).
The wise one should meditate upon the entire path of the principles (tattvādhvan) dissolving in due order into Hari, the unmanifest fire which is the abode of all principles. 10.83.
One should unite the pure [soul] with the supreme reality by means of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having thus purified the principles (tattvas), one should dissolve primordial nature (prakṛti) into the Supreme Self.
Having dissolved [the deity] through the yoga of knowledge, the wise one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having burnt away primordial nature (prakṛti) during the ritual of dissolution, he should unite it with the Supreme by means of the final oblation.
One should install an ordinary man as the presiding authority over the temple;
however, if one is unable to do so, one may install a deity equipped with all its ritual implements.
Having performed the preliminary consecration immediately on the twelfth day, one should initiate [the disciple] either on a sacrificial altar or even upon a leveled mound;
first, one should purify the principles (tattvas) in their proper order with sixty-four oblations.
This latent impression (vāsanā) of the mind is the obstacle to liberation;
through its purification the knower of the field (kṣetrī) becomes pure, and by its corruption he is defiled. 10.88
The eradication of the mind's latent impressions through liberation from the bondage of karma is declared to be its purification, which renders it seedless. 10.89.
Constantly joined by the Guru, the yogi should practice yoga thoroughly;
without him, yoga is not perfected—of this there is no doubt. (10.90)
Having drawn forth that [being] whose limbs were scorched and who resembled sparks,
he— thus ends the eleventh chapter.
Now I shall describe in brief the consecration of one who has been initiated—
whether he be a *putraka* or a *deśika*— by which he attains the status of an *ācārya*.
First, at the initial stage, there is initiation into the knowledge of the Tantra, and then into worship;
for these three initiations are to be employed for the increase of righteousness.
Having first drawn the mandala together with its retinue, the preceptor should show it to the disciple; such a person is known as a "vowed practitioner" (samayin). || 11.3 ||
Having propitiated the deity in the maṇḍala preceded by an offering of handfuls of flowers, whoever is shown [the mandala] according to the rite shall become one initiated into the tantra. || 11.4 ||

Having offered all the mantras into the fire and having worshipped that Lord according to the prescribed rule, he who reveals [the deity] is to be known as the preceptor-officiant (deśikārcaka). || 11.5 ||
The son, having studied the tantras, should receive the second mantra;
he should worship the deity for the third time—such is the threefold sequence.
Indeed, by a single ritual application alone, three initiations for the sake of grace—
intended for the worship of the Samaya-granthi— should be performed by one who knows the reality.

Having first performed the sacraments in their proper sequence, beginning with the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) and ending with the investiture of the sacred thread (vratabandha), the preceptor indeed [performed them] according to the supreme reality.
Then, by means of ten oblations for each, one should dissolve the principles (tattvas);
indeed, the principles beginning with vaikāra are composed of the five elements.
Having meditated upon the sixth principle, characterized as the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), within the body of the disciple,
and having purified it through the fire-oblation, one should finally unite it with the Supreme by means of the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
There, Māyā is established in the form of the five elements;
but the sixth reality is, in the ultimate sense, unbound.
Since there can be no cessation of intrinsic nature, just as there is none of fire's heat, therefore the bound soul is like a jar and the supreme state is like space. 11.12
Having thus understood that which is distinct and stainless,
the wise man should destroy through the fire-oblation that which is known as bondage, like a jar.

Beginning with earth and the other elements, one should purify each of the principles (tattvas) in sequence by means of the five [mantras] beginning with vaikāra, using one hundred oblations for each.
Having offered five full oblations, one should contemplate the severing of the bonds;
at the conclusion of the hundred oblations, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is freed from the bondage of Māyā.
Meditating thus, one should offer the final oblation; this is the supreme initiation of devotion.
Whatever ritual action has been prescribed for each according to the divisions of the *samaya* and other rules, [it should be performed].
That same duty belongs to him again even in the performance of penance;
and initiation must be performed year after year for the sake of bestowing grace upon his disciples.
He who has been initiated by twelve sacrifices is Hari himself;
he desires to make that disciple, endowed with virtuous qualities, his preceptor.
The knower of mantras should perform his consecration according to this rite;
one who knows the mantras should perform the king’s consecration according to this rite. 11.19.
For the practitioner who is childless, poor, or diseased,
having prepared the maṇḍala as before— possessing all its characteristics yet unobserved by others— (he should proceed).
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods here and offered oblations into the fire according to the rule,
one should place before him faultless water-pots encircled with threads.
Endowed with the five jewels, accompanied by gold and sprouts,
and wrapped in pairs of cloths, [he placed them] in the four directions in due order.
In the center, one should place the fifth [syllable], together with the beard and the lid;
one should place the Praṇava, which embodies all mantras, upon the eastern pitcher.
The wise one should place the syllable *a* in the south, which embodies all tantras;
likewise, in the west, he should place the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, consisting of its specific authority (*adhikāra*).
In the north, one should also place Viṣṇu, the all-pervading one whose form is knowledge;
and in the center, the Vaiṣṇava seed-syllable, the eternal Śabdabrahman.
Then he should worship them all in due order with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
for they are endowed with mastery in yoga, the meaning of the tantras, and all branches of knowledge.

As it has been said: having meditated upon all the luminaries, beginning with Tārā, who reside within the lotus of the Mātṛkā, in the form of mantras, tantras, and so forth, one should contemplate the deity individually and in due order. (11.27)
The preceptor, being well-composed, should thus perform the ritual of one thousand recitations or indeed one hundred recitations for each individual pitcher.
Then the lord of practitioners should perform the fire oblation (homa) according to rule,
by way of reabsorption, as previously described for that which is called Nirvāṇa.
Having thus performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) there according to the rules of yoga,
one should then properly perform the empowerment (abhiṣeka) for the practitioner.
On the northern side of the pavilion, having first constructed a very beautiful altar (vedī) measuring one cubit,
two cubits, or four cubits [in size].
In a pavilion four pillars high, as tall as a palm tree, provided with a roof, covered with canopies and cloths, and adorned with garlands and wreaths; (11.32)
Having decorated it as beautifully as possible with jars of parched grain on all four sides, and having drawn a svastika in the center and a very beautiful square; 11.33.
There, having placed upon it a new, auspicious, and square throne made of śrīparṇī wood, covered with white dust.
Upon that [lotus], one should worship the infinite [deity] together with the lotus, consisting of Dharma and the other [qualities].
Then, standing in front facing east, one should meditate upon the Lord seated upon the throne.
Having worshipped with the mind, one should present this request:
"O Blessed One, it has been stated that for one who is initiated, there is an empowerment into the office of the preceptor. (11.36)
"Authorized by you, I shall perform that for the sake of accomplishing all goals.
Then, having received permission, he should perform the consecration according to the prescribed rite.
Having meditated upon the path of the principles (tattvādhvan) according to the sequence of emanation and having cultivated it well,
the Guru should cause the disciple— facing east and wearing white garments— to enter.
Having meditated upon that imperishable Viṣṇu, who is seated upon the infinite throne and has been worshipped,
one should bring the water-pots here and place them in their respective directions.
Then, while auspicious songs were being sung by women with melodious voices,
accompanied by the sound of conchs and trumpets and preceded by the ritual waving of lights (nīrājana), [the procession proceeded].
Then the preceptor should perform the consecration together with the chanting of the Vedic hymns,
having meditated upon the water as being identical in essence to the mantra, using the very mantras previously mentioned.
Having thus worshipped each jar in turn and incensed them in due order—
with four [mantras], then with the fifth, which consists of supreme knowledge— 42.
Having performed the lustration ceremony once more, he should worship him with perfumes and flowers,
having clothed him in two beautiful new garments as he approached.
Having offered water for sipping and having first provided a seat of grass (bṛsī), the preceptor himself sat down;
he too, having bowed to the Lord of Gods, sat upon it with his speech restrained.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon him with mantras, he should worship him again as before;
[offering] the yogapaṭṭaka, the uṣṇīṣa, the cakra, and the aṅgulīyaka.
He should announce his own office and the essential truth to him,
and he should bestow the Vaiṣṇava knowledge which is the cause for severing the cycle of worldly existence.
The supreme teacher should cause these pledges (samayas) spoken in the Tantra to be heard:
"Disciples who are Vaiṣṇavas and of virtuous conduct are indeed to be favored by you. (11.47)
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or even women;
those who are devoted to another deity, as well as those who are outside the four castes—11.48.
O Vaiṣṇava, you must never show favor toward those who are hypocritical, performers of evil deeds, and revilers of the gods and Brahmins. 11.49.
However, where the guru is nearby, one must not exercise independence;
even when the teacher resides at a distance of many yojanas, [one remains under his authority].
In this matter, O sinless one, initiation must not be performed by you unless it has been prescribed;
furthermore, the worship of the guru must be performed by you just as that of Viṣṇu.
The teacher must always be remembered during times such as explanations and the like;
never should the word of the teacher be treated by you as lacking authority.
If negligence occurs, the expiation must be performed according to his command;
O sinless one, you must never cause distress to the world.
You must follow the Vaibhāṣika doctrine of the Vaiṣṇavas, even that which is censured in the world, and you must act according to the scriptures in accordance with the conduct of the elders.
You must never harbor pride, even in your dreams, my child! And you must observe the rules and the modes of conduct that have been declared by me. (11.55)
"You must protect [these teachings] with effort according to my command for as long as you live; indeed, become an Ācārya in the Vaiṣṇava Tantra, beloved by all living beings. (11.56)
Let your disciples approach you; treat them according to the scriptures.
Do not act out of greed for gain, nor out of hope, nor out of fear.
Especially during the five nights, constantly remember the God;
at times such as the solstices and others, the imperishable Viṣṇu is to be worshipped.
Teachers are to be honored through the actions of mind, speech, and body;
one should not commit useless violence, and they should be supported according to one's ability.
The poor, the helpless, the blind, and the Brahmins should always be honored;
one should remain ever-diligent and unwearied in the performance of daily rites.

One should perform a small amount of recitation daily, offer a small amount as an oblation in the fire, and practice a small amount of meditation; this is the perpetual sacrificial session for the teacher.
Having spoken thus to the disciple of pure mind who stands before the deity,
the Guru should impart the entire Tantra and the mantra itself to the practitioner.
Having filled a handful of water mixed with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata) before the deity,
one should recite the mantra and pour it into his hand.
"May the fruit born of the mantra, which you desire, be swiftly accomplished.
Having been addressed thus, he himself arose, circumambulated the preceptor, and [prostrated]. (11.64)
Having seated him on a seat and having washed his feet with devotion, one should gratify the guru with wealth and grain according to one’s power and devotion. (11.65)
Having satisfied him and clasped his feet with both hands, one should request permission from the guru, saying, "Please honor the deity yourself. (11.66)
Having received permission, that disciple may also eat from that time forward.
But the man who performs worship without being thus authorized by him— || 11.67 ||
"Success does not come through the worship of that [image]; such is the certainty of the scripture.
Therefore, [one should worship] the deity situated in the center of the maṇḍala, who has been worshipped by the preceptor. (11.68)
Having seen [the proper time] and obtained the permission of his guru, he should worship Puruṣottama;
thus, whoever performs the Vaiṣṇava initiation, or whoever causes it to be performed—|| 11.69 ||
Both of them go to heaven, and in the reverse case, to hell.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, one should worship Viṣvaksena in the northeastern direction.
The god with tawny beard and wide-open eyes, holding a mace in his hand, four-armed,
bearing the conch and the discus, stands intent upon the protection of the world.
Threatening the world with his left index finger held near the tip of his nose,
he should worship the deity along with his limbs within the circle of Varuṇa using the remaining materials.
Having released [the deity] according to the prescribed rite, one should collect all the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) from Madhokṣaja situated within the mandala and present them to him.
For that [mantra], one should likewise arrange the syllables in their proper order as follows: *viṃ*, *vaṃ*, *namaḥ*, *ṣvāṃ*, *vīṃ*, *svāhā*, *kṣeṃ*, *vaṣaṭ*, *viṣvaṃ*, *vaiṃ*, and *hum*. (11.74)
With the syllable *phaṭ*, these five limbs [are consecrated] for that worship;
then, having sprinkled the water contained in the *praṇīta* vessel upon the sacrificial grass (*prastara*), one should do so with that [water].
Having sprinkled water upon himself along with his disciples, he should dismiss the fire;
then, having dismissed Viṣvaksena, he should offer him all the remains of the offerings.
One should cause that which was previously given to be deposited by others in unfathomable water;
one should worship the Vaiṣṇavas according to one's ability, and especially the Brāhmaṇas.
He should cause food and other provisions to be provided without restriction for all people;
thus the initiate, who is devoted to dharma, attains the status of a teacher.
Devoted to his caste and stage of life, faithful, humble, and observant of the rules of conduct,
he should worship Hari once, twice, or thrice a day.
Then, one should favor the disciples through initiation, worship, and consecration;
likewise, one is worthy of the office of an ācārya in rites such as the installation of images.
At the conclusion of the initiation and at the conclusion of the consecration, having honored the Vaiṣṇavas according to one's ability,
one should go at dawn to the avabhṛtha bath where there is a supreme sacred ford (tīrtha).
Having bathed there and performed worship, one should have the Brahmins recite benedictions.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, named "Consecration," in the Viṣṇu-saṃhitā.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Now I shall briefly describe the characteristics of the sacrificial ground, where, having worshipped the God according to the rules, all perfections are obtained. (12.1)
The earth is of three kinds—superior, inferior, and middling—and likewise of four types according to the distinction of their birth: Supadmā, Bhadrikā, Pūrṇā, and Dhūmrā. (12.2)
A field with much soil and dried-up water is excellent for the rapid growth of rice and other crops;
it is best when the water flows clockwise and when the soil remains even during both the cold and hot seasons.
Where the river flows eastward, where the trees bear milk, flowers, and fruit,
and where cattle and men delight together in equal affection— that land is most excellent.
The sound and gestures of a conch-shell, a cloud, and so forth, should match the caste of all castes;
in the absence of such [natural qualities], they may be artificial, but otherwise they would be inferior. (12.5)
And she is said to be all-floating, characterized by auspicious and inauspicious marks;
her proportions are square, or eight, six, or five parts, with her length being one-quarter greater than her width. (12.6)
The ground prescribed for the Brahmins and the other castes is that which is best for all;
likewise, the ground for the Brahmin and the others is white, red, yellow, and black respectively.
Sweet, sour, astringent, bitter, and pungent are their tastes in sequence;
they possess the scents of ghee, blood, raw meat, and excrement, and are rejected because they are multicolored.
At night, one should know [the result] by lighting and surrounding a *vardhamāna* lamp with ghee and wicks placed in a jar full of grain, using white and other colors, by means of observation.
One should know [the outcome] by flowers that have withered overnight, as well as by white and other such [colors];
likewise by anthills, gravel, mud, husks, charcoal, bones, and ashes. (12.10)
One should avoid ground that is infested with hair, mud, and insects;
ground that is smoky-colored, parched, foul-smelling, and hard is inauspicious.

The *adikṣṭhā*, the waterless (*jalahīnā*), the crooked (*kuṭilā*), the double-length (*dviguṇāyatā*), the circular (*vṛttā*), the five-, three-, or six-cornered (*pañcatriṣaṭkoṇā*), the half-moon (*ardhacandrā*), and the winnowing-basket-shaped (*śūrpikā*). || 12.12 ||
With *pīlu*, *śelva*, *akṣa*, bamboo, *arka*, *snuk*, *piśāca*, and bitter trees;
and with hawks, vultures, bears, jackals, boars, crows, and monkeys. (12.13)

A river that flows toward the north is censured as being haunted by Rākṣasas, while one that flows toward the south is condemned for its fiery and windy nature; a river that is low in the middle, contains pools, or flows in a contrary direction is not desired.

The ground for the Brāhmaṇas and the other classes is to be known by its kuśa grass, śara grass, dūrvā grass, and kāśa grass, as well as by flowers and lamps; having bowed and addressed that Lord, [one should prepare it]. 12.15.
"O Lord, tell me the sign described in the Kalpa regarding the twice-born and others, when it is applied to the four wicks for the sake of the noble castes. (12.16)
If, after a short time has passed, his lamp continues to burn, then the ground belongs to him;
for it is desired that the site be free from obstruction, since it illuminates everything for all.

The Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Plakṣa trees, situated to the east and so forth, are auspicious; whether taken individually or all together, they are praised, whereas those on the left yield no desired fruit.
Water that is not drinkable is the worst, even if situated in all directions;
water from a well is best in the directions of Indra, Agni, and Soma, but water from a single source is not auspicious.

Water, mountains, trees, and shrubs situated in the east and other directions are auspicious; however, trees such as the *śigru* and *nimba* should be cut down within a distance of one hundred cubits.
Those situated outside are not a fault; they should be made auspicious within.
Having left a space twice the height of the house's chest, they do not stand as a fault.
Outside the double height of the houses, there were likewise fruit and flowering trees:
bakula, aśoka, punnāga, nāga, candana, and campaka.

The *bilva*, mango, jackfruit, and others, as well as the *palāśa* and other beautiful trees—those with internal pith, those with external pith, those without pith, and those that are the essence of all. || 12.23 ||
Among those, the four types of stationary plants are worthless; they should not be kept in front of the house.
Plants such as the plantain tree should be maintained outside, on the back or the side of the dwelling. (12.24)
The essence of all things is proclaimed everywhere to be the tamarind and so forth;
one should know that which has internal essence as such, while that which has external essence is like something without essence.
One should not even keep a golden tree near one's house;
however, such a rule does not apply exclusively to shrubs, creepers, and medicinal herbs.
It was completely covered with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, kadamba, tilaka, and arjuna trees, as well as betel nuts, coconuts, kuśa grass, and darbha grass.
The earth, strewn with groves of lotuses and water-lilies, rich in water and abounding in islands,
filled with ketaka and sugarcane, and graced with beautiful lotuses, bestows peace.
It was situated at a sacred ford and sanctuary extending as far as the rivers and the ocean;
it was thickly covered with milk-exuding trees and crowded with fruit-bearing trees.
It was provided with gardens and groves, filled with flowering shrubs and creepers;
on the west it was bordered by sacrificial trees, and on the south by fields of rice.
That ground is declared to be auspicious and bestows happiness upon those who perform sacrifices there;
it is filled with *kiṃśuka*, *aśoka*, *bakula*, *aṅkola*, and *nimba* trees.
It was filled with khadira, rohitaka, and plakṣa trees, as well as mādhavī, campaka, and asana trees, along with kula, stha, tila, niṣpāva, and kodrava plants.
Land situated on the slope of a mountain or resting upon a mountain peak,
even if it has little water, is full and bestows nourishment.
It was filled with groves of pilu and veṇu trees, abounding in snuhi and śleṣmātaka plants; it was crowded with vibhītaka and arka trees, hard and strewn with gravel.
Crowded with hawks, vultures, bears, jackals, boars, and crows, saline, and containing embryos, such a smoky-colored land brings about destruction.
Having thus examined with care by means of its fragrance, color, taste, and other qualities,
one should clear away the shrubs and such from this site and then plow it with auspicious plows.
One should sow all kinds of grains, either fivefold or tenfold;
then, after having cultivated the land, one should once again make it endowed with flowers and fruits.
Now, the purification for her who has been utterly defiled is being described:
having caused her to undergo a hundred fasts, one should cause her to dwell there with a herd of cows.
Then, having stayed for the rainy season and ploughed the field, one should sow sesame seeds and other crops there;
indeed, when the plants have produced flowers and fruits, [the harvest is ready]. (12.39)
Then, having first offered the *bhūtakūra* oblation there, the wise man should plough the ground again; it will undoubtedly attain purification. (12.40)
One should establish the enclosure as far as the edge of the rampart,
[driving away] whatever beings or even rākṣasas may dwell therein.
"May they all indeed depart; I shall prepare a place for Hari.
Having thus requested permission from the spirits and other beings, one should then perform that ritual procedure. (12.42)
The practitioner of mantras should perform the stretching of the lines from Indra to Īśāna by wrapping the peg twice around it, using auspicious signs as the occasion.
Strong, pitiless spikes produced from a single *punnāga* tree should be worshipped and struck eight times with iron hammers by one facing the east.
Having dug a pit one man’s height deep, or even down to where water or stone is reached,
he should then place a jar in the center, filled according to the ritual rules and duly honored.
At an auspicious moment, he had a pit dug with excellent earth and filled it up to the brim with a heap of grain containing jewels, and then covered it with stones.
Having flooded it with water to the depth of three-quarters, and having struck and rubbed it with palāśa, aśvattha, and mudgara stones, one should cause the floor to be made very firm.
One should worship the deity at the doorway and satisfy the fire upon the sacrificial mound;
having made it square and level, one should there also satisfy the Vāstu deity.
Furthermore, one should lay out the lines so as to form eighty-one squares;
a dwelling site that is perfectly level brings happiness, whereas an uneven one does not lead to well-being.

For the sake of auspiciousness, one should first draw [the diagram] clockwise using curd, unbroken rice, clarified butter, flowers, water, gold, and jewels; never with the fingers or similar means. 12.50.
One should worship with kusha grass, flowers, unbroken grains, water, and fragrant blossoms those [deities] situated there upon the head of Ishvara and the foot of Nirriti, while lying on one's back.
Brahmā should be in the center of the nine; in the six directions [there are] two each, and elsewhere;
