thirty-two deities are to be worshipped outside, starting from the northeast (Īśāna) in sequence. || 12.52 ||
Brahmā is to be worshipped in the central square; then Āryaka in the east of that, and Sāvitra and Savitṛ in the southeast. After that, two deities residing in two squares each are prescribed.
Vivasvān is in the southern group of six; Jayanta and Indra are in the two pairs [of the north-east];
Mitra is in the western group of six, and again in the two pairs of the north-west.
Rājayakṣmā and Rudra are in the sixth [cell] on the northern side of the mountain;
likewise, Āpavatsa and Apa are in the two [cells] outside of that, where Śiva resides.
Parjanya, Jayanta, Indra, Sūrya, Satya, Bhṛśa, and Ambara;
I shall describe those beginning with Agni in the east, as well as Pūṣan and Vitatha.
One should worship Gṛhakṣata, Dharmarāja, Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarājaka,
and Mṛga in the south-western corner (nairṛta), and thereafter worship the ancestors.
And [he addressed] Sugrīva the gatekeeper, Puṣpadanta the lord of the waters,
the Asura Tvaṣṭṛ, Śoṣa, and Pāpayakṣman as well.
Likewise, one should worship Vāyu, Nāga, Mukhya,
Bhallāṭa, Soma, Aditi, Diti, and Kubera, in sequence, starting from the northeast (Īśāna) and proceeding outward.
Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā the evil Rākṣasī,
Śarva, Skanda, Aryaman, Jambhaka, and Pilipiñchaka— [these he subdued].

Having offered the bali-oblation to them in the various directions, one should then offer a bali to all beings in every direction, beginning from the center and proceeding in due order throughout the eight quarters.
The fifty-three deities residing within the body of the site (vāstu), when worshipped, lead to success; but if they are not worshipped, they bring misfortune to the inhabitants of the house.
Having resolved upon the fast, well-bathed and accompanied by a worthy companion,
he should sit upon the ground at night, facing north, on a well-smeared surface.
Having recited the mantra that grants dreams until he has fallen under the power of sleep,
he then sees a dream that indicates the fruit of that [action] upon the ground.
Having had a good dream, one should construct a house here during an auspicious lunar mansion, day, and time of sunrise;
having prepared a very beautiful sacrificial altar of four cubits with excellent clay.
One should place a beautiful water-pot, smeared [with unguents], situated in the center of a lotus, filled with all medicinal herbs, containing jewels within, and adorned with sprouts.
His limbs were anointed with white sandalwood paste, he was adorned with a garland of lotuses,
covered by a pair of white garments, composed, and marked with the svastika sign.
Having first visualized a radiant lotus at its opening with the *praṇava*,
the mantra-practitioner, with a finger-ring upon his hand, should arrange the planets there.
One should worship them, joyful and seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), by their respective names:
the Sun as red, the Moon as white, and Mars as red again.
One should visualize Mercury as resembling gold, Saturn as black in color,
Jupiter as yellow, and Venus indeed as white.

Rāhu should be worshipped with flowers having a dark-yellow luster, and Ketu with black flowers; all of them are to be honored according to the prescribed rule with flowers characterized by their own respective colors.
At the conclusion, one should perform a fire-oblation and a ritual offering accompanied by song and instrumental music;
having offered praise to the planets, one should recite the purifying hymn.
O Lord of Planets! Reveal to me, who am asking, the auspicious and inauspicious signs of great significance—those celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial omens.
Having spoken thus and lifted up that pitcher while reciting the Śākuna Sūkta,
one should carefully circumambulate it, accompanied by shouts of victory and other such sounds.
Even when facing an undesirable sight, having thus placed and worshipped [the image] upon the ground, one should lift it up and whirl it again; then a marvel is seen in the sky.
The vision of perfected beings (siddhas), their voice, or even rain accompanied by warmth;
[the appearance of] jewels, flowers, fruits, food, grains, honey, clarified butter, and garments. || 12.76 ||
The fall of curd, pāṭhīna fish, frogs, urine, meat, or tortoises from the sky onto the surface of the earth is auspicious. (12.77)
The king saw the maiden of the Brahmin and the previous water-jar; her voice was like that of an elephant, a horse, a peacock, a swan, a cloud, a conch, or a flute. || 12.78 ||
These and other such [omens] should be recognized by the discerning at the time of ritual action;
when something undesirable is clearly smelled, heard, or seen, one should avoid the ground.
Having reached another day and having recognized an auspicious omen, the performer should indeed cause the rite to be performed according to the method previously described.

Having thus worshipped the fire and said "Forgive me," and having had the Brahmins recite benedictions, he should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) and dig as before; he should then fill that earth back up again. || 12.81 ||
In the center of the house, the wise man should place the auspicious tortoise-stone previously prepared, upon which the tortoise is to be set.
One should place a silver tortoise and likewise a golden one;
as before, one should fashion a lotus and the Mātṛkā consisting of the eight groups of letters.
Having worshipped and bowed to the power of the support (ādhāraśakti), he should then make this request:
"You alone are the supreme power; you alone are the sustainer of the seat. (12.84)
O Goddess, you must always remain here with a satisfied mind,
supporting the king of tortoises, Makūpāra, as well as the entire universe.
Having meditated upon him seated on the previously mentioned lotus, one should worship him by his own name:
"Salutations to you, Viṣṇu, in the form of the tortoise, the sustainer of the universe. (12.86)
"You ought to support the temple that is to be built here.
Having thus petitioned him with devotion, one should worship Gaṇeśa there as well. || 12.87 ||
Having fashioned a lotus on the right side of the tortoise as before,
one should worship it in due order with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the seed-syllable joined with the name.
One should perform the five-limbed rite for the seed-syllable using the [vowels] ending at the twelfth [position], elongated threefold;
having especially offered sweetmeats (laḍḍuka), cakes (apūpa), parched grain (pṛthuka), and so forth. 12.89.
One should meditate upon the elephant-faced one, red in color, with a large belly and four arms,
holding a noose and a goad, and bearing food as well as a tusk.
Where Gaṇeśa is thus constantly worshipped with devotion, there no obstacles arise and prosperity increases. (12.91)
One should worship this Gaṇeśa according to the prescribed rite in the mandala, on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), and at every sacrifice.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Now I shall briefly describe the supreme method for constructing a temple, the mere undertaking of which immediately destroys all sins. (13.1)
Even when eight bricks have been laid, it is impossible to state the result; for by that very [measure], the result must be inferred according to the extent of the temple. (13.2)
Whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, sacred fords, and the Vedas—
all that arises for the sacrificer multiplied ten millionfold.
Moreover, through the excellence of its substance and configuration, the fruit of this [gift] increases further;
there is nothing more beneficial than this, therefore it should be performed in every way by those who are capable. (13.4)
Facing the east, the preceptor, having ploughed the ground with two tawny bulls of equal size using yoke-poles made of wood, [should proceed].

Adorned with new garments and other ornaments, and having cultivated a crop on ground leveled with a wooden pin and prepared by oxen, he should eat it while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra. (13.6)
Having dug again, one should perform the laying of the bricks once the door has been prepared;
the first brick should be placed on the southern side of the door.

Having performed the rites from the *ullekhana* up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he should, in due order, offer the cooked oblation upon a mound of earth situated to the north with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī, and then offer the oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) in sequence. (13.8)

Then, with the eight syllables of the *gāyatrī* mantra distributed individually, he offered oblations to the eight *vyāhṛtis*, and thereafter to Indra and the others, as well as to Agni, Soma, and the planets, in their proper order.
The teacher [should offer] to the constellations, to the spirits, and likewise to the nāgas;
and to all the deities, and to the Viśvedevas. (13.10)

Having offered oblations with "And to Viṣṇu," one should then offer the Vyāhṛtis; thereafter, having offered fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge, one should recite the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.
Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and completed the remainder of the *homa*,
one should pour the residue of the clarified butter (*sampātājya*) upon the bricks while reciting the root mantra.
Having drawn eight lines with a shoot of the *aśvattha* tree—oriented toward the east and the north—using a star as a guide, he, facing the east and well-composed, [should proceed]. (13.13)
In a square divided into four compartments, one should place [the syllables] in the compartments of Agni and Anila;
likewise, along the line directed toward the east and the line directed toward the north, as well as in the compartments of Nirṛti and Īśa.
Standing thereafter with palms joined in reverence, he meditated upon the Lord Adhokṣaja and recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, as well as the twelve-syllable mantra.

Then, having bowed to that Lord and meditated upon Him within the eight compartments by means of the eight syllables, the wise man should recite the eight-syllabled mantra as many times as there are letters in his own name.
One should place those eight bricks in sequence, beginning with Agni and ending with Indra;
one should employ them like a foundation, avoiding anything that is low or high.
Having thus laid down the bricks and filled the pit with pure, fragrant waters, rich with the scent of gems that had fallen [into them]. (13.18)

Having first placed white flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata) upon jars that are filled, honored, and consecrated with mantras, one should cause [the disciple] to gaze at the vessel while reciting the Tāra mantra.
The clockwise and counter-clockwise revolutions of the auspicious and inauspicious [winds] are to be known as being on the right and left;
then, one should cover the pit with clay from fields of rice and other crops. (13.20)
Having dismissed the artisans, one should also have a dream-vision performed here:
in a favorable [dream] there is gain; in an unfavorable one, release; but upon seeing [the deity], peace should be performed. (13.21)
Then one should perform the rite of conception (garbhādhāna), for there can be no prosperity in a dwelling that is devoid of a child.
Ten types of earth and aquatic roots should be collected. (13.22)
The elements are considered the seeds of jewels as well as metals and so forth;
[the stūpa] should be eight cubits high, with its upper covering (uttaracchada) half that height and reduced by one-quarter.
It was thick, made of copper, smooth, and a beautiful inner vessel;
it was well-secured, as if it were fixed within a wall or by means of a partition.
The sandals of a Brahmin are placed upon the ground; those of a king upon the ground; and those of others below it.
On the right side of the door, at the third part remaining after two have been set aside.
One should place [the vessel] beside the base of the door after it has been drenched with cow’s urine;
once washed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), this purified vessel [is ready].
Having meditated according to the rule upon the syllable-lotus on the seat by means of the dhāraṇās,
[one should contemplate] the circle of the earth situated upon Ananta, together with its mountains, oceans, and directional elephants.
Having performed circumambulation from left to right, one should first place earth from the ocean within [the enclosure], and then,
with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should distribute earth in the cardinal and intermediate directions as well as in the center.
And [the earth] was brought respectively from mountains, sacred bathing places, rivers, a lake, the abode of Karkaṭaka, an anthill, a threshing floor, an elephant, and the horns of a bull. (13.29)
The preceptor should likewise place four [seeds] in order at the roots of the red lotus, the blue lotus, the white water-lily, and the red lotus in the cardinal directions.
Realgar, yellow orpiment, collyrium, black lead, antimony, saurāṣṭrī, gorocanā, red chalk, and mercury—these likewise [should be used]. (13.31)
Diamond, pearl, topaz, lapis lazuli, conch-shell, crystal, and puṣyaka; moonstone, sapphire, and likewise ruby. (13.32)
He also offered śāli rice, nīvāra grain, kaṅgu, māṣa, and kuluttha; as well as niṣpāva, sesame, mung beans, and sarṣapa seeds, all fully cooked.
In the cardinal directions, there were images made of gold, silver, iron, tin, and gold;
and in the intermediate corners, there were figures of Garuḍa, a tortoise, a conch, and a discus.
A bow, a mace, and a lotus, each made of gold,
should be brought together and placed in the center of the womb-vessel.
Having performed this and sprinkled [the materials] with the five products of the cow while reciting the twelvefold vidyā,
one should place them to the south of the fire and offer oblations in the prescribed sequence as before.

Ghee [should be offered] with twelve names—those of the world-protectors (dikpatis) and Nārāyaṇa—beginning with "Tāra" and ending with "Huta," along with the names that will be mentioned hereafter. || 13.37 ||
All seeds, all elements, and all the worlds, as well as the mountains,
oceans, all sacred fords, rivers, and lakes.

Then, having offered oblations with the mantras beginning with "pātālāḥ" and ending with "vyāhṛti," [he should offer] the nāgas, the elephants of the quarters, and likewise the bulls, according to the very procedure for the *sampāta* [offering].
Having offered the clarified butter and placed that vessel before his hand,
the preceptor, facing eastward at night, should recite the mantra and meditate upon the earth.
After a short while, having obtained the permission of the twice-born, and with the sounding of musical instruments and the like,
he meditated upon Śakti, worshipped her, and reflected that this [universe] had become the embryo within her.
Having meditated upon the bright earthly egg of Brahmā as a dwelling for the manifestation of forms,
one should slowly recite the mantra within it, as before, over the earth.
O bearer of all beings! O beloved one! O you adorned with mountains for breasts!
O goddess whose garment is the ocean, take refuge in this womb! 13.43.
When the embryo has been thus deposited, there shall be happiness everywhere;
then, having given gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should cause a temple to be built.
Having established the door-keepers as before below, and having worshipped the Vāstu deity in due order,
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and, after touching [the site], deposit gems and other substances according to one's capacity.

Having covered the door with two cloths washed with cow-products and other substances, having worshipped it well with perfumes and other offerings, and having performed the rites of pacification and oblations; 13.46.
The wise man should establish [the image] for a moment, having released it from the center to the center;
he should place the *ātmatattva* below and the *vidyātattva* on the two branches.
And that supreme reality (paratattva) is situated within the center of the well-formed cavity;
one should then establish it with the syllable Om (praṇava) and worship it again in due order.
Stability, immeasurability, pervasiveness, awakening, eternity, indestructibility,
and contentment— these seven should be offered in sequence as seven oblations.
The deities such as the Pratīhāras who are stationed there should be offered oblations here by their names, and then their sacrificial offering (bali) should be given.
In the arrangement of walls, pillars, and so forth, one must by all means avoid injuring veins, vital points (*marmans*), and the like; otherwise, there will be a disturbance of the site.

Having led [the thread] slightly to the north or to the east, one should place the pillars and other elements according to the measurement of the veins and so forth; in this way, the defect of piercing (vedhadoṣa) does not arise.
The [liṅga] situated on a bull should face east, and that situated on a banner should face west;
otherwise, there will be total destruction due to defects in the site—of this there is no doubt. (13.53)
The eastern gate should be in the center of the village, as should those to the west and north;
however, a western gate is generally preferred for the south, east, and southeast.
One should have it made thirty cubits long, starting from three cubits in width, with seven stories at most and one at least; it may be circular or square, but it must be beautiful to behold.
Through the increase of the elements, Vāyu, Vahni, Indra, Varuṇa, Arka, Indu, and Viṣṇu are to be known as the deities of houses; they are the other forms of the earths.
The former yogis—whether lying down, sitting, standing, or walking—are to be known as the deities of the [four] quarters; those situated in the intermediate directions are the others. (13.57)
Varāha, Nārasiṃha, Śrīdhara, Hayānana, Rāma the son of Jamadagni, Vāmana, and Kṛṣṇa. (13.58)
Above that, one should fashion Vainateya in the four directions;
Brahmā should be in the center, Śiva at the end, and Hari himself in the pitcher.
At the end of the pitcher is Mahāviṣṇu, and Sadāviṣṇu is in front of him;
these are to be known as the images within the interior of the house, consisting of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme self.
One should know that the infinite *pāduka* is the Lord, the Sovereign of the Reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*).
Above this is the foundation of the Reality of Knowledge (*vidyātattva*), and likewise that which is beyond it.
Indra and the other [deities] are situated in the directions upon the altar; Viṣvaksena is in the spout.
From the sandals up to the feet, the shanks, and the thighs, extending to the end of the pedestal, is the *prati*; the waist is [the *kaṭi*].
The girdle is the waistband, the belly is the interior chamber, and the arms are the pillars;
the middle part is the navel, the heart is the pedestal, and the downward breath is the outlet for water.
The pedestal is the ego (ahaṃkāra), and the base (piṇḍikā) is said to be the intellect (buddhi).
At its end is the lotus, which is primordial nature (prakṛti); the image is traditionally held to be the Puruṣa.
The bell is the tongue, the lamp is the mind; the wood is the sinew, and the stone is the bone;
the plaster is the skin, the mortar is the flesh, and the liquid therein is the blood. (13.65)
The eye is on the side of the peak, while the crest-jewel (śikhā) should be at the tip of the banner;
the hand is the base-pitcher (talakumbha), and the door is known as the generative organ (prajanana).
The *śukanāsa* is called the nose; they know the *gavākṣa* as the ear; likewise, the *kapotālī* is the shoulder and the *āmalasāraka* is the neck. (13.67)

The jar, the head, clarified butter, marrow, speech, the mantra, the sprinkling, milk, the name, coldness, and so forth—these objects are situated within the letters, the sounds, and the incenses. (13.68)
The apertures, windows, the dwelling, and the plastering are the cavities;
the joints are to be known as the articulations, while the iron fastenings and nails are likewise [the joints]. (13.69)
Its hair and body hair should be understood as brushes made of wool;
its surrounding wall should be as high as the base of a palace. (13.70)
They know the maṇḍapa to be equal in height to the gopura minus one quarter;
the maṇḍapa for Garuḍa has a width double that of the pedestal (pīṭha).
There were as many palaces for the world-protectors and for Viṣvaksena;
behind Ananta and in the south-east was a sacrificial hall of equal size.
The abodes of the Mothers should be constructed to the south and likewise to the north;
all these dwellings should face westward and be situated toward Indra, Agni, and Īśa.
Those facing the Rakṣas, Varuṇa, and Vāyu should likewise face the east;
those in the south and north should be made so as to face the palace.
With eight middle-sized barley grains that are husked and not flattened,
the best [measure] is seven [of such grains], while the middling-inferior is six finger-breadths.
A cubit (hasta) is established by exactly as many finger-breadths (aṅgula) as there are syllables in the Gāyatrī; everything of the three kinds is intended to be measured by that. 13.76.
One should construct the width of the temple using stone, brick, wood, or even clay; however, one should avoid that which possesses defects.

Having abandoned a stone that is worn out, too small, from a Caṇḍāla's dwelling, pregnant, produced from impure soil, or otherwise inauspicious, one should take another auspicious one according to the requirements of its color.
The image is declared to be in the masculine gender, while the pedestal is remembered as being in the feminine;
however, the stone placed below the installation of the gems is considered to be neuter.
The worship should be performed in accordance with the house, or the house should be in accordance with the worship;
this same principle should be understood by the wise regarding the pedestal and other such elements as well. (13.80)

One should not have a Vaiṣṇava temple, a pedestal, or an image constructed using stones and other materials that are worn out or already in use; otherwise, it will result in malevolent magic (ābhicāra).
The bricks used here should not be old, discolored, or unburnt;
nor should they be hollow, naturally dried, fallen, or damaged by fire. (13.82)
Trees situated in wicked lands are pithless, corrupted, and likewise [unfit], such as those with bitter thorns, those inhabited by *piśācas*, and small shrines (*caityas*). (13.83)

One who knows the scriptures should not employ in his house those who have made their living by means of spears, needles, banners, pillars, wheels, or staffs; nor should he employ a person of the highest caste in a low occupation.
One should cause wooden parts such as those of a water-wheel to be made from the Kapittha tree or the Akṣa tree;
one should pull them by the root and not by the tip, nor should one join new wood to the best part.
One should not employ [the vessel] facing downward, nor likewise facing south;
for the subsequent sacrifice, the auspicious substances must indeed be placed face upward.
If the stone foundations and other auspicious elements beneath the palace are disturbed by chance,
then the original pedestal must be re-established as it was before.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Now, for the benefit of practitioners, I shall briefly describe the supreme characteristics of images, as well as the distinctions of their origins and postures. 14.1.

An image is to be known as being of seven kinds, according to the distinctions of precious stones, metals, stone, minerals, clay, wood, and painting; those made of precious stones and metals are faultless. (14.2)
That stone, however, possesses many defects; it is said to originate from the Meru mountain.
It is of four kinds: Vāruṇī, Aindrī, Āgneyī, and Vāyavī. (14.3)
Of the first two [types], that stone which is sunken in the earth—beautiful, glossy, and free from the rays of the sun—is faultless, but not so the other two. (14.4)
A stone that is of a single color, golden, well-proportioned, exceedingly beautiful, with the luster of a white lotus, and gentle—such a stone is to be taken for a Brāhmaṇa. (14.5)
The Aindrī [lunar mansion] is red and belongs to the Kula-sthā; for a Kṣatriya, it is Jyeṣṭhā.
For a Vaiśya, it is Bhaga-devatyā in Phalgunī, being either yellow or green.
In the asterism of Aśvinī, the voice is black, resembling mung beans; it belongs to a Śūdra and has the Aśvins as its presiding deities.
It is wide, not very thick, resonant with holes, and sweet-toned. (14.7)
A woman shaped like a plantain leaf would be cool and charming;
she who has a deep resonance, is weighty, firm, and emits sparks [of light]. (14.8)

One that resembles the leaves of the *aśvattha* or *vaṭa* tree, which is broad and thick, indicates a male; one with the appearance of both is a hermaphrodite; and one that lacks these qualities and resembles a *parpaṭa* leaf is female. (14.9)
With closely knit limbs, supple, with a steady voice and very cool, rich in fragrance, flavor, and touch—that young woman was most beautiful. (14.10)

A girl who is too young, unable to endure the touch of a weapon, soft, slippery, or as unstable as a tender sprout—whether she be a Caṇḍālī or one subject to toll—his mind finds no delight in her. (14.11)
For she was like a piece of a frog—old, coarse, and extremely worn out;
multicolored, very dark blue, smoky, and covered with thick hair.
One with a low voice and censurable limbs, who is hot-tempered, is known as a Caṇḍālikā;
she is like an anthill clinging to a tree, struck by fire, wind, and heat.
Standing near a funeral pyre or a shrine, standing in an outer line, or associating with outcasts;
possessed by spirits, discolored, or dwelling in water at a crossroads—(14.14)
It is fashioned elsewhere and refined by anyone who is skilled;
it possesses an interior, a circular frame, openings, joints, pins, and a lattice-work. (14.15)

A palm marked with eruptions, whirlpools, prominent veins, or knots is to be avoided; one with few lines is inferior, while one with many lines is superior; and that which has both [many lines and auspicious marks] is most excellent. (14.16)
The lines on Śilāsavarmā’s skin were golden and exceedingly beautiful;
they were as delightful as the rainbow, a banner, a lotus-bud, or a water-pot. (14.17)
It should be known as always bringing about prosperity and conferring welfare upon cows and Brahmins;
it is auspiciously marked by the Śrīvatsa, the conch, the discus, the lotus, and the clockwise-turning Nandyāvarta.
It resembled a gateway, a parasol, a garment, a bull, a maiden, a garland, and a flower;
it was like a palace, a svastika, a horse, an elephant, a prospering woman, and a fish.
A chariot, an eye, a finger, a tortoise, a chowrie, a goad, a lion,
jewel-ornaments, a cow, a tree, a leaf, the moon, the sun, and the stars.
Auspicious signs include a sacred thread, a water-pot, a mirror, a deer, a swan, and so forth;
however, if these appear broken into one, two, or many pieces, there will be the loss of a son, a lord, or a wife.
Those that are crooked, thick, thin, rough, or broken at the tip are not auspicious; likewise, a stone that is mottled or possesses many flaws is not desired for this purpose.

The letter *vṛddhi* (ai) causes the destruction of enemies, while *saṃvṛta* (a) is inauspicious; *vṛddhi* occurs among the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*), and *sampad* (prosperity) is found among the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*.
In the *yogavāha* letters, there is eradication (*uccāṭa*) at the beginning; in the *rādi* group, fear, nourishment, and pacification;
in the *ūṣman* letters, accomplishment; and in the last group, liberation. Horizontal lines, however, are inauspicious.
One should discard that [vessel] which, when opened while containing its contents, breaks with a dull sound; or that which is marked with circles and the like, is hot, or is discolored.
If, when the stone has been washed, nothing at all is perceived, that stone should be known as mediocre; it is inferior, being joined with both auspicious and inauspicious qualities.
Where there is a sound like that of a bell and sparks are constantly seen during the cutting, that is her head; its back is upward and its face is downward.
Whatever a twice-born man, a craftsman, or a consecrated maiden may say, that shall be the head; from that, one should fashion the face without hesitation.
For houses with doors facing east or west, the grass-blade should be taken with its tip pointing east or west;
if these are unavailable, it may have its tip pointing south or north, but one with a tip pointing toward a corner is not recommended.
Having first worshipped the deity upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should have the Brāhmaṇas recite benedictions;
then, on an auspicious day, having partaken of curd-rice preceded by protective rites and auspicious ceremonies.
Having worshipped the weapons with the Astra-mantra and having addressed auspicious words to them,
one should face either the east or the north while worshipping the weapons with the Astra-mantra.
Having observed auspicious signs and examined the omens,
the preceptor should go forth with the artisans for the purpose of the image.

Constantly meditating upon the Queen of Vidyās while standing before her with the water-offering (arghya) in hand, one should proceed when auspicious signs appear; otherwise, one should do so differently.
Once he has emerged, the maker should look at the stone from that time forward constantly;
he should have an image fashioned, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) until the completion of that work.
If such an auspicious stone is not found among the Somas, Indras,
or Īśvaras, one should proceed to Siddhaśilākara after again performing the sacrifice to the quarters.
Having surveyed the directions and performed the protection and auspicious rites with mantras,
the preceptor, being self-restrained, should perform the consecration there at night.
Having constructed a pavilion of stone and enclosed it on all sides,
he adorned it with banners of four colors in the four directions.
Having worshipped Hari and the deities of the quarters, he should offer a bali-oblation to the spirits and the cruel beings;
having fasted with his senses restrained upon a bed of darbha grass before the deity, he should remain there.
The preceptor, being well-established, should meditate upon Viṣṇu and utter the mantra:
"Salutation to Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Lord of all the worlds. (14.39)
"Salutation to the Lord of Dreams, who is all-pervading and possesses every form;
by means of this [mantra] recited one hundred and eight times, he then beholds a dream. (14.40)
If an auspicious dream occurs, it would be good; otherwise, a rite of pacification (śānti) should be performed.
Having recognized that the stone is beautiful, one should examine its color, its characteristic mark (liṅga), and likewise its head.
With the mantra "Awake! (udbudhyasva), the preceptor should mark it here and there with the weapon-mantra (astra); having done this, he should then have it taken up by artisans.
Having worshipped the gods, offered oblations, and performed the recitation of auspicious prayers,
he should then carefully place the stone upon the chariot and lead it forth with diligence.

One should perform a hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra over the chariot, its artisan, and its modifications; then, having circumambulated it amidst the sounds of banners and other instruments, one should place it in the northern part of the hall.
Having conceived the image of one [deity] upon a stone or even on a tree, one should not make another image; if made, it becomes fruitless. (14.45)
The primary [type of woman] is one who has produced herself; the middling is one purchased with wealth;
and the inferior is one who is pure and found in lakes and such places by those who know her limbs.
Just as one prepares a carving on stone, so should one proceed with the work of wood:
the *dārucandana*, *śamyāka*, *madhūka*, *āsana*, and *bilvaka* trees. (14.47)
The *sarala*, *spandana*, *sāla*, *stabaka*, *stambhaka*,
*timi*, *varaṇa*, *tinduka*, *aśoka*, *parṇī*, *panasa*, and *śiṃśapā* trees.
Other trees suitable for sacrifice are also excellent if they possess pith;
[the ideal tree] is straight, glossy, even, branchless, grown in a auspicious location, and dense.
A site that is not hollow, without wounds or cavities, and possesses firm roots is considered auspicious;
whereas one that slopes toward the south, is parched, burnt, or inhabited by birds and predatory animals is inauspicious.
One who has fallen [from caste] and one residing in a shrine, an anthill, a funeral pyre, or similar places, is not accepted;
however, having purified the lower part [of the body] and having strewn darbha grass all around, [the rite may proceed]. || 14.51 ||
Having sprinkled water from all sides purified by the Gāyatrī,
he should offer oblations with this very mantra using fuel-sticks from milk-exuding trees.
Let it be understood that whatever supreme Vaiṣṇava reality there is, and furthermore whatever Bhāgavata reality there is—all that is entirely contained within this body. 14.53.
May Dharma, merit, and likewise truth all abide together in one place.
O Tree! For the sake of the world’s peace, go to the auspicious abode of the gods.
There you shall attain divinity, free from burning and cutting,
through the offering of water and flowers, as well as with incense and ritual oblations.
The people will honor you, and through that you shall attain peace;
having worshipped with perfumes and flowers and offered the oblation as before.
Having seen a dream, having told it to a brahmin, and having described auspicious things, the reciter, facing either east or north, should mutter this verse: "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ. (14.57)
Having remembered the Astra-mantra, one should begin to cut with an axe smeared with honey and clarified butter;
by doing so during the day or at night, one shall surely remove its poison.
Its falling upon the lords of the soma [constellations] is auspicious; elsewhere it is not praised.
When this [pole star] is broken, one should perform a propitiatory rite through the offering of the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
One should purify the fallen tree with the *agnir āyāhi* mantra;
then, having fashioned it into a square, one should carry it away on a chariot as if it were a stone.
In this same manner, clay should be brought that is of the same color and free from defects; it should be taken from a sacred and beautiful site, with the words: "Thou art extracted. (14.61)
An earthen vessel that is uncooked is praised; one that is cooked here is censured.
[One should prepare it] with the powder mixed with the decoctions of *kapilā* ghee and linseed oil. (14.62)
Having repeatedly ground it together with śrīveṣṭaka and other ingredients,
and having allowed it to remain for a month or a fortnight, one should then fashion the image.
Having consecrated the image-pike in the principal pavilion according to the ritual rules,
and having first performed the deposition of jewels, the Guru should install it at an auspicious moment.
Having caused an image made of lac to be fashioned from iron and covered with clay, and having purified gold and other materials by melting them again like charcoal; 14.65.
One should have it made with effort by skilled artisans so that it is complete and dense on all sides.
An image made of gold is known to bestow nourishment, while one of silver is said to bestow fame.
One made of copper brings wealth and sons; one made of jewels bestows happiness;
one made of wood should be known as a bringer of prosperity; and one made of clay grants all desires.
An image may consist of a single piece of stone, metal, or precious gemstone; however, those consisting of many pieces are made of clay, wood, or even painted.
However, an image made of stone, wood, or clay should be installed in a temple;
any other image may be worshipped according to the prescribed rules either in a house or in a temple.

One should install and worship [the image] in a house at a height from the thumb up to a span; in a temple, however, it should be from one cubit upwards, but beyond that, it must be in a temple alone.
One should always worship the mobile [form] with both invocation and dismissal;
however, for a single installed image (ekabera), there is neither invocation nor dismissal.

Having fashioned an image of the deity made of metal, one cubit in height and with a beautiful face, its proportions corresponding to the root-mantra, and having purified it according to the prescribed rule; 14.72.
Having invoked [the deity] into it and worshipped it, one should release it again into the plastered area and so forth.
On the height of the door, reduced by one-eighth and divided into three parts, the image should occupy two parts.
Whether measuring one full ninth-part less, or the whole, or even three-quarters, that measurement is equal [in merit].
For a stone temple, this is the best measurement; for a wooden one, it would be middling. (14.74)
In the case of a gem, the lowest [image] is to be known; one may conceive of others according to one's desire.
An image ten tālas high is the best, while one nine tālas high is the middling. (14.75)
The goddesses should be known as being at least eight tālas in height; having divided the desired measurement into ten or nine parts, one should take a single part [as the unit]. (14.76)
Having divided [the height] into twelve parts, one should understand that by which it is measured as one's own finger-breadth (svāṅgula);
one should fashion [the proportions] from the neck to the heart, the navel, and the private organ according to the measurement of the face.
Having broken that [posture], one should place [the hands] evenly upon the head, throat, feet, and knees;
the shanks and thighs should be made double [in length], and the arms should hang down past the knees.
The upabāhus should be known as slightly less than that in measurement;
one should make the crown, the lotus, and the stalk according to their proper proportions.
One should arrange sixteen horizontal lines and seven vertical ones;
when the face has been divided into twelve parts by these horizontal and vertical lines, [the proportions are established].

The two eyes should be placed at the interval of one unit between the two feet, as specified in the *Keśapañcama-sūtra*, and they should be drawn with a width equal to the measurement of a single foot.
Between those two, the auspicious nose should be made twice the length of the eyes;
the pupils should be situated on the line between the corners of the mouth, and the nostrils should be equal in measure to the [outer] folds.

One should place the two ears upon the brow-line; the eyes should be as long as the distance between the brows; the pupils should be situated at one-third of that [distance], and the luminous points (jyotis) should be at one-third of those [pupils].
The tip of the nose is as high as the eye; its base is lower by half that amount.
The nostrils are like flat beans and are sunken; the space between the eyebrows is at the level of the middle of the eyes. (14.84)
The lower lip is equal to that [upper lip], and the gojikā (the upper lip's protrusion) is half its measure;
the length of the ear is like that of the nose, and its width is like that of its tip.
The two *tuṭukas* are situated at the eye-threads and are equal in measure to their width;
the width of the forehead and neck is considered to be double that of the nose.
The chin is twice as long as the distance from the root of the ear;
one should know that the face is twice as long as the space between the breasts, and likewise twice as long as the distance between the armpits.
The width at the region of the navel is desired to be exactly double that of the neck;
they know the distance between the breasts and the armpits to be two and one-third parts, with the eyes as the additional unit.
One should fashion the space between the armpit and the shoulder, with the shoulder raised;
the forearm, from the joint at the armpit to the tip of the nose, should be shaped like the hip. 14.89.
In that regard, one should fashion the measurement of the two middle fingers from the junction of the lower lip and the nose; likewise, the index and ring fingers should be less by half a joint.
Of those two [hands], with the thumb and little finger half-bent, the palms have a length exceeding that of the eyes, and their width is equal to their length.
In that position, the distance between the thumb and the index finger should be equal to the span of the eyes;
the distance between the middle finger and the little finger should be equal to the space between the wrist and the base of the little finger.
The wrist is like the nose, and the distance from there to the tip of the thumb is likewise;
the width of the forearm is twice that, and the elbow is one eye-measure less.
Everywhere it has a triple circumference; its two arms are beautiful like the tail of a cow; the middle and the rear joints are equal, while the remaining parts are half that size.

The joints of the ring finger and the middle finger should be reduced by one-eighth from that [length], while those of the little finger should be reduced by one-quarter; these should be applied according to proportion.
The two thumb joints should be level with the joints of the ring finger and the middle finger;
the nails on all fingers should be made to end at half the length of the uppermost joint.
The day [measure] for the thumb is not less than one-eighth of the nose; for the other two [fingers], it is likewise reduced.
Thus, when the circle of the little finger is equal to the forearm, the buttocks [are properly formed].
The thighs were slightly less than the face; the knees and shanks were half the length of the face;
the feet were as long as the face, and in front, they were level with the shanks. (14.98)
When raised like a tortoise, the two big toes are successively higher, each being half the height of the one preceding it;
the two fore-toes are equal to those, and the remaining toes are shorter, each being less than the nail of the one before it.
The nails are without a thumb-nail joint, red like half-moons, and without a ridge;
the thumb is as long as the middle finger, and the index finger is as long as the thumb. (14.100)
One should fashion the others in due proportion, each reduced by one-eighth in succession:
the ear-lobes, the hair, the ornaments, the garments, and the weapons.
And the arrangement [of the eyes] should be applied according to the specific characteristics by one who understands them:
the eyes should be large, white, coppery, and possessed of eyelashes. (14.102)
The vision of those who behold it would be as if common, neither ascending nor descending;
or else, having had such a painting made upon a cloth, the practitioner himself [should worship] that cloth. (14.103)
Having established it in a solitary place, one should worship it daily with devotion;
the height of the pedestal should be half the height of the image, and its length according to the measurement of the image.
The reservoir should be equal in size to the face up to the hairline, resembling a lotus;
however, for a movable vessel, a pedestal larger than six finger-breadths is not desired.
A [liṅga] made of metal must not be less than two finger-breadths in height and should be of a single substance;
a stone liṅga is to be understood as being otherwise, while those born of jewels are indeed made of metal.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter of the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Now I shall explain in brief, in due order, the ritual for consecration (pratiṣṭhā), which must especially be performed with the mantras beginning with Parameṣṭhin. 15.1.
Sthāpanā, tāpanā, and likewise saṃsthāpanā, as well as prasthāpanā together with pratiṣṭhāpanā—these five are declared. (15.2)
The fivefold activity pertaining to those who are standing, sitting, lying down, moving in a vehicle, or walking— which has been described in five ways— is proclaimed as *pratiṣṭhā*.
The image should be gentle in its standing posture, likewise gentle when seated;
it may be fierce in the reclining posture, or otherwise one may arrange it according to one's desire. (15.4)
The form is sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasic respectively;
it may be white, red, black, dark-blue, or indeed all colors at once. (15.5)
The divine form of the Supreme Self remains established; however, another [form] is perceived as seated, joined with a slight degree of humanity. (15.6)
Viṣṇu is the pervader in the standing posture; he is both the pervaded and the pervader in the sitting posture;
and he is to be known as the pervaded in the reclining posture—these are the deities of the three daily libations.
On his two sides were Brahmā and Rudra, with the Sun and the Moon near them;
at his back were Śrī and Sarasvatī, and on his sides were Śānti and Rati.
On its back, he stood with ten arrows aimed at Varāha and Hayagrīva;
likewise, on its sides, he struck Aja, Bhṛgu, and Dakṣa, as well as Rudra, Agni, and Manu.

Seated, he was surrounded by twelve [attendants]: Sanatkumāra and Skanda, those who have attained perfection while remaining in their respective stations, and those whose hands are joined in the añjali gesture.
He was lying down with Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and him who resides in the navel-lotus;
he was accompanied by the five [attendants] and honored by Mārkaṇḍeya standing before him.
Of all these [elements] mentioned as being of three kinds,
one should arrange whichever ones serve as the retinue for the vehicle in due order, according to one's desire.
Likewise, he was surrounded by his common attendants bearing bows, maces, discs, conchs, swords, arrows, plows, shields, and lotuses.
The deity may stand with four arms or sit with eight arms;
for one who is reclining, the arms may be joined according to one's desire, or in all cases, they may be arranged as desired.
These five extremely subtle divine powers, which are the five Upaniṣads, are celebrated by the exponents of the Vedas under the term "five tanmātras. (15.15)
Since these five powers joined together are the causes of all things,
he alone, endowed with these five, proceeds at the beginning of creation.
The Lord, though himself inactive, effects both restraint and favor;
for he whose sovereign power is complete acts thus in all matters, such as establishing [the world], and not otherwise.

Due to the distinction between the subordinate and the primary [qualities], a fivefold division is to be understood as existing only within the powers that are conjoined; it does not exist individually, because they do not abide separately.
"The connection with various effects and instruments is the cause of experience;
so say others, as are its powers along with their respective effects and instruments. (15.19)
Therefore, those [mantras] should be employed in combination by preceptors who are skilled in consecration and have mastered the tantras, for the sake of attaining mastery over the image. 15.20.
Therefore, the classification into *sthāpanā* and so forth may also arise from the arrangement of the image;
those who know this [teach] that the statement of these divisions is solely for the purpose of indicating their relative importance. 15.21.
Furthermore, within that subtle and common body composed of the five powers (pañcaśakti),
his forms are recorded as manifold, according to the distinctions of the primary limbs and their specific parts.
The bed should be placed in a palace that is either circular or square; otherwise, it should be used by those who are standing, sitting, or about to depart.
Whether at that time or at any other, the consecration for the sake of liberation should be performed;
however, it should be carried out during the northern course of the sun and in the bright fortnight for the sake of liberation.
It is also recommended under Punarvasu, Aśvinī, Śravaṇa, Puṣya, Hasta, the three Uttaras, Revatī, Rohiṇī, Svātī, and Bharaṇī. (15.25)
The second, the fifth, the tenth, the thirteenth, the full moon day, and the twelfth—these are the lunar days (tithis) for the practice. (15.26)
Soma, Bṛhaspati, Bhārgava, and likewise Budha—these are the gentle planets (saumyagrahāḥ) to be employed in consideration of the day of the week and the rising of the signs. || 15.27 ||

The sowing of the seedlings should take place on an auspicious day, either on the seventh, the ninth, or even earlier than that; or it may be on the fifth day, accompanied by the sprinkling of the three worlds and worship.
Three kinds of vessels are prescribed for sowing the seeds of auspiciousness:
the *pālikā*, the *ghaṭikā*, and the *śarāva*, according to their distinctions. (15.29)
The lords of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva are faultless in all rites;
twelve or sixteen *pālikās* should be taken for each of them. (15.30)
They are twenty-five finger-breadths in height, and their mouth is sixteen finger-breadths wide;
the pedestal is six finger-breadths [in width] and four finger-breadths in height, with a joint of one finger-breadth between them.
The measurement of the *ghaṭikā* is sixteen or twelve finger-breadths;
it has five faces, measured by four finger-breadths in each of the cardinal directions and upwards.
The pedestal is like that of the *pālikā*;
its stalk is four finger-breadths [in height], while the shallow bowl (*śarāva*) is one *tāla* in height and has a pedestal of four finger-breadths.
Having tripled the vessels and placed them with great care in a well-protected northern location, from the southeast to the northeast.
Filled with soft sand and cow-dung, each succeeding one higher than the last,
they are adorned with dūrvā grass and other plants, and placed upon bundles of grain.
Barley, mung beans, sesame, rice, black gram, peas, horse-gram, and lentils, together with millet, mustard, śyāmāka, kidney beans, and adzukis.
One should wash these auspicious items with the twelve-syllable mantra, after first having the Brāhmaṇas proclaim a "day of merit" (puṇyāha) and recite blessings (svasti). || 15.37 ||
The attentive Guru should sequentially deposit the seed-syllables within them using the eight-syllable mantra, proceeding clockwise according to the previously mentioned order.
Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one! Salutations to you, the creator of the universe!
O Subrahmaṇya, may there be salutations to you; salutations, O Primordial Puruṣa!
With that same mantra ending in "namas" and preceded by the three *tārakas*,
he should sprinkle [the disciple] during the three daily libations with water scented with *hāridra* while holding a *kūrca* in his hand, in the prescribed order.
One should worship those [vessels] with the names of the deities and with fragrant flowers.
The deities of the vessels have been declared; now hear those of the seeds. (15.41)
Brahmā, Rudra, and Hari are to be worshipped respectively in barley, mustard, and mung beans; Vāyu is to be worshipped in the case of *niṣpāva* beans, and Skanda in the case of *priyaṅgu*.
Indra resides in the māṣa beans, Agni in the kuluttha, Arka in the śāli rice, Yama in the sesame seeds,
Varuṇa in the rājamāṣa beans, Śrī in the āḍhakī, and the Moon in the śyāmāka grain.
Having worshipped within the mandalas provided with kusha grass according to the sequence of the eight directions,
one should offer the bali-oblation, accompanied by water, to the Lords of Night (Rātrīśas) ending with their attendants (pārṣadas).
One should first offer a bali-oblation to the spirits that delights them, consisting of husks, powdered turmeric, parched grain, curd, and roasted barley flour. 15.45.
One should offer the second portion, pertaining to the ancestors, consisting of rice mixed with sesame seeds;
then, one should present the bali-offering to the Yakṣas using grains, udumbara fruits, and wild rice.
On the fourth night, the wise man should indeed offer the Nāga-bali, consisting of coconut milk, parched grain flour, and rice flour, all mixed together.
One should offer the fifth oblation to Brahmā, accompanied by lotus flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata);
one should present the sixth oblation to Śiva with sacrificial porridge (caru) joined with cakes (apūpa).
Rice mixed with sugar is for Viṣṇu; immediately after that, as the seventh, one should likewise offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and rice with sesame (kṛsara) as the eighth and ninth.
Having become pure, with a self restrained and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should offer an oblation every night; thereafter, one should perform the ritual bath.
Having given [the materials] on the morning of the ritual day, one should subsequently employ them in the rite;
here, only the Guru himself should enter, and no one else whatsoever under any circumstances. (15.51)
One should diligently avoid all impure things, such as food remnants;
moreover, one should not perform the rite of the *pālikās* there without having first offered the *bali* oblation.

Since the offering of the bali alone is fruitless, the planting of the sprouts must by all means be performed with effort along with the bali-offering by those who are most excellent in their direction. 15.53.
At the commencement of the rites, one should place vessels containing well-sprouted sprouts at the bases of the pillars within the pavilion, which are filled with grain.
If they are dark, there will be loss of wealth; if red, conflict is certain;
if slanted, there will be disease; and if unformed, death shall occur. (15.55)
It is auspicious when the lines are yellowish, white, even, upward-pointing, and straight.
Therefore, with every effort, these must always be guarded by those who are unwearied.
From the time the sprouts begin to grow,
one should daily sweep the village streets and sprinkle them thoroughly on all sides.

Having diligently expelled from there atheists, the insane, heretics, those who have fallen [from their caste], those initiated [for improper rites], and the impure, he should collect the materials for the sacrifice.
Having constructed a square pavilion in front of the palace,
adorned with canopies and the like, provided with four gates, and well-furnished with all necessary equipment.
Then there were four archways, each five cubits high;
eight banners, nine flags, and the ninth bearing the emblem of Tārkṣya.
One should take palaces of wide extent and height, banners ten *dhanus* long with ten doors,
and auspicious jars made of gold or other precious materials, or even those made of clay, all new.
A large iron vessel, as well as a water-jar with a capacity of one droṇa, four vessels each with a capacity of one prastha, and beautiful sacrificial pots. || 15.62 ||
He brought the vessel for clarified butter and the *praṇītā* water-vessel, as well as fuel-sticks, *darbha*, and *kuśa* grass;
and two other vessels made of gold and silver, each with a capacity of two handfuls.
And other items for the purpose of the *arghya* offering and so forth, as well as weapons made of metal resembling lotuses, and others made of pure gold.
A tortoise, a garuḍa, and a lotus, as well as various jewels,
metals, minerals, seeds, and sacrificial implements such as the darvī, sruva, juhū, and sruc ladles.
Clay pots, threads, colored powders, and flowers; fragrances, guggulu resin, oils, curd, milk, molasses, and honey. 15.66
Cow-derived ghee for the purpose of the fire-oblation, as well as cow-dung and urine;
blankets, skins, and couches, along with a new and auspicious bed.
It was provided with two pillows and both sides of the headrest,
covered with a white spread and various kinds of garments.
A tawny cow with her calf, pure, with horns adorned with gold and yielding abundant milk, as well as four other Surabhi cows and auspicious milking vessels. (15.69)
He also provided astringent decoctions, tree barks, and all kinds of materials for the fire-oblation,
as well as beautiful ornaments and lotus-stalks with their sprouts.
Various kinds of herbs beginning with dūrvā grass, sweet fruits, roots for use as unguents and the like, and a golden sacred thread (yajñopavīta). 15.71.
The eight auspicious and pure items: a water-pot (kuṇḍikā) and a sprinkling-vessel (vardhanī), dry fuel, lamps, thread, grains, and rice.
Likewise, he provided four kinds of musical instruments, as well as singers and dancers, and especially peaceful Brahmins who were knowers of the Vedas and devotees of Viṣṇu. || 15.73 ||
[He honored] those who knew the science of grammar and logic, those who knew the application of Vedic rituals,
those who knew the auspicious moments, those who knew the divisions of time, those observing vows, and those who recited the mantras.
He should observe the ascetics of pure knowledge and especially the Takṣakas;
having seen everything, both what has been said and what has not been said, he should carry it out in action.
All the implements for sacrifice, and especially the locations and so forth—all these would become defiled by use; therefore, everything should be new and auspicious.
Purity for worldly purposes is achieved merely by washing away dirt;
however, for the worship of the gods, the bath prescribed in the scriptures serves to purify the body. (15.77)
In worldly transactions and in other treatises on dharma,
the purifications prescribed therein should be adopted by a wise devotee of Viṣṇu.
They know that digging and other such acts are for the purification of defiled ground;
however, even ground that is already pure should be smeared with cow dung for the sake of sacrifice.
That fresh ghee produced from a cow, situated on the ground, well-strained even from milk and the like, melted, purified, and especially fragrant and desirable—[is to be used]. (15.80)
Having smeared the ground and struck it with the Astra-mantra, one should wash one’s hand and touch [the site];
having sprinkled it with unbroken rice grains and white mustard seeds, one should scatter them—this is the purification of the place. || 15.81 ||
Copper is purified by water with the paste of *āmla* (tamarind), gold by water, silver by house-soot or by the embers of straw. (15.82)
Silver is purified by ash, and conch-shells and the like by salt;
fruit-vessels by earth and water, but wooden ones by planing. (15.83)
But earthen objects may either be burned or replaced with new ones;
for all such things, purification is declared to consist in the removal of stains and odors. (15.84)

Having meditated upon the light consisting of the mantra within water that contains kusha grass, is rich with fragrance and flowers, and has been consecrated by the Tārā-mantra, one performs the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), which is the purification of the ritual substances.
Water that is free from salt and impurity, pure, abundant, originating from rivers and such sources, delicious in taste, and untouched by the wicked—such water is fit for all ritual acts. (15.86)
An image made of metal is purified like a vessel; one made of stone is cleansed with powders;
and the purification of a wooden image, as well as one that is painted, is achieved through the removal of impurities.
The cleansing of gems is like that of minerals, while that of stones is like [that of] rock;
having thus purified and gathered them, one creates [the deity] and performs the ritual identification with its limbs.
A non-stationary image is purified [by bathing], while a stationary one is purified by ablutions and the like;
likewise, items such as *kuśa* grass are purified simply by wiping or by washing.

Seated upon a seat of sacred grass (darbha) below the place of worship, the wise one, with darbha grass in hand, [should sprinkle] with water from a vessel (kūrca) empowered by the splendor of the mantra. (15.90)
One should purify everything by sprinkling water and by means of tearing [the skin] and other such acts;
furthermore, the ritual placement (nyāsa), the sacred syllable Om (praṇava), and darbha grass are recommended for the purification of mantras. 15.91.
The counting of repetitions, the mudrā, and meditation are proclaimed;
likewise, speech characterized by truthfulness, kindness, and benefit, as well as knowledge and contentment of mind. (15.92)
For all [practitioners], devotion alone is to be known as the singular purifier.
[This includes] land-born [flowers] such as the oleander (karavīra) and so forth, and water-born [flowers] such as the lotus (kamala) and so forth. 15.93.
One should offer fresh, fragrant flowers that have not yet been plucked—whatever is yellow or white in color and brought with purity. (15.94)
A flower that has not been plucked by hand, which is unfaded, and which has fallen naturally, may be accepted;
however, one that is perforated, still in bud, withered, fallen to the ground, or devoid of its stalk should be rejected.

That which remains after being tasted, that which lacks fragrance, that which is mixed with hair, insects, and the like, as well as flowers found even in times of distress, and likewise those fallen upon the leaves of the Arka plant, must be rejected.
If one should touch flowers that are forbidden, even if he has bathed well, he must bathe again;
if he is unable to do so, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and worship the Lord.
Either the wife herself, or the son, or a disciple should gather the flowers;
with clean hands, placing them in a suitable vessel, she should cover it and set it in a place not exposed to the sun. (15.98)
One should worship with night-blooming flowers at night, and likewise with day-blooming flowers during the day;
however, in times of distress, worship according to what is available at the time that presents itself is praised.
Even if it lacks fragrance, whatever is praised— such as the mandāra, pītaka, koraṇḍaka, and so forth— that too should be accepted, provided it is devoid of girikarṇī and similar plants.
Of dūrvā grass, apāmārga, bhadrā, tṛṇa, sīgu, gandhapūrṇa, tamāla, aśvattha, bilva, śamī, kuśa, and palāśa. || 15.101 ||
He also ate the leaves of the *dhātakī*, *brāhmī*, and *bhṛṅga* plants like flowers,
as well as the sprouts of barley, *priyaṅgu*, *niṣpāva*, mung beans, black gram, and chickpeas.
In the absence of flowers, one should prepare [offerings] from well-gathered tips of uncut [grass or leaves].
A flower grown in one's own garden is the best; that gathered from the forest is middling. (15.103)
The fruit for the giver is inferior when purchased for an image;
it is the same whether received separately or together with flour, sugar, sandalwood, moonstone, and gold. (15.104)
Or he should worship with artificial, auspicious fragrances devoid of animal parts,
or with the wood of the sāl, sarja, purāṇa, sevya, and indrayava trees.
One should offer incense combined with clarified butter and other substances in an auspicious vessel;
or one should offer a lamp with oil, clarified butter, or, in times of distress, with the resinous exudation of wood.

Provided with a wick made of thread, ignited by the breath from the mouth, [it should be offered] with pure, unhusked, and non-sweated grains of *śāli* rice that have been washed three times. (15.107)
One should offer cooked food accompanied by ghee and side dishes, as well as sweet fruits that are ripened in their season and free from defects. (15.108)
If these are not available, one should worship with flowers alone, or with water, or even mentally.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter of the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Now I shall explain, in brief and in due order, the purification of the image (bimbaśuddhi).
First, one should select a preceptor (ācārya), and thereafter have the rites performed. 16.1
A deity should be known to be of two kinds: stationary and mobile;
an image is the stationary deity, and likewise, the preceptor is the mobile deity.
The Blessed One, compassionate toward his devotees, accepts the worship of those two, which is preceded by ritual and mantras; for Hari does not accept worship from anyone else.
An action should be performed by one who understands only with the teacher’s approval;
through that very worship, the God becomes a granter of boons, and not otherwise.

Refined by initiations and other rites, tranquil, learned, free from anger, youthful, observant of the rules of conduct, eloquent, and endowed with the virtues appropriate to his caste and stage of life. (16.5)
The preceptor must be accepted in every way by the sacrificer during the installations and other rites—by one who is wise, of auspicious appearance, and free from all diseases. (16.6)
A deity should be installed by a learned householder for the sake of spiritual success;
[the officiants] should be of noble birth, pure, skillful, initiated, and masters of the Tantras.
Devout, skillful, and humble Brahmins are known as the bearers of the [divine] forms;
they should not eat in a temple, in a house, on a riverbank, in a cow-pen, or at the foot of a tree.
Or else, in another auspicious place, free from the sight of wicked people, smeared with cow dung and purified with the five products of the cow and other substances. (16.9)
On a seat covered with cloth and furnished with darbha grass, he [should approach] the requested guru together with four,
eight, or twelve image-keepers (mūrtipas).
Having seated him according to the rule, one should then honor him with water for the feet and other offerings,
on kusha grass with its tips pointing eastward in the north-eastern direction.
The sacrificer, having become pure, should set out the articles of worship and the auspicious vessels along with the kūrca-grass mats, accompanied by the syllable Om (praṇava). 16.12.
Having sprinkled the garments, the pair of earrings, and the auspicious ornaments with water consecrated by the *kūrca* grass, he should place them face upwards in their proper order.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the grass mats with the *praṇava* alone, one should arrange the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and so forth,
using the tips of *kuśa* grass, barley, white mustard seeds, sesame, black gram, fruits, and unbroken rice grains.
Having prepared the *arghya* with milk, fragrance, and flowers, one should worship it;
likewise, one should provide water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) in two other vessels.
Furthermore, one should consecrate these with the root-mantras and the limb-mantras, or with the form-mantras;
then, having restrained one's speech, one should offer *kūrca* grass-bunches for their seats.

One should wash the feet with water containing a purifier while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra; one should offer the water for sipping (ācamana) with the Śiras-mantra, and the water for respectful offering (arghya) with the Śikhā-mantra.
One should present pairs of garments and ornaments to the remaining two;
having honored them according to the prescribed rite and bowed down, one should feed them milk-rice with clarified butter.
Having saluted and propitiated the preceptor who has sipped water and wears a turban,
one should give gold and other gifts as available while recollecting the deity.
Having likewise given [gifts] to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), he should request them after prostrating before them;
having stated the purpose according to the rule, he should honor them again individually.
Having gratified them with pleasant words and having bowed down, he should then make this request:
"May you, who have been fully honored by me here and satisfied with sacrificial fees... (16.21)
"Let a sacrifice to Viṣṇu be performed for me; I pray that he be gracious.
Having said this, she should choose [the groom] in due order, taking him by the right hand.
In that regard, the preceptor should say, "Om, I shall do so.
Thus, indeed, in all sacrifices, one should diligently worship the guru.
Having prostrated before those officiating priests and offered them the arghya water, the wise man should choose them;
likewise, he should choose again those who are experts in the ritual manuals (tantra), as well as the initiated ones and the performers of the fire-oblations.
The patron of the sacrifice should appoint those who are pure reciters of mantras and students of the Vedas, who remain steadfast in the word of their teacher.
Beginning with the selection of the building site and ending with the ritual bath at a sacred ford, one should perform all this with devotion, as if worshipping Hari himself. 16.26.
Having first placed the well-examined image upon the bed,
and having honored the artisans there with gifts of wealth, one should proceed.
One should cause the opening of the eyes to be performed by those who are satisfied, according to the prescribed rite;
the grasping of the image’s gaze must be performed with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having uttered the *praṇava* with a protracted tone (*pluta*), he should then touch her on the feet;
first washing them with water, he should rub them thoroughly with *darbha* grass. (16.29)
Having touched it with cow-hair, he should then wash it while it is smeared with ghee;
then, into the consecrated fire, he should offer grains mixed with Śamī leaves.
One should offer oblations one hundred times each with the mantras beginning with *bhūḥ* and ending with *satya*;
for Viṣṇu is the gross body (*sthūladeha*), as seen in the Vedic revelation concerning the Vairāja. (16.31)
Therefore, when the oblation has been thus offered, the image of Viṣṇu becomes complete;
then, the Brahmins should pronounce the benediction (svasti) while reciting the Śākuna Sūkta.
Having placed dūrvā grass and unbroken grains upon the head with the syllable Om while remaining composed,
he should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and display auspicious objects.
When the afternoon had arrived, the preceptor, accompanied by the image-bearers,
went to a river, a pond, or a delightful natural pool.
Alternatively, having worshipped Varuṇa again in a vessel filled with water,
one should prepare a bank adorned with a banner, purified and enclosed on all sides.
Having withdrawn the fire and meditated upon the image through the path of reabsorption,
he covered it with darbha grass and cloths and placed it upon a wooden board.
Accompanied by the sounds of conchs and drums and shouts of victory,
while recollecting the seat of yoga as a sphere of light, one should place it within the waters.
Having visualized the world-protectors outside [the mandala] and protected [the image] with the five mantras,
one should thus place the image in water for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) with its head facing east.
For three nights he should carry a stone, for one night iron, and for one night a jewel;
having bathed, sipped water, become pure, and adorned with garments and ornaments. (16.39)
Having approached the temple together with the image-makers and performed circumambulation,
he— pure and facing east— performed the rites of installation and so forth in due order on the right side.
One should thoroughly cleanse the palace immediately after it has been cleared by the carpenters,
having encircled it on all sides with a measuring-line and a cord of darbha grass.
Having surveyed the inner chamber once more with the "weapon-vision," he should sprinkle it with water cleansed by the *kuśa* grass-mantra and smear it with fragrant scents.
One should again scatter mustard seeds, unbroken rice grains, and dūrvā grass all around;
then, having sprinkled [the area] with the Astra-mantra, one should likewise perform the three claps of the hands (tālatraya).
One should scatter durvā grass, unbroken rice, and tips of kuśa grass with the five powers (śaktis),
using resin, śrāveṣṭa, lac, lotus, white lodhra, fruits, and so forth.
Having offered incense with a lamp everywhere using the eight-syllable mantra,
and having placed a full water-pot and grain, one should discharge the flower-weapon.
Having prepared [the ground] on all sides with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Rākṣoghna hymn,
and having sprinkled it with water while reciting the Cakra mantra, [one should perform the rite] upon a surface smeared with cow dung.
One should begin the fire-oblation on a sacrificial mound in the southeast according to the prescribed rule;
one should offer the cooked clarified butter with the two mantras beginning with "rakṣohaṇa."

One should perform [the rite] further with the eighteen [verses] beginning with "kṛṇuṣva," with the five beginning with "yad devāḥ," with those beginning with "jātavedas," and likewise in sequence with the vyāhṛtis. || 16.48 ||
Then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations of apāmārga wood with the Cakra mantra, he should complete the rite by offering clarified butter as the sacrificial oblation.

Having brought [the materials] in a vessel with a cloth, together with the ashes from the fire-oblation, the remainder of the clarified butter, the remainder of the water, and the juices of apāmārga; || 16.50 ||
Then, one should recite the wheel-mantra one hundred and eight times;
having sprinkled [water] everywhere in the temple with branches of the *palāśa* and *aśvattha* trees.
One should subsequently scatter barley and mustard seeds with the hymns beginning with "kṛṇuṣva," and again perform the triple clapping of the hands as well as the enclosure of fire.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times again, one should worship the wheel and the pit;
having done this, one should then feed the Brahmins at night with food that destroys demons.
Having established that very fire upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains,
one should place a water-pot upon a previously prepared mound covered with cloth.
One should place therein water filled with bunches of kuśa, dūrvā, and śamī leaves, along with jātī flowers and gold; according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the propitiatory worship.

Then, having offered oblations of cooked food with the ritual substances such as water for the feet in their proper order, and with the verse "śanno devī" and the two mantras beginning with "vāstoṣpate," he should offer oblations of clarified butter.
One should offer oblations with the six mantras beginning with "vāstoṣpate dhruva," with the five mantras beginning with "jāta," with the group of "śam" mantras, and likewise with the vyāhṛtis.
One should offer oblations of śamī wood, ghee, rice, and clarified butter with that same verse;
then one should conclude with dūrvā grass and roots together with products of the cow.
Then, one should offer the remnants of the oblation upon the *kuśa* grass in front of the fire;
with water and clarified butter, one should perform the sprinkling while reciting the *vipra-yajus* mantra beginning with "namo rudrebhyaḥ. (16.59)

One should perform the recitation for well-being (svastivācana) accompanied by water for peace (śāntitoya), and together with the image-keepers (mūrtipās), one should cause the declaration of "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) and "May there be welfare and stability" (śivaṃ vāstu) to be uttered.
Thereafter, one should feed twelve excellent Brahmins with milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having established [the deities] within the purified pavilion, the Ṛgveda and the others are to be placed upon the internal pillars.
And at the gates, there were well-proportioned archways in due order:
the one named Suśobhana was made of aśvattha wood, and the one named Subhadra was made of udumbara wood.
With the mantra "syonā pṛthivi," he should scatter sesame seeds along with rice grains at the Nyagrodha tree called Sukarman, at Suhotra, and likewise at the Plakṣa tree. || 16.63 ||
Having consecrated it with the mantra "ucchrayasva" (Arise!), one should worship it while circumambulating to the right;
in the directions [the colors are] yellow, reddish, dark, black, clear, and blackish-white.
Padmavarṇa and Citra—these eight banners should be established in due order;
as well as Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana. (16.65)
Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita—
these are the deities presiding over the banners who are to be worshipped.
Surrounded individually by many crores of bhūtas and saṃghas,
one should worship after placing two full jars at each door.
First, Pūrṇa and Puṣkara were to be worshipped in waters of ruby and coral;
then likewise, Ānanda and Nandana in waters containing beryl and lotuses.
Vīrasena and Suṣeṇa were appointed over Nīla and Marataka,
while Sambhava and Prabhabha were placed over Muktā and Sphaṭikatoya.
Having first performed the worship of the site (vāstupūjā), as well as the worship of the arches and banners,
the demarcation of the ground and the consecration of the fire are prescribed to follow immediately thereafter.
The verses beginning with "trātāram indram" and "yad ulūkaḥ" and "imaṃ me gantum" are the mantras proclaimed here for the worship of the pitchers of the guardians of the directions.

The Bahvṛcas, Adhvaryus, Chandogas, and Atharvaṇas— these twice-born ones, who know the true meaning of the treatises on dharma, are traditionally prescribed for the recitation of the entire Veda (pārāyaṇa) in the various directions.
Those who know the true meaning of historical narratives and are most excellent in the knowledge of Brahman—
such image-priests (mūrtipāḥ) should be appointed in the corners for the oblations in due order.
Each reciting his own sacred lore, they remained awake at night with their minds fixed upon that [task],
on a svastika-marked spot where grain had been sown and eight blades of kuśa grass were placed.
One should prepare the bed there with the twelve-syllable mantra;
one should place eight water-pots in order around the pedestal.
All of them were filled with water, placed within heaps of grain, auspicious, with their openings covered by sprouts, and wrapped with thread and cloth. || 16.76 ||
One should worship these with scents and flowers using the eight syllables individually;
having fashioned the yoga-pīṭha here, one should worship it up to the Śakti.
One should offer all kinds of grains and flowers around the perimeter of the pedestal;
here, the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyādhipatis) are to be worshipped on all sides.
Then he placed Viṣṇu in the eastern quarter, Madhusūdana in the southern,
Trivikrama in the western, and Vāmana likewise in the northern.
Likewise, one should place Śrīdhara in the southeast, Hṛṣīkeśa in the southwest,
Padmanābha in the northwest, and Dāmodara in the remaining [northeast] direction.
To the northeast of that pedestal, one should place a water vessel;
wearing a turban and an upper garment, and remaining silent, one should filter the water.
With a new, hairless cloth sprinkled with water while reciting the mantra,
one should fill the vessel with flower-water using the *praṇava* itself.
Having filled [the vessel], one should worship it with the twelve-syllable vidyā;
it must be protected by canopies and the like, properly covering it on all sides.
One should arrange auspicious vessels containing the sprouts of auspiciousness,
as well as a conch, a discus, a banner, the śrīvatsa mark, a mirror, and a bull.
A pair of fish and a water-pot are declared to be auspicious signs;
one should construct a square pavilion on the northeast side, equal on all sides.
It was four cubits in extent with four pillars, provided with a central pedestal,
and equipped with bathing materials filled in jars in their proper order.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the eight-syllable mantra,
