he should touch the jars with the residual ghee and consecrate them with mantras.
Having brought all the images there in their proper order, beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāṃ hariṇīm," one should bathe them in the case of a single-liṅga shrine.
When an image made of plaster is being fashioned after the previous installation of jewels has been performed,
another image made of metal must be produced for the sake of the ritual work.
One should perform the installation, the placement of the mudrās, and so forth, upon the primary image (mūlārcā);
the remaining rites, such as the ceremonial bathing and others, are to be performed upon the ritual image (karmārcā)—this is the established rule.
Having carefully lifted either the primary image (mūlārcā) or the ritual image (karmārcā), which has been consecrated in water and held by four bearers of the [divine] forms, || 16.91 ||
Standing with darbha grass in hand, the wise man should worship her as she stands still:
"Homage to you, O Arcī, O Sovereign of the Gods, in the likeness of Viśvakarman! (16.92)
O Mother who has manifested the entire world! Salutations, salutations to you! In you, I worship the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all ailment.
"May you always be free from defects of the womb and endowed with supernatural powers.
Having thus made this request, [he offered] auspicious items consisting of fine linen cloth, water, and white mustard seeds.
One should bind the protective amulet with a woolen thread on the right hand;
having drawn it through [the fingers] with the thumb and the ring finger, using the *jitādya* mantra.
Having consecrated it seven times with the eight-syllable mantra for the pacification of obstacles,
one should then lead that image, adorned with fine garments, by means of the Brahma-vehicle.
Having adorned it with canopies and other ornaments according to the Śākuna Sūkta,
and having placed her upon a seat while reciting "trīṇi," he should then proclaim "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ."
Having anointed [the image] with cow-ghee while reciting "Tejo 'si," the practitioner should wash it with powders and water, and then bathe it with those same substances in due order.

Having gathered earth from the two banks of the river, as well as earth from an anthill, along with clay, astringents, medicinal herbs, and products of the cow—either individually or combined—he [prepared the bath]. (16.99)
It was known from the field where the crab lived and from the tip of its horn;
[the wood of] Śamī, Palāśa, Khadira, Bilva, Aśvattha, and Vikaṅkata [were used]. (16.100)
Indeed, there are udumbara and nyagrodha trees, as well as parts of plants with astringent properties;
likewise, śaṅkhapuṣpī, priyaṅgu, viṣṇukrāntī, and śatāvarī.
One should take dūrvā grass, amṛtā, rajanī, and vacā, reciting respectively the verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ" and "samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ. (16.102)
One should apply these waters to this bathing place of mine; with the Gāyatrī one should take cow's urine, and with "gandhadvārā" the cow dung. (16.103)
With the mantra "āpyāyasva" one offers milk; with "dadhikrāvṇe," curd;
with "tejo 'si śukram," clarified butter (ājya); and with "devasya tvā," water from kuśa grass.
One should offer the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), milk from the *payasvatī* plants, and likewise scented water with the hymn "āpo hi ṣṭhā"; thereafter, one should provide pure water.
One should bathe [the image] with the Parameśvara mantra and the Sakala mantra;
and having combined honey and clarified butter in a metallic vessel, one should recite the verse "madhu vātā" over them.
Then, having opened his eyes with a golden probe,
he [should do so] with the verse "The wondrous god" (citraṃ devī) and also with the verse "Swell up" (āpyāyasva).
The patron should then give a cow, saying, "May Govinda be pleased.
Afterwards, he should bathe [the deity] with four jars located at the corners.
The practitioner of mantras [should worship] with Brahmaśrī, Campaka, Kṣīra, Nīpa, Āmra, Balu, Lārjuna, and Aśoka trees with their sprouts, using the Ṛgvedic verse beginning "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat. (16.109)
One should offer padmaka, rocanā, dūrvā grass, a cluster of darbha blades, white mustard seeds, sandalwood, jāti, āvartaka, and kunda flowers with the *viṣṇorarāṭa* verse. || 16.110 ||
Barley, rice, sesame, gold, silver, earth from both riverbanks, cow dung, and earth untouched by the ground— [one should offer these] with the verse beginning "Soma, the King" (RV 1.91.1).
One should perform the ritual bath with *samī*, *varya*, *amṛtākrānti*, *sahā*, *bhṛṅga*, *mahauṣadhī*, *syāmāka*, and [the mantra] "viśvataścakṣuḥ. (16.112)
Then one should invoke the god Hari, who wears yellow garments:
"Come, come, O Blessed Viṣṇu, you who bestow grace upon the worlds! (16.113)
"O Vāsudeva, accept this sacrificial portion; salutations, salutations!
Then one should indeed offer water for the feet, water for sipping, and the respectful offering (arghya) with the root mantra. (16.114)
One should give two unwashed garments and a purifier with the Aṣṭaka hymn;
furthermore, one should cause a golden thread to be given while reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
Then one should offer ornaments with the twelve-syllable vidyā;
thereafter, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings.
One should worship with garlands, incense, lamps, fruits, gorocana, and collyrium; and with sandals, fans, umbrellas, and honey-mixture offerings.
One should pour a stream of water from the root mantra onto the feet of the deity;
then offer water for rinsing the mouth, incense, mouth-perfume, and a mirror.
Then one should offer body-unguents and a garland, followed by a handful of flowers;
having praised him with the Sāman chants, one should then recite the purifying hymn.
There, the knower of mantras should perform the rite for an auspicious day together with the Vaiṣṇavas;
and sesame seeds and sacrificial fees should be given to the Vaiṣṇavas according to the prescribed rule.
Then, being composed in meditation, he should remember Puruṣottama with devotion;
having done this, he should bring that image toward his bed.
With the Pauruṣa Sūkta, the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments,
and with the twelve-syllable mantra, one should lay him down upon the bed.
Having said "This is he," at the end one should mutter the eight-syllable mantra "sarvayogeśvara oṃ" and arrange the auspicious symbols.
A wise man should place a golden vessel filled with clarified butter at its head-position,
and a silver one filled with honey at its foot-position.
One should place a copper vessel containing milk on the right side,
and one should set down water for pacification contained in an iron vessel on the left.
In an earthen vessel, one should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and a fifth [vessel] before them;
one should perform the ritual touching (ālabhana) of these in sequence with the mantras beginning with Parameṣṭhin.
A skillful preceptor should cause four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to be made in the cardinal directions, respectively square, bow-shaped, circular, and triangular. 16.127.
At a distance of one cubit all around the pedestal, measuring one hand in width,
all [the altars] should be made with three tiers and half-cavities.
Having drawn [the fire] from the preceptor’s pit, he should subsequently deposit it into the other pits;
having consecrated the fire in those pits, he should perform the ullokha and other rites in due order.
But for one who is free from birth and so forth, having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the primordial nature (prakṛti),
they should offer food in due order with the Gāyatrī mantra at the conclusion of the fire-ritual of their own Vedic branch.
One should place the heart-mantra in the eastern pit, the head-mantra in the southern,
the crest-mantra in the western, and likewise the armor-mantra in the northern.
In this rite for the two weapons, Netra and Astra, no fire-oblation (homa) should be performed; however, it may be done with the [six] forms (mūrtis).

[The materials are: sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), sacrificial porridge (caru), parched grain (lāja), mustard seeds (sarṣapa), barley (yava), and sesame seeds (tila). || 16.132 ||
One should likewise offer oblations of rice and clarified butter into all the sacrificial pits;
then the preceptor should perform eight thousand oblations with the root mantra.
And here, for every hundred [recitations], one should offer one hundred and eight full oblations.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter of the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Now I shall describe in brief the supreme consecration (adhivāsana), through the application of which Hari is always present within the image. 17.1.
One should contemplate that the two hands, having been consumed by the weapon-mantra, have become composed of reality (tattva).
The thumbs should be made into the *praṇava*, and those two [thumbs] should have the vowels as their finger-joints. (17.2)
Having separately assigned the consonants to the left and right hands, with the *bindu* on the palms and the *visarga* on the backs, one should assign the *nāda* to the two thumbs.
Having retained the breath there, the knower of mantras should then enter it through inhalation;
thereafter, he should [place] the treasury of knowledge in due order.
Having meditated upon the body composed of the great elements, endowed with merit and demerit, as gradually withered, burnt, and then flooded by its own seed-syllables; 17.5.
One should meditate upon oneself as established in space, endowed with the form of the *bindu*;
just as a sprout arises from a seed that has been moistened, so it is with the self.
One should contemplate the divine source that has attained the state of the syllable Om (praṇava);
the wise know that to be Prakṛti, which consists of the three qualities and is joined with the eightfold intellect.

The first two vowels, A and Ā, are called Intellect (buddhi); the two I-sounds are Egoism (ahaṅkāra); the Mind (manas) consists of the two following them; and the five elements beginning with space (vyoman) are the vowels ending with the nasal (ṃ).

The self, the life-force, the belly, the ear, the tongue, the nose, the eye, and the skin are, in order, the sibilants, the semivowels, the head, the crown-lock, and the arms and shanks, respectively, according to their groups. (17.9)
The entire group of gutturals (ka-varga) represents all the fingers; such is this gross body.
One should meditate upon Vāgīśa, seated upon a lotus in the sun, accompanied by Vāgīśvarī.
One should meditate upon Hari, who possesses all powers, who has eight arms,
and who shines like a thousand suns, being difficult even for gods and asuras to behold.
One should contemplate [the deity] entering the interior of the body through the aperture of Brahmā;
one should then install the pervasive root-mantra and the limbs in their proper sequence.
Having meditated upon himself as the all-pervading, omniscient, and immutable Viṣṇu,
one who is filled with devotion should perform the supreme consecration (adhivāsana) of Viṣṇu.
Having brought the individual soul— which is imagined as a reflection, conceived as the stars, and drawn forth—
into a state of oneness with the Self through meditation, one should dissolve the elements beginning with earth.

One should contemplate the universe, composed of the five elements, as dissolved into earth, which is dried and burnt; then into water; that [water] into fire; that [fire] into air; and that [air] into space. Thus, one should meditate on the dissolution of the universe into space.
Through the sequence of that mind, ego, intellect, and māyā, one should lead [the self] to the Lord of Tārā;
having presided over that māyā, which is his own unmanifest nature, with the desire to create.
The Self of Sound (nādātmā) creates the entire pentad beginning with Parameṣṭhin;
Viṣṇu himself is the Self of the Praṇava, while his forms reside within the syllables beginning with 'na'.
Vāsudeva and the others, along with the five elements beginning with space and ending with earth—
this is declared to be the gross body of that Viṣṇu who consists of six aspects.
He, born from the unceasing lotus, the soul of the earth, the lord of creatures, is called "the Unborn" (Aja) because he was born from Viṣṇu, who is distinct from the creation. || 17.19 ||
Having first created the element of water, he created the earthly egg;
having thus created it, she became born as the fourteenfold world.
Then, having meditated upon that egg— which consists of the five elements, is radiant, and golden as a reflection— Viṣṇu himself should cause the individual soul (jīva) to enter it.

That Viṣṇu, the individual soul transcending the stars, becomes endowed with eight arms when accompanied by the five powers beginning with Nāda, through the arrangement of the limbs which are the root of the script.
Having placed the image upon the bed, one should then offer ghee in sequence;
one should perform the sixteen-fold ritual placement (nyāsa), for it is not desired to perform the placement without having offered oblations.
The *tāra*, the *vyāhṛtis*, the *lipis*, the *ṛks*, the asterisms, time, color, the *jāla*, the *śruti*, the *vairāja* deity, sacrifice, qualities, and weapons, in their respective order.
The sixteen-fold ritual placement (nyāsa) is said to consist of those [syllables] ending with the power-mantra (śakti), the mantra, and the life-force (jīva).
One should first offer oblations of the Praṇava, divided into three measures (mātrās).
One should place Brahmā, Keśava, and Rudra at the feet, the heart, and the head respectively;
here, one hundred and eight oblations should be offered by them in that sequence.
One should offer the three vyāhṛtis for the gratification of the three worlds,
and then one should offer the mātṛkā, beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa'.
They are open in the palate, the mouth, the eyes, the ears, the teeth, the lips, the neck, and the tongue; and they are closed in the two nostrils and the two cheeks.
The navel, heart, hips, belly, ears, tips of the teeth, nose, sight, skin—these are the primary parts; likewise the arms, shanks, and fingers. (17.29)
Having offered oblations to the lunar mansions, planets, and stars, one should assign them to the limbs:
the planets to the two eyes, the chest, the navel, the face, the forehead, and the feet.
In this manner, one should likewise offer oblations to the lunar mansions,
beginning with Rohiṇī, [assigning them] to the heart, the two arms, the hair, the forehead, the mouth, the nose, and the teeth.
In the two ears, the two arms, the pair of hands, the two breasts, the belly and the sides, the hips, the eyes, the genitals, the testicles, the anus, the two thighs, and the two shanks. (17.32)
In this manner, the arrangement of the constellations ending with Kṛttikā is established in the feet;
Dhruva is situated in his navel, and likewise the Seven Sages are in his throat.
The circle of the Mothers (mātṛmaṇḍala) is to be known as situated at his waist;
the three steps on his foot are the forest garland (vanamālā), while the path (vīthikā) is [the space] between them.
One should first worship Hari, whose body is the year, as the form of Time— his body hairs being the clusters of stars, his eyes the sage Agastya, and his gem the Kaustubha.
Thus, the twelve months, beginning with Caitra and ending with Phālguna, are situated respectively in the heart, the two breasts, the chest, the hips, the two thighs, the shanks, and the two feet.
Utpūrva, ānupūrva, paripūrva, and saṃpūrva—these four years are to be known as his four arms. (17.37)
Its joints are the joints of the year, and the seasons are known as its limbs;
the days and nights are its bones, and the minor units of time, such as kṣaṇas, are its body hairs. (17.38)
One should arrange the four ages— Kṛta and the others— in sequence upon the face, heart, hips, and feet, and likewise distribute the Manvantaras across the two arms.
They know the two lower joints of the shanks to be two *parārdhas*, and the head to be a *mahākalpa*;
the two solstices are the two feet—thus is he described as having the form of a year.
The castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas are to be known as originating from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet; the mixed castes are to be understood as being located in the toes of the feet. 17.41.
Those who are the most excellent among the mixed castes (saṅkara) should be known as his cows in all the joints of his limbs;
and goats and sheep are to be understood as being in his two breasts. (17.42)
The single-hoofed animals are on his feet; domestic and wild beasts are established upon his thighs;
the clouds are to be known as being in his hair, and the mists are indeed his body hairs.
All the rivers are his limbs and members, and the oceans reside within his belly;
his head is to be known as the sacrifice, and the Ṛgveda is his right arm. (17.44)
The Sāmaveda is remembered as his left side; all the Upaniṣads are in his heart;
the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are his shanks, and the Yajurveda is remembered as his chest. 17.45.
The Atharva-Angirasas are his navel; the Kalpa-sūtras are at his feet; Phonetics and Grammar are his mouth; and Logic is situated in his throat. (17.46)
Mīmāṃsā and Nirukta are his heart; Chandas and Jyotiṣa are his two eyes;
and Gāruḍa and Bhūtatantra are established in the pair of his ears.
The science of archery (dhanurveda) and the science of medicine (āyurveda) are said to be in his two hands;
the treatises on yoga are in his heart, and the treatises on ethics (nītiśāstra) are in his feet.
Speech is his song, the hands his dance; the arts and sciences reside in his pores.
The sky is his head, the moon and sun his eyes, and the vital breath, whose nature is wind, is in his nose.
One should place the sky and the four oceans at the navel, the earth with its moving and unmoving beings at the base of the belly,
Hiraṇyagarbha on his head, and serpents in his hair.
Having placed Rudra on the forehead, Antaka between the eyebrows, the two Aśvins in the ears, Vaiśvānara in the mouth, and Sarasvatī on the tongue; 17.51.
One should place the Rudras in the teeth, the Vasus in the throat, and the Ādityas in the visible [face];
Indra and Bali in the two arms, and Prahlāda on the left breast.
On the right [side], he saw Viśvakarman and Nārada situated in the belly;
Ananta was situated in the left belly, and Varuṇa was situated in the bladder.
He placed Mitra at the anus, Tārkṣya on the hips, the Viśvedevas and likewise the Uragas on the thighs;
the Pitṛs on the two knees, the Yakṣas on the shanks, and the Rākṣasas on the ankles.
One should place the Piśācas on the forepart of the feet and the Pārṣṇis, and likewise the Vidyādharas;
the Grahas on the soles, and the Jambhakas along with the Pūtanās on the nails.
One should place the Apsarases on the fingers, Kārttikeya and Gaṇeśvara on the hips, the Gandharvas on the two lips, and all beings on the back.
One should place Matsya on the feet, Kūrma on the shanks,
Narasiṃha on the forehead, and Vāmana in the middle of the face.
One should place Rāma and Kṛṣṇa upon the navel, heart, hips, and private parts; Kalki upon the region of the knees; and Nara and Nārāyaṇa upon the feet.
One should likewise assign the Thousand-Armed one to his arms;
the Horse Sacrifice is his head, and the Human Sacrifice is his forehead.
The Rājasūya is his mouth, the Gosava is situated in his throat; the Dvādaśāha is his heart, and the Ahīna is situated in his navel. (17.60)
The Viśvajit and the Viśvamedha are situated in the region of his hips;
the Agniṣṭoma resides in his penis, and the Atirātra in his testicles.
The Aptoryāma sacrifice was situated on his thighs, the Ṣoḍaśī on the region of his knees;
the Ukthya and Vājapeya were on his shanks, while Agni was in his feet.
One should assign the Cāturmāsya sacrifices to his two arms;
having placed the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice upon his palms, one should assign the animal sacrifice to his fingers.
The New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices are her eyes, and her movements are the ritual hair-offerings;
the utterances of Svāhā and Vaṣaṭ are established upon her two breasts.
The fingers of the two arms are proclaimed as the five great sacrifices;
his heart is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the darbha grass is his hair, and his skin is his garment.
His mouth is the Āhavanīya fire; his heart and navel are the two fires of the Dakṣiṇā and the western altar;
the Pravargya rite is his ornament, and the three Soma-pressings are his three states of existence.
The *pākayajñas* and *haviyajñas* are said to be his feet and toes;
the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāgau*) are to be known as his eyes, the sacrificial altars (*vedī*) as his hips, and the oblation (*havis*) as his mouth. (17.67)
First, one should gratify his body, which consists of the qualities (guṇas), by means of oblation;
then, one should place Dharma, established in ten ways, upon the head.
One should place knowledge eightfold in the heart, detachment ninefold in the secret organ, and sovereignty eightfold in the feet; this is the body composed of the qualities (guṇas).
The placement (nyāsa) of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus is considered common;
those which are specifically mentioned in the Tantras according to the different forms (mūrti) are also [to be performed]. 17.70.
Peace resides in his heart, prosperity on his forehead, and Sarasvatī in his mouth; delight is in his private parts, love in his navel, and fame shall encompass him entirely.
Contentment in the belly and nourishment in the body—this is declared to be the placement of power (śaktinyāsa).
The placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa), consisting of the syllables and the limbs [of the deity], has already been explained previously.
Having placed the Śrīvatsa on the chest, the Kaustubha gem in the region of the navel,
and the forest garland upon the neck— this is declared to be the placement of the mudrās.
Having raised [the breath] from below the navel, endowed with the organs, and having pervaded the body with the subtle elements, the bodies, and the five vital breaths; 17.74.
Endowed with sovereignty, the knowledge of dharma, and dispassion,
he pervaded the entire expanse of the quarters with a mass of shimmering rays.
Having reached the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) by means of the *iḍā*, which shines like a thousand suns,
one should contemplate it entering slightly into the interior of the forehead.
Remaining there, he should also direct the ten vital breaths located in the head;
having entered the heart-lotus by way of the door of the pericarp.
One should join the vital breaths, beginning with prāṇa, there by means of the fivefold division of their functions;
one should place prāṇa between the feet and apāna at the back of the nose.
Vyāna is indeed all-pervading, while Udāna moves upward from the abdomen;
Samāna is at the navel and heart, and then there are the five beginning with Nāga.
Having placed the city of eight constituents (puryaṣṭaka) within the heart, [one should meditate] upon Puruṣottama in its center—
He who bestows grace, who is gentle, omniscient, and faces in all directions.
One should meditate in this manner; thus, in the Kṛta age, that image becomes infused with life in an instant.
No preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) is required for it, for there are only fifteen ritual depositions (nyāsa). || 17.81 ||
One should perform the rite of enlivening once Madhusūdana has been installed;
however, one who does not know the sequence for the installation of the life-force (jīvanyāsa) from oral instruction [should not do so]. || 17.82 ||
That teacher should not be regarded [as such]; he should be restrained like a thief.
At that very time, however, one should consecrate the *piṇḍikā*.
Now, let the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) described therein also be understood:
having first purified [the site] in due order with *darbha* grass, earth, bark, products of the cow, and water; (17.84)
Therein, the wise one should cause the primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of the egg-form, to abide;
he should place the Mātṛkā there and conceive of her as being of the form of Śakti.
One should place the Praṇava in the center, the sixteen vowels outside of that,
and the consonants outside of those, starting with Parjanya and proceeding clockwise.
One should place the lotus in that very [space], and the Śaktis should be established upon the lotus;
endowed with which [Śakti], the Lord constantly performs the act of grace (anugraha).
The imperishable Hari, the Supreme Self, is eternally present and worthy of worship therein;
one should worship the Goddess with water for the feet, perfumes, and other offerings, as well as with sacrificial oblations. 17.88.
One should fashion the form of Lakṣmī with unwashed garments;
the preceptor alone should perform the fire-oblation for those ending with the eight Śaktis.
The arrangement of the principles (tattva-vinyāsa) for the *ayana*, the *śakti*, and the *prāsāda* has been previously explained there; now it is recalled in due order. 17.90.
Likewise, having visualized him in the form of a person in due order,
one should afterwards worship the temple with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Then, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) here upon the purified Brahma-stone;
the placement of the seat of Ananta is upon the Napuṃsaka-stone.
The supreme Brahman is said to be the neuter, the support of all;
here one should draw a mandala with five-colored rice grains.
The most excellent preceptor, having first performed the ritual of complete identification (sakalīkaraṇa) upon the image, [should prepare] a square area with four gates and a lotus in the center.

One should worship the God together with his limbs (sāṅga) in due order using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, according to the method prescribed for one's own ritual manual, by means of the division of major and minor limbs.
With ornaments and offerings, according to the extent of his wealth,
the wise man should worship the Lord Adhokṣaja together with His limbs [attendants] within the mandala.
One should conceive that very form which has been installed in the image there, having worshipped Acyuta according to the prescribed rite, together with his limbs and his retinue.
Having offered oblations into the fire according to the rule, he should present the bali-offering to his attendants,
as well as to those primordial beings and those born of action who abide in the eastern quarter.
"Being serene and fully satisfied, may they accept this offering;
one should assign [the offerings] to the south, the west, and the north. (17.99)
One should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food, and water in due order; and likewise, one should present the bali offering to the intermediate directions according to the rule.
Those who are situated upon trees, on mountain peaks, and in the intermediate directions;
those who dwell upon the earth and in the sky—may they too accept this offering.
May the Vināyakas, the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas), and others who desire offerings,
as well as the attendants (pārṣadas) beginning with those of the east, accept this bali-offering.
One should indeed offer [the oblation] all around, circumambulating it clockwise;
then, having sipped water (ācamana) and entered within, one should remain composed, having performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa).
Having offered oblations for peace with the *vyāhṛtis*, one should then touch the deity in due order;
having offered clarified butter with the mantra "bhūḥ," one should touch two feet of the deity.
Having offered curd with the mantra "bhūvaḥ," he should then touch his navel;
having offered milk with the mantra "svar," he should then touch his heart.
Having thus offered oblations with "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ," one should touch the head with honey;
having offered everything with the root mantra at the end, one should touch all the limbs.
In this rite for pacification, sixty-four oblations are prescribed;
and here, the touching [of the vessel] with the *sruva* ladle filled with the ritual substance is also enjoined. (17.107)
When each substance has been touched in that manner, one should worship it with fragrant flowers;
then, having washed the *sruva* ladle, the oblation of the other substances should be performed.
Four cows, peaceful, bound with ropes, and accompanied by their calves, should be stationed facing north near the southern gate. (17.109)
Having honored the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, as well as the Godāvarī and the Sarasvatī by their names with perfumes and flowers in due order, [he should proceed]. (17.110)
Having milked with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, he should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) with that same mantra;
he should offer it with that same mantra, and at the end, he should present the bali-oblation with that same mantra. || 17.111 ||
There, one should feed twelve devoted Brāhmaṇas with milk-rice (pāyasa);
on the northern side of the pavilion, gold shall be the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One should offer fragrant substances to the preceptor, saying, "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me.
Having performed this, one should thereafter keep a vigil at night.
Accompanied by conchs, trumpets, and other instruments, and joined with dance, song, and the like,
he should pass the night with recitations of the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Kathās.
At dawn, on an auspicious day and weekday, when the rising of a mass of merit occurs, the wise man should establish [the image] according to the *lagna* (ascendant) indicated by the astrologer.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, on the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), in the *Viṣṇusaṃhitā*.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Now I shall explain in brief the supreme procedure for consecration: having first performed the sacrifice to the site (vāstuyāga), the installation should take place at an auspicious moment. 18.1
Having performed the Nāndīmukha rite according to one's ability, one should feed six, eight, or twelve peaceful Brāhmaṇas, especially Vaiṣṇavas. (18.2)
One should give garments, rings, and so forth, as well as gold, according to one's capacity;
thereafter, one should cause the entire temple to be swept clean.

Then, having diligently sprinkled the interior with Darbha grass and its stalks, and with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and fragrant scents consecrated by the root mantra, [he purified it]. 18.4.
For the purpose of the fire-oblation, one should cause square sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍilas) to be made with sand all around the temple, in the proper sequence.
Having thus performed this in the eight directions, one should place eight jars filled with water and flowers, provided with lids and sprouts. (18.6)
When the inner sanctum was divided into forty-nine sections,
there were the stations for the Brahmas, gods, humans, and piśācas.
Starting from the center, one should diligently recognize [the divisions] in order on all sides:
the portion of Brahmā shall be fifteen parts, and the portions of the gods thirteen.
Eleven and nine degrees [are measured] from the rear of the remaining two;
movement is said to be of three kinds, distinguished as rearward, leftward, and forward.

One should conceive [the forms] according to the proper rule through the application of substance and configuration; one should arrange the postures of those who are standing, sitting, or lying down. 18.10.
In the Brahma portion, having set aside the middle [space] and also the second from behind, the third position is desired for the single installed image (ekaberabimba). || 18.11 ||
When the width of the door is divided into three parts, one should lay out a cord for the purpose of movement at the middle of the seven parts of the third [section],
and at half of that middle section toward the north.
Having established the ear-line at the junction of the west and north,
one should move it toward the northeast by two finger-breadths of the image, or by two barley-corns.
If the worship of the site is performed while omitting the portion for Brahmā, the king who is the lord of that mandala and the one who established it shall both perish. (18.14)
And the ritual action would indeed be fruitless; therefore, one should measure with care.
Relying on some human [scale], one should perform the work of preparing the seat.
A wise person should prepare the bed using portions of both divine and human [measurements];
when the pedestal for worship is of the Brāhma type, the installation is performed according to the Daivika [standard]. (18.16)
His attendants belong to the human realm, while his weapons belong to the Piśāca realm;
having fashioned the site for the foot-stone into either a circular or a square shape.
Then, beneath the footstool, one should place the Brahma-śilā with the mantra:
"You alone are the supreme Śakti; you alone are the sustainer of the throne. (18.18)
"O Goddess! By the command of the gods, you must remain here at all times.
Having thus informed her, he first worshipped her with perfumes and flowers. (18.19)
Having meditated, the preceptor should place the earth into the pit with this mantra:
"In whom the moving and unmoving world resides, and who is the inexhaustible treasure of jewels. (19.20)
"O Earth, remain here firm as the Brahma-stone!
Having thus established her and worshipped her again with perfumes and flowers, [he performed the rite]. (19.21)
Then one should perform the deposition of jewels according to the path prescribed by the rules; four pits, covered with low mounds, have been prepared in succession. (19.22)
In the eight directions, including the center, eight [seals] should be placed in due order;
within them are the seed-syllables, jewels, minerals, metals, and weapons.
Having combined all the substances, one should place them in the station of Brahmā;
these are the qualities of Viṣṇu renowned under the name of the eightfold sovereignty (aṣṭaguṇaiśvarya).
At the time of the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should contemplate those jewels as situated in the directions;
their seed-syllables (bījas) reside within the wind and the ether, and they are the [five] qualities (guṇas). || 19.25 ||
In this context, they are correctly remembered as being in the directions starting from the east in the order of lordship (īśitva) and so forth;
however, in the center, the Person (puruṣa) endowed with the eight qualities should be known as the Praṇava.
One should purify the pit with the five products of the cow using the eight-syllable mantra,
and sprinkle it with scented water using the twelve-syllable vidyā.
Then one should perform the fire-sacrifice (homakarma) on the northern side of the temple;
having brought the common (laukika) fire, one should place it in a shallow earthen bowl (śarāva). || 19.28 ||
One should perform the rite of Vaiṣṇavīkaraṇa and bring forth the consecrated fire;
one should offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the eight-syllable mantra.
Then, having offered fuel-sticks with the twelve-syllable vidyā and clarified butter with the Gāyatrī, one should touch the precious gems.
Or one should perform a thousand oblations of clarified butter here with the Gāyatrī alone;
alternatively, there may be eight hundred, which constitutes the superior, the middling, and the inferior [levels].
Having touched them with that [water], he should place the jewels into the pits;
he should arrange neither more nor less substance than the pit. (19.32)
In some cases, the skillful preceptor should cause a pit to be made equal in size to the substance [to be buried],
using the syllables of the eight-syllable mantra, arranged individually and in their proper sequence.
Having placed barley and the other grains in the cardinal directions, one should place white mustard seeds in the center; then, one should place the vajra and other gems, with the ruby in the middle.
One should likewise place the minerals such as realgar (manaḥśilā) and mercury (pārata);
the eight [metals] beginning with gold in the directions, and a golden lotus in the center.
Then, with the Viṣṇugāyatrī mantra, he should touch the pit while offering a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
even if seeds and other materials are unavailable, at their respective locations in due order.
The wise one, knowing the mantras, should place rice, pearls, yellow orpiment, and gold;
first, he who knows the mantras should cause the Vaiṣṇavas to proclaim an auspicious day.
Then, having performed the placement of the jewels, one should install the pedestal there;
having brought the Vaiṣṇava fire to the northeast with the root mantra.
One should offer a thousand or even a hundred fuel-sticks of the *brāhmī* plant,
or else eight more than that [one hundred and eight], with clarified butter while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra known as Viṣṇu.
Having offered ghee in due order with the Mūrti-mantras, the Śaktis, and the Aṅgas,
the wise man, according to his capacity, should then collect the water of pacification (śāntitoya).
Then, having brought forth the fire, oblations should be offered into the eight directions with fuel sticks by those most skilled in the Vaiṣṇava mantras, using the root-vidyā.
Likewise, those born from palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, plakṣa, and nyagrodha;
as well as kāśmarya, rohitaka, bilva, and udumbara, in their respective order. || 19.42 ||
Those sacrificial fuel sticks are proclaimed to be twelve finger-breadths in measure;
those measuring the size of the little finger are for the separate eight-thousand-fold [recitation].
Having thus performed the oblation to the quarters, one should collect the water of pacification in a copper vessel belonging to Viṣṇu, having gathered it from all the jars.
Then the preceptor, having consecrated it one hundred times with the root mantra and having filled it with the syllables of the eight-syllable mantra, should circumambulate it clockwise.
Having worshipped it in due order with the syllable Om, along with perfumes and flowers,
one should take up that [vessel] which is secured by the hand, provided with a lid, and wrapped in cloth.
Having meditated here upon Viṣṇu, the supreme, whose form is splendor and who is free from ailment,
one should then pour [the water] upon the head of the ritual image while uttering "Om."
Having sprinkled water containing the essence of all sacred fords upon the head of the image,
and having discarded the two previous garments, one should clothe it again with two new pieces of cloth.
One should worship properly with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings according to one's means;
then, having raised [the image] with the sounds of conchs and drums, [one should say], "Arise! (19.49).
The wise preceptor, accompanied by the image-makers, should lead the image around the temple in a clockwise direction while reciting the hymn beginning with "ato devā. (19.50)
Then, having offered the arghya at the entrance during an auspicious moment,
the most excellent preceptor should carefully lead [the image] into the temple.
Having inserted it inside so that it touches neither below nor above,
and having circumambulated the seat clockwise, one should then deposit it with the whole [mantra].
The wise one, most proficient in mantras, should meditate upon Viṣṇu, the supreme and partless,
and having visualized Him as consisting of all principles, should install Him at an auspicious moment.
For the sake of favoring the world, remain steadfast for our happiness;
O Lord, increase your presence here daily. 19.54
"May there be no opposition to the subjects here; may the sacrificer prosper, as well as the kingdom along with its protector, free from all calamities. (19.55)
"May they attain security, incomparable growth, and imperishable happiness.
Having spoken thus, one should recite before him the Ṛgvedic verse beginning with "viśvataścakṣuḥ. (19.56)
Having performed the ritual of endowing with life (sajīvakaraṇa) according to the five Upaniṣads in sequence,
and having offered the peace-oblation (śānti-homa) in accordance with the rules, one should consecrate that deity.
Having meditated upon Viṣṇu as partless (niṣkala), one should then contemplate him as having form (sakala). Space shall be his body, and the earth his pedestal.
One should conceive of a body for that splendor by means of its atoms;
then, having meditated upon it as consisting of light, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Then one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) according to the distinctions of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
thereafter, having meditated upon the Lord of the Manifested (sakaleśvara), who is entirely composed of light.

Then, having restrained [the breath] with the syllable *praṇava*, one should [meditate on the Self] whose form has its senses and limbs distinguished, who is endowed with all powers, and beautiful in every limb. (19.61)

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should then worship [the deity] resplendent with the yellow garment, crown, and other ornaments, and possessing radiant weapons, together with his limbs (aṅgas) and retinue (āvaraṇas).
Then, having displayed the mudrā, one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground;
one should then install the attendants beginning with Brahmā and the weapons by their respective names.
Having worshipped [them], one should display one's own mudrās to the attendants individually;
then, having worshipped the God and bowed with the añjali-mudrā, [one should proceed]. (19.64)
Having obtained permission from that Lord, he should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
then, having gone out and turned toward [the deity], he should take water mixed with flowers and other offerings.
Having installed both Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, the two divine doorkeepers at the entrance by uttering their own names preceded by "namaḥ," one should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali).
Having installed Vainateya, Ananta, Gaṇeśa, Dakṣiṇeśvara, and the world-protectors, one should worship Viṣvaksena.
Having consecrated the image made of clay, having performed the ritual worship and entered the divine temple, one should place it there, saying: "O Lord, this is that very form of yours; Om. (19.68)
All [rites], beginning with the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa), should be performed here as before;
however, one should employ the rites such as bathing and so forth in the ritual worship of the deity (karmārcā). 19.69.
The established rule is that all procedures, such as the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa) and so forth, are performed upon the primary image;
however, one should then assign all the attendants of Viṣṇu to the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha). 19.70.
Having sipped water and performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa), the wise one should enter the inner chamber;
having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, he should pay homage to that deity.

Having praised him with various kinds of hymns preceded by the names of the Great Beings (Mahāpuruṣa), and having thereafter prostrated with the eight-limbed salutation in the gesture of reverence; 19.72.
Then one should cause various dances, songs, and instrumental music to be performed;
there, one should also diligently provide food and other provisions without restriction.
Thereafter, one should honor the preceptor together with the image by means of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
one should present to him all the materials used for the sacrifice. (19.74)
Thereafter, one should worship the Vaiṣṇavas according to the extent of one's means.
Lac, resin of the Sarja tree, conch shell, sand, and Kuruvindaka [gems]— 19.75.
Mercury (hiṅgulaka) and borax (bola) are bound by means of a decoction of *phalaka*;
the eight substances beginning with *vimalā* are to be ground together; these liquid substances are the *anugrahas*.
The bond consisting of the nine powers (navaśakti) belongs to Lakṣmī and Mādhava;
having thus performed the eightfold bond with the five powers beginning with ghee (ghṛta), [one should proceed]. 19.77.
One should perform the offering with *dūrvā* grass upon the heart, the secret parts, and the feet of the bronze image;
then, having worshipped it and withdrawn [the offerings], one should wrap it with *darbha* grass and cloths.
The mantra-practitioner should likewise perform the oblation for the lunar day (tithi) and for the presiding deity of that lunar day;
he should also perform the oblation for the asterism (ṛkṣa), the oblation for the day of the week (vāra), and the oblation for its presiding deity.
The oblation to the deities of the muhūrta and likewise the other oblation to the planets—
one should repeatedly pour their combined residue (sampāta) into that water-pot (kalaśa).
Then, having worshipped the preceptor along with those bearing the [divine] forms, and having performed the auspicious *puṇyāha* rite, he should take up the water-pot and bathe the deity. (19.81)
Accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and conchs, as well as shouts of "Victory!", one should then cause the place to resound with Vaiṣṇava hymns and cries of "Victory! (19.82).
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, garments, incense, and lamps;
then one should offer the fourfold food-oblation to the deity.
One should diligently scatter the sacrificial offering (bali) and have the Brāhmaṇas recite benedictions (svasti).
When this is done, the evils arising from the lunar day, the asterism, the day of the week, the zodiac sign, and the planets [are neutralized]. (19.84)
All defects are destroyed; therefore, it must certainly be performed.
Thereafter, one should sprinkle the patron with the water from the Viṣṇu-pitcher.
Having bathed [the image], the preceptor himself should perform the worship;
then, together with his guru, his wife, his sons, and likewise his younger brothers. (19.86)
Wearing white garments, he should reverently salute that God;
having divided his wealth into three parts, he should assign one portion to the deity.
A share for his wife, sons, and others; a share as the teacher’s fee (dakṣiṇā); a gift of affection; and articles for worship should be given. 19.88.
Whatever one gives at that time, all of it shall yield great fruit;
having offered incense, lamps, and the like, one should indeed sweep the temple of the deity.
After that, no one should open it for three days;
there, worship is prescribed with sacrificial fees, offerings of food, and oblations.
Once Puruṣottama has been installed, one should perform the propitiation of the mantra with ghee, milk, curd, or pure water, even once. (19.91)
Having bathed the ritual image,
[this concludes] the nineteenth chapter.
Now I shall briefly describe the rites to be performed immediately following the consecration.
As before, one should prepare eight sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*) in the cardinal directions for the purpose of the fire-oblation (*homa*). (19.1)
Having performed the rites of scraping and so forth in due order according to the previously stated procedure,
the initiated ones should offer oblations into the consecrated Vaiṣṇava fire in the various directions.
"In the eastern direction, 'indrakratum'; in the southeast, 'agnim dūtam';
in the southern direction, 'suparṇam'; and in the southwest, 'mo ṣu ṇaḥ parā'. (19.3)
In the western direction, [he offers] "They who protect" (yaraṃkṣanti); in the north-west, "O purifier, come hither" (vāyavāyāhi pāvane);
in the north, "Soma the King" (somaṃ rājānam); and in the north-east, "Tryambaka. (19.4)
Having recited the five Tāraka mantras in front, the officiating priests should, according to the rule, offer the cooked oblation from the eastward direction in succession, using these mantras.
He offered one hundred fuel-sticks each, separately, made from palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, plakṣa, nyagrodha, bilva, udumbara, and kāśmarya wood.
Having offered clarified butter, rice, parched grain, and so forth, one should complete the remainder;
one should offer fuel sticks and other materials as available, along with oblations to Indra and others using their respective weapons-mantras.
Having thus offered oblations to Indra and the other deities in the eight directions with their respective mantras,
[he should sprinkle] with water contained in jars, consecrated by mantras and mixed with the residual clarified butter from the offerings.
Having bathed these [images] upon their pedestals, one should worship them in sequence with perfumes and other offerings;
having installed Skanda in the southeast, one should do so with the mantra "To the Six-faced One."
The Teacher [is represented] by the syllable *bhāṃ* in the fire; "Homage to the Lord of Beings.
Likewise, Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī. (19.10)
Vārāhī, Aindrī, and Cāmuṇḍī, along with the Seven Mothers on the southern side,
together with Vīrabhadra and Gaṇeśa, [are stationed] by the side of the enclosure wall.
Vīrabhadra, all the vowels, the seven groups [of consonants], the Mothers, Kūṭa, and Gaṇapati— thus the Mātṛkā should be known in this sequence.
One should worship the Sun in the southwest (nairṛtyā) with the syllable *praṇava* or with his own mantras;
or the mantra "ghasotkāya" may be used at the end of the oblation in that ritual procedure.
Afterwards, Brahmā [is worshipped] with his own *ṣaṭka*, and likewise another with "Tat Sat";
then, with the seed-syllable "Bhūḥ," Varāha [is worshipped] in the region of the wind.
Durgā is worshipped with the syllable *hrīṃ* placed before her name, followed by it at the end;
likewise, Śrīdhara, Hayāsya, Vāgīśvarī, and the other Mothers [are worshipped]. (19.15)
Vāgīśvarī, Kriyā, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, and Sṛṣṭi as the fifth—these should be known as Vidyā and Kānti, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace. (19.16)
The fourth and sixth [syllables] end with the *bindu*; then the twelfth and thirteenth;
and the first and eleventh are to be known as the vowels belonging to Indra (the second group). 19.17.
Viṣvaksena, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, should be established upon Aditi;
he threatens the world with his left index finger, which is positioned near the tip of his nose.
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, as well as with the remaining sacrificial materials,
[he should take] the flowers and other items used by the deity that remain within the temple.
Having given all of that to him, one should finally wrap it with two cloths;
then, one should install Īśāna in the northeastern quarter with his own mantras.
Kumuda and the other deities of the banners, starting from the east, should be stationed upon the pedestals outside the enclosure wall; they are to be worshipped in sequence with offerings.

Having established Bala at the sacrificial pedestal and the leader of spirits (Bhūtanāyaka) along with his retinue in front, and having worshipped them all, he should then make this petition: || 19.22 ||
"As long as the Lord of the World remains here, residing within this image, so long must you all remain right here at all times for the sake of protection. (19.23)
The inner necklace (antahārakā) should be half a staff (daṇḍa) from the edge of the inner circle;
the middle necklace (madhyahārā) is two staffs long, and the four boundary walls are likewise [two staffs].
Then, a boundary wall should be constructed, seven *daṇḍas* in length;
its width should be one-third, one-fourth, or even one-half of the length of the entrance. (19.25)
The height of the *balipīṭha* (offering pedestal) is declared to be equal to the height of the inner sanctum (*garbhāgāra*),
or equal to the height of the worship-pedestal (*pūjāpīṭha*), or even six units less.
Having divided the height into ten parts, its width shall be seven parts;
having likewise divided that height into twenty-seven parts, [the width shall be] exactly equal to those.
One should know the *pāduka* to be one part; then the *jagatī* again with four parts, the *kumuda* with three parts, and likewise the *paṭṭikā* with one part.
They say the neck is one-tenth [of the height]; by two parts are the conch-shell and the bud;
by three parts they call it the pigeon-niche; and by one part, the front fillet.
The lotus at the end should consist of two parts; this is the characteristic of the pedestal (pīṭha).
One should determine its superior, inferior, or middling nature according to its association with the image (bimba). || 19.30 ||
In the case of the best images, the middle and lowest [types] are excluded;
likewise, in the middle and lowest [images], eight pedestals are excluded. (19.31)
Since the overturning of the pedestals would lead to the destruction of the lineage, those who desire happiness must not allow the displacement of one thing for another. (19.32)
The height and the projection of the *pāduka* are declared to be equal;
it should be situated within that same measure at the junction of the *jagatī* and the *kumbha*.
Having made one part for the *kumbha* and half a part for the *paṭṭikā* thereafter,
one should indeed make the neck-base (*kaṇṭhapāduka*) with one part and one-third of a part.
The neck is situated within half a part;
the girdle is one-quarter of a measure (pāda) in width, and its breadth is said to be one-eighth of a part.
Either four or twelve throat-ornaments (kaṇṭhapādukā) should be made;
one should fashion the neck-band exactly like the band for the water-pot.
The outer portion should indeed be curved at its midpoint, while the inner portion should be curved like a bow;
the water should flow from all sides.
Above that, a band should be known [to be placed], and within it, a lotus-shaped form;
having constructed that pedestal in the center, one should build a pavilion endowed with the proper characteristics.

Preceded by the sowing of seeds, the raising of the banner, and offerings for auspiciousness, it was joined with festivals, food, the declaration of a holy day, the purification of the site, and other such rites.
Having drawn an auspicious eight-petaled lotus with a base extending all around, one should fill eight jars with ghee, or with grains, or with water. (19.40)
Adorned with all kinds of jewels, one should wrap it in pairs of cloths;
whether made of metal, clay, or otherwise, one should place it upon the pedestal.
Beginning with the Lord of Beings (Bhūtanātha) and performing a circumambulation of the spirits,
one should worship them on all sides with perfumes and other offerings, as well as with fruits and flowers.
Provided with various kinds of food, both solid and soft, as well as water-jars as before, he should wrap them all in new cloths that are free from hair and other defects. (19.43)
For the sake of the fire sacrifice, eight or four Brahmins should be selected;
or the preceptor himself may perform it alone according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Engaged in the study of the Vedas and likewise keeping a vigil at night,
one should worship the God within the temple according to the prescribed rites.

Having performed the offering of the bali-oblation according to one's capacity, as previously described, one should perform the fire-offering (homa) for all the image-protectors (mūrtipās) with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā). || 19.46 ||
Just as with his own name-mantra, he offered sacrificial fuel,
clarified butter, oblations, parched grain, mustard seeds, as well as groats, barley, and sesame seeds.
Curd, milk, honey, flowers, and fruits—all these, together with clarified butter, should be offered as oblations; this is auspicious and brings about all forms of peace.
One should offer one thousand and eight or one hundred oblations separately for each substance;
and here, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) according to the rule for every material.
Accompanied by conch shells, trumpets, and other instruments, he should offer the bali-oblation to the spirits in all directions:
"Oṃ! Salutation to the spirits of the east, to the spirits of the universe!
Salutation be to those of universal form, and salutation to you who are of diverse forms! (19.50)
Om,
salutations be to the southern spirits of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
salutations to the Hāhā spirits, and repeated salutations to all of you!

Oṃ, obeisance to the western beings, the Bhairavas who protect Viṣṇu and dwell within the belly of the celestial spheres; Huṃ Phaṭ! Oṃ, depart! Ṭhaṭha! From this [offering], I present a bali-oblation to the hosts of Viṣṇu; grant us prosperity, be pleased, Svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Viṣṇu-beings of the north, who act for the welfare of all creatures and protect the universe; obeisance to you, Svāhā!
Then, having bathed well and having had the benediction recited, with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas—
Having performed a great worship of the god with devotion and a concentrated mind.
Having worshipped Vainateya and his retinue according to one's capacity,
and having propitiated Bhūtanātha, one should then worship the guardians of the images (mūrtipās) in due order.
Having prepared all this in due order— consisting of cakes, parched grain flour, fried grains, fruits, and various foods— one should perform the satiation of the Brahmins.
And here, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability;
then, being composed, one should worship the altar of offerings (balipīṭha) with perfumes and flowers.
Having established the Lord of Beings (Bhūtānātha), one should sprinkle him with water from the pitcher;
the others, the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās), one should sprinkle in the directions in their proper order.

The preceptor and the sacrificer, having circumambulated the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) and worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, should prostrate before the Lord of Beings (bhūtanāyaka). || 19.57 ||
One should worship the Lord of Beings with milk-rice, rice mixed with sesame, and rice with jaggery combined with ghee, along with curd, honey, and fruits. (19.58)
Then the preceptor should cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given to the guardians of the image;
thereafter, he should perform the ceremonial bath (snapana) of the God of gods according to his ability, as previously described.
Then, with the remnants of the bath water held in jars, the preceptor, together with the image-keepers,
should sprinkle those attendants and worship them with perfumes and other offerings.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
Now I shall explain in brief the supreme ritual for the festival, without which Keśava, even though installed, does not become propitious. 20.1
A year, half a year, or three months; or a month, or a fortnight in the event of impossibility;
or even nine days, seven days, or five days—beyond this, it is not permitted.
In the month of Māgha, or Mārgaśīrṣa, or indeed Caitra or Vaiśākha,
or Pauṣa or Phālguna, one should perform the festival with great elaboration.
One should regularly perform every year, according to one's ability, the accomplishment of all goals;
on an auspicious day at the commencement of a festival, one should carry out the installation of the banner.

Having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the planting of auspicious mango sprouts on the first day of the four-week period, ending with the Śravaṇā constellation and concluding with a ritual bath at a sacred ford (tīrtha), [one should perform the rite]. 20.5.
Devoted to Viṣṇu, one should perform the festival for Viṣṇu with devotion;
at the commencement of the festival, one should erect a banner bearing the emblem of Garuḍa.
And in the eight directions, according to rule, he should erect eight radiant banners and other ornaments;
once the raising of the flag has been performed, one is not overcome by any obstacles whatsoever.
Then, together with the water-pot, the hoisting of the banner should be performed;
having constructed a pavilion as before, one should prepare a well-surrounded altar.
The generation of the fire and the ritual preparation of the pitchers and the images should be performed;
the flagstaff must be made straight, firm, and free from blemishes or cracks. (20.9)
One who is not engaged in other work, who is not withered, and has not fallen of his own accord,
should be accepted during the conjunctions of Puṣya and so forth, at an auspicious moment, accompanied by favorable omens.

Having first had the Brahmins recite benedictions and the like, being pure, bathed, and well-adorned, he was accompanied by such twice-born men and joined by shouts of "Victory! and other auspicious sounds. (20.11)
Facing the northeast, the Guru, having cut down a bamboo pole with an axe smeared with honey and clarified butter,
should bring it forward and bathe it with auspicious jars.
One should worship with clay, astringents, medicinal herbs, and sacred waters, as well as with perfumes and flowers;
and an auspicious white banner should be made to hang from it.
It should hang down level with one-third of the peak of the temple;
it should be encircled by *darbha* grass and provided with bells, chowries, and mirrors.
There, one should have a portrait drawn in the presence [of the deity], delighting the family of the Vinatās,
with [the body] extending from the knees to the navel and neck, and colored white, yellow, reddish-brown, and black respectively.
Difficult for both gods and daityas to behold, with eyes ablaze with flames,
supporting the eight primordial serpent-kings beginning with Ananta, and possessing a dark-tipped nose.
Having mentally invoked him who resembles a thousand suns, the knower of mantras should place him [there] and worship him with perfumes and flowers using this mantra: 20.17.
The eight-syllable mantra beginning with "Tārā" and ending with "pakṣirājāya hūṃ" should indeed take the form of the vocative case during both the invocation and the dismissal.
Having worshipped [the deity] on the bed with sandalwood paste, garlands, offerings, and meditations, one should cause it to dwell there;
and one should perform the fire-oblation according to the rules with mantras beginning with the consonants of the first class and ending with those from *ka* to *sa*.

With oblations ending in the word *huta* and preceded by the *praṇava*, one should offer sesame seeds mixed with rice in the four directions using the four syllables following the *ca*-group, excluding the nasal (*ṅa*).
One should offer one thousand and eight oblations of clarified butter mixed with the foot-mantra of Vainateya, as well as all four kinds of food offerings.
And one should offer a bali-oblation all around to the spirits dwelling upon the banner,
as well as to the attendants who are spirits numbering many tens of millions.
Having thus worshipped at dawn, one should satisfy the Brahmins;
for he is the very embodiment of Viṣṇu’s banner and vehicle, possessing the prowess of Viṣṇu.
"May Suparṇa, the delighter of Vinatā’s clan, be pleased with me.
Having uttered this, one should then proceed toward the temple of the deity. 20.24.
Taking up the banner together with those twice-born ones who bear the forms of the gods,
one should consecrate the banner at an auspicious moment amidst the sounds of Vedic recitations, musical instruments, and the like.
Having placed pearls, emeralds, and gold in the pit, one should cause it to be filled. [One should worship] with this hymn of praise for the Lord of Birds: "Oṃ!

Salutations to the one adorned by the serpents of the eight families; to the one whose limbs are smeared with the blood of serpents; to the one who causes agitation among the inhabitants dwelling in the seven netherworlds; to the one capable of shaking great mountains; to the one with reddish-brown eyes; to the vehicle of Puruṣottama; to the one who brings joy to Vinatā; to the one who agitates the three worlds; to the subduer of gods, dānavas, gandharvas, and uragas; to the churner of the nectar; to the one who bewildered the serpents for the sake of his mother—slay, slay the obstacles! Destroy them! Svāhā! Having praised that Lord of Birds with this hymn of praise, [one should proceed]. (20.26)
One should always invoke the presence of that king of birds there;
from that time forward, the rākṣasas do not approach that place.
Because of the Piśācas and the venomous serpents, the raising of the banner should therefore be performed,
as well as the ceremonial bathing of the temple.
One should fill a bright water-pot with various auspicious fruits, all kinds of grains, as well as white flowers and fragrant scents. (20.29)
The manner in which the principles (tattvas) are to be installed was first explained to you;
furthermore, the sacrificer, together with his followers, [performs this] for the banner and the temple.
Having performed three circumambulations, he should then proceed to the avabhṛtha bath;
having entered a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), he should there again invoke the Gaṅgā.
O Goddess! O Viṣṇupadī! O Pure One! O Dispeller of all sins!
Your names are indeed Nandinī, as well as Nalinī and Mālinī.
O daughter of Dakṣa, O bird, O beloved of all beings!
I have come to you for refuge; release me from my sins without delay.
Having meditated and recited this mantra, one should stir the water with the hand and immerse oneself;
all others who immerse themselves here shall likewise be freed from sin.
There, one should satisfy the sages, gods, and seers with the root-mantras and their limbs;
thus, there shall be for them satisfaction lasting twelve years.
At the conclusion of the initiation (dīkṣā) and at the conclusion of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), one should likewise perform the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha);
it becomes meritorious, equal to all sacred fords (tīrtha)—of this there is no doubt.
Having likewise erected other banners marked with the insignia of the guardians of the directions,
one should worship them in the quarters with their respective mantras and offer a sacrificial oblation (bali) to all of them.
Having swept the village streets and sprinkled them with scented water,
one should then scatter beautiful and fragrant flowers all around.
And in the regions on the outskirts of the village, at the boundaries of the village, at crossroads, in sacred groves, in cow-pens, and in temples of the gods. (2.39)
One should adorn it with arches, banners, and circular pavilions,
as well as with plantains, coconut palms, sugarcane, betel-nut trees, and trees bearing flowers and fruits.
One should create beauty on all sides with lamps, pavilions, and mechanical devices;
at the sacrificial sessions, one should offer oblations accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having worshipped according to the rule, especially during festivals,
and having bathed [the deity] with pure water, milk, curd, clarified butter, and scents.

Having smeared him with products of the cow and coconut water, and having anointed him with well-blended fragrances, he was clothed in beautiful, freshly dyed silken garments and perfumed with excellent incense.
With various beautiful and meritorious flowers, especially with garlands and wreaths, and by fumigating [the area] on all sides with incense and the like, [one should worship]. 20.44.
One should worship with devotion using ornaments of gold and jewels, as well as lamps, and abundant, delicious foods accompanied by side dishes and mixed with clarified butter. (20.45)
With four kinds of offerings such as curds, milk, and molasses,
it was filled with song, music, and instrumental performance, bringing great joy to the devotees.
Then, one should cause a festival to be held, abounding in various kinds of food;
having performed the daily offering, one should further present the festival offering there.
And everything should be performed with particular care, accompanied by all auspicious rites;
women and twice-born men should be joyful, and there should be devoted reciters of victory-hymns. (20.48)
Having circumambulated the deity, they are liberated from all sins;
and here they should celebrate a grand festival with dance, song, and other such performances. (20.49)
The preceptor should proceed slowly in a clockwise direction and offer the sacrificial oblation;
he should perform this in the same manner for as many days as are ordained for the festival.
Devotees should scatter perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, garlands, and various auspicious fruits over the marriage-thread (kautuka) or the wheel of time (kālacakra).
Having thus performed the circumambulation three times according to the rule for six days,
one should then, on the seventh day, perform the flower-sacrifice dear to Hari.
Having slept on the ground the previous day, self-restrained and eating only sacrificial food,
he should fast through the night and perform the binding of the protective amulet for the deity.
Having worshipped the image of the deity in a well-decorated pavilion,
[one should perform the rite] with vessels containing sprouts placed in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Having first had the offering of ghee performed by Vaiṣṇavas,
and having displayed the auspicious mirror amidst the sounds of victory and auspiciousness, [he should proceed].
One should tie the protective amulet on the right hand while reciting "jitaṃ te" (Victory to you!);
at that time, the binding of the amulet must also be performed for the preceptor.
One should fan the image with yak-tail whisks and palm-leaf fans amidst auspicious rites,
having placed it upon its bed while lamps are kept burning without being extinguished.
One should remain seated for the remainder of the night, fumigating with incense and the like;
then, having bathed in the morning, performed worship, and recited auspicious verses, [one should proceed]. || 20.58 ||
And here, one should have flour-dust prepared for the circumambulation of the village;
[this should be done] at a new, clean mortar, adorned with dūrvā grass and other such items.
Having smeared that image or the original icon with very auspicious substances mixed with clarified butter by Vaiṣṇava female servants or by Brahmins, [one should proceed]. (20.60)
Having thoroughly rubbed [the image] all over with gold powder and other substances,
one should place it upon the heads of the devotees, who are mixed with turmeric and mung beans.
One should likewise rub the image with fragrant powders,
and then bathe it in the center of the altar with waters filled from sacred fords (tīrtha).
And that water, mixed with fragrant substances, should be poured upon the heads of the devotees;
having given it, one should again worship according to the prescribed rite while offering gold dust.

Having bathed and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should again scatter mustard seeds and unbroken grains (akṣata) upon the altar that has been purified on all sides and equipped with four archways (toraṇa).
One should adorn it with water-pots, sprouts, lamps, mirrors, and so forth; and one should hang garlands there, including strings of pearls on all sides.
Having first performed the ritual demarcation of the ground for Kumbheśa and Vardhanī,
and having traced the lines here as before, one should have a flower-mandala constructed.
With auspicious flowers of five colors that were unfading and fragrant—mandāra, yellow koraṇḍa, lotuses, and even bilva leaves—(he honored him). 20.67.
Free from recitation and other such rites, purified according to the division of their respective armor-mantras,
there is in the center a beautiful eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
One should fashion it with either six or twelve petals;
the pericarp should be made yellow, and the filaments red in color.
In this case, the joints should be green and the petals white;
one should draw either a *bhadraka* or a lotus-wheel (*cakrābja*) there, according to one's preference.
In the outer enclosure, there are eight lotuses with eight petals each,
made of flowers for the forms of the deities and likewise for the goddesses.
In the same way, for the mudrās, the world-protectors (lokapālas), and likewise for the two enclosures (āvaraṇa),
one should fashion the lotuses of their forms with the measurement of half an initial padma.
One should fashion the seals for Indra and the other [deities] with half that size;
likewise, one should fashion those for Vainateya and Viṣvaksena with the same measure.
One should cause the western door to be opened, and there should be pathways all around;
in the region of Puṣpadanta, there should be a passage for those carrying the images.
In this manner, one should fashion lotuses made entirely of flowers in every respect;
all the exterior parts, such as the doors and so forth, should be arranged according to what is aesthetically pleasing.
Having worshipped the Yoga-pīṭha together with its limbs and its equipment,
one should place the image of the Primordial Lotus within the pericarp.
One should worship the deity as before, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the rules;
and upon those lotuses, the forms, powers, weapons, and world-protectors are to be worshipped.
Having worshipped according to the rule with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and excellent food, one should commence the fire-rite.
Having first placed four offering-bowls to the four directions around the fire,
he prepared four sacrificial pots according to his means.
As before, having divided the consecrated firewood into four parts— or even one—
having performed the rites of spreading the base (upastaraṇa) and so forth, he should first offer it as an oblation.
One should offer the second oblation into the fire, smeared with clarified butter, just as before;
having given the third to the attendants, one should finally present the bali offering.
One should cause [the child] to eat the fourth portion mixed with clarified butter, leaving the remainder as before;
one should give gold as a sacrificial fee and feed the Brahmins. (20.82)
One should please the Lord of All with dances, songs, and other such offerings, with abundant hymns of praise and Vedic recitations, and with the worship of Vaiṣṇavas. 20.83.
On the twelfth lunar day and likewise under the Śravaṇa asterism, the wise man should perform the sacrifice;
he should perform the Viṣṇu-sacrifice every seventh [day] without weariness.
Having performed it likewise for a year, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
as also during the solstices, the equinoxes, and during lunar and solar eclipses.
By performing the desired rites on the Viṣṇupañcamī at the time of the transit [of the sun], one shall obtain the fruit;
on the first day, during the night, one should perform the circumambulation of the village.
One should perform circumambulation during the day and on the remaining days as well;
and one should offer oblations to all beings everywhere, both inside and outside.
During the time of circumambulation, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) within the mandalas; those who present the oblation must proceed in front of the sacred thread (kautuka). 20.88.
One should perform the scattering of the bali offering, provided with perfumes, flowers, and the like, accompanied by the gift of water, and display the bali-mudrā.
Of the lords whose banners bear the kumuda and other [emblems], there are fifty leaders of the gaṇas;
likewise, they exist by the hundreds and by the thousands. 20.90.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
Now I shall describe in brief his auspicious and inauspicious journey:
a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrtha) is to be known as auspicious, while that which takes place within one's own home is inauspicious.
Having performed a festival on the preceding day, one should offer a great oblation at night to the attendants of Viṣṇu, saying: "Salutations, salutations to the Pramathas! (21.2)
"Salutations again and again to the Mothers and to all their attendants!
Having thus offered [oblations] in every direction, he should enter and offer prayers as before.

On a seat provided with a covering, having worshipped the deity with recitations for a holy day and auspicious blessings, and having performed the tying of the marriage-thread (kautuka), one should then recite hymns of praise and so forth.
Having bathed and being well-adorned in the morning, and having performed the sacrifice previously described,
he offered oblations with the six mantras beginning with "kanikradat" and the five beginning with "svasti."
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of sacrificial wood, clarified butter, and cooked rice in sequence with the root mantra,
and having examined the omens, he should then undertake the ritual bath and procession.
One should bring for him a chariot or an elephant as a vehicle for his journey, as well as many attendants skilled in various musical instruments. (21.7)
Having summoned the umbrellas, banners, and flags, as well as the soldiers, servants, attendants, and brahmins, the preceptor [performed the rites] at an auspicious moment.
Having had the "auspicious day" (puṇyāha) proclaimed there and having received permission from the best of the twice-born,
he circumambulated the deity, prostrated himself, and stood before him.
Having placed the ritual image upon the pedestal, one should gently inform it of the task:
"O Hari! This ritual image has been prepared for the purpose of a pilgrimage. (21.10)
"Perform a pilgrimage to sacred sites, departing from here for our benefit;
then, having withdrawn that image and having produced it according to the prescribed rites," (21.11)
In that [image], one should invoke the deity in sequence with the five Upaniṣads;
having recollected the deity as invoked, and having offered the arghya water and performed worship, [one should proceed].
One should wrap [the image] in a pair of new, high-quality garments;
wearing a turban and an upper robe, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), and being composed in mind.
Taking him by the right hand himself, remaining silent,
and surrounded by his disciples, he should proceed to the well-decorated pavilion.
There, all the twice-born ones should perform an auspicious rite endowed with every blessing, and they should likewise say, "So be it. (21.15)
Having reached the door of the pavilion and offered the arghya water together with the image-keepers (mūrtipāḥ),
and having circumambulated the temple, he should then go outside once more.
The best of the twice-born would break the water-pot, the sacrificial oblation, the parasol, the implements of sacrifice, and other vessels containing sprouts. (21.17)
Having gone outside with a great clamor, he himself, remaining silent,
meditated upon his vehicle Garuḍa, worshipped him, and ascended it.
One should go within a yojana to a river or another body of water;
having first performed a circumambulation to the right outside the enclosure wall with the directional mantra (diṅmantra).
Let them all proceed, restrained in speech, wearing upper garments and well-adorned; let the people along the path raise a clamor with musical instruments and the sounds of song and dance.
They should also perform [the rites] with various vehicles for the satisfaction of the gods;
having gone within the archway to the pavilion situated beside the sacred bathing place (tīrtha). || 21.21 ||
Having constructed an enclosed altar, one should seat the deity upon a pedestal;
there, in some secluded place, those who have been initiated should have milk-rice cooked.
Having offered water for the feet and other honors, and taking everything with him, he should go to the river;
there, having invoked the purifying Vaiṣṇava sacred site (tīrtha) by means of water.
Having immersed himself three times at this sacred ford with the mantra of Parameṣṭhin,
