he established [the deity] upon the pedestal and offered the arghya, water for the feet, and water for sipping.
Having sprinkled [the water] with the five verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," being composed in mind,
he should take that [water] and plunge again into the water after performing the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite.
They know that bathing there is of great merit and removes all sins;
having seated [the image] upon a pedestal and personally clothed it in two new garments. (21.26)
Having sipped water and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), he should worship again according to the prescribed rule;
having offered the food to be presented along with clarified butter, he should give it to him according to the rite.
O Supreme Person, you have bathed in this meritorious Vaiṣṇava tīrtha;
therefore, favor us by taking up residence in our own abode. (21.28)
Having thus prayed and taken him, one should lead the vehicle as before;
having mounted it, one should quickly lead him to the palace as previously described.
On the very day of the procession, one should bring [the deity] home and then transfer it into the image;
otherwise, a great fault will certainly befall the performers here. || 21.30 ||
Having entered the inner sanctum and seated [the image] upon the pedestal,
being well-composed, he should mentally invoke [the deity] with water, perfumes, and flowers, accompanied by mantras.
One should install everything in the primary image according to the rule;
this is remembered as the procedure for invocation at the beginning of a procession and likewise at its conclusion. || 21.32 ||

Having worshipped [the deity] who has been made manifest through the sakalīkaraṇa rite, having offered the arghya water, and having prostrated, one should exit while blocking the door; and here, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas.
One should likewise offer the bali-oblation at night; thus has the auspicious journey been described by me.
Now, let the inauspicious [journey] for the purpose of securing a dwelling be explained and understood.
When the temple has become dilapidated and decayed— whether it be a clay image or a painted one—
one should transfer the deity to a new house according to this ritual procedure.
Whether it be Parjanya or Jayanta, because of their origin from Diti and Aditi,
he stood as the gatekeeper at the eastern or western gate, stationed like a deer at the entrance.
A new, auspicious, small house facing the door of the palace,
having a single story and a prominent neck, constructed either of mud or of wood.
Then, one should have a beautiful wooden pedestal made with a hollow cavity;
subsequently, one should fashion an image made of metal or wood, or even of clay in times of distress.
When the time limit has been properly established, a complete transference is desired here;
they declare that the duration of time in this case extends from one month up to twelve years. (21.39)
Having thoroughly cleansed the new house and performed everything as previously described,
one should first perform the rite for the destruction of Rākṣasas and then carry out all other rituals.
Furthermore, one should have a pavilion constructed according to the prescribed method for its installation;
it should be provided with banners and arches and adorned with sprouts and other offerings.
Having sprinkled [the ground] with cow products and with the Astra-mantra, one should draw a svastika in the center;
having prepared an altar (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains, one should spread cloths over it.
One should place rice grains upon it and spread it over with blankets and the like;
then one should worship it with kuśa grass, garments, flowers, perfumes, and so forth.
Having bathed the image of the deity in water and having washed it with auspicious waters—
namely, water mixed with clay, water from leaves, decoctions, and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)— [he should proceed].
Having adorned it with perfumes and flowers and covered it with cloths,
one should lay it down amidst the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and the like.
For seven nights, during the twilights, one should offer oblations to the deities:
"May all the deities who have taken refuge in this palace hear me! (21.46)
May you favor what we are saying;
for this temple of the gods was previously built by our ancestors, yet it is devoid of substance.
Having once again come under the power of time, we are now prepared to perform that very same act;
after all this time, once more in this newly renovated palace.
Having said, "We shall fulfill the truth," the wise man should make the proclamation;
however, if the time is less than a month away, a reduction in that period is permitted.
Having likewise extracted all the principles (tattvas) situated within the body of the palace in their proper order,
as well as the deities together with their retinues, [one should place them within the lotus].
Having meditated according to the path of withdrawal, the supreme teacher should duly dissolve all that form of radiant energy into the primary image.
Having performed that likewise above,
the Guru, accompanied by the image-keepers (mūrtipās), should enter the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) and begin the rite of transference.
Then, having caused the Brahmins to pronounce "an auspicious day," he should have them recite blessings;
and having performed a great worship of the God with devotion according to the prescribed rite.
Having prostrated and stood before him, he should announce his business slowly:
"O Blessed One! Your new temple and the image are beautiful. (21.54)
Your devotees will have it made for you; therefore, O Lord, you ought to grant us permission.
You, who dwell in hardship, must now be pleased to reside in this small dwelling.
"Once we have fashioned a new and beautiful one, we shall restore it;
meanwhile, let us prepare an iron jar, cleansed and wound with thread. (21.56)
Having placed the unhusked rice grains (*akṣata*) and other items along with the *pavitra* grass before the deity,
he should then go out together with them and begin the consecration of the image (*bimba*).
Having meditated upon the principles (tattvas) in their proper sequence through the yoga of dissolution and emanation,
and having offered those principles into the fire according to the prescribed rite in the order beginning with birth, [he should proceed].
Having gone out, the preceptor should again ask the performers:
"For how long, O Lord, will you dwell here in this temporary residence? (21.59)
The period of time is traditionally held to be from one month up to twelve years;
Vāsudeva does not permit a residence of suffering for less than that, nor for more.
Thus questioned, they shall state the limit of time without hesitation;
having proclaimed the fixed duration, the deity is led outside.
Then, having entered with a well-composed mind, he should inform the Lord of the time appointed by the officiants; thereafter, he should perform this rite.
At an auspicious moment, the preceptor, having performed the fire-oblation and other rites associated with the journey,
and having sacrificed to Vāstoṣpati, should immediately lead the deity outside.
Having worshipped the water-pot (kalaśa) filled [with water] and wrapped in cloth,
one should, according to the prescribed rule, fashion the Yoga-pīṭha within that jar.
Having invoked the eternal God of gods into that golden lotus— which was filled with water scented with gold and jewels— according to the prescribed rite, [he placed him there].
Having offered the arghya and worshipped him here with scents and flowers, accompanied by the five upaniṣadic mantras and the mantra-form, and having prostrated; 21.66.
Having carefully fashioned the image wrapped in cloth and other materials,
the Guru, maintaining silence and carrying a water-pot upon his head, should depart.
Accompanied by the sounds of conchs and drums, abundant shouts of victory,
and the chanting of the Vedas, they circumambulated the house.
Adorned with garments and ornaments, he should proceed slowly and with care,
accompanied by the recitation of auspicious hymns concerning birds, benedictory prayers, and invocations to the gods.
Having brought Hari into the inner pavilion, one should place him upon the bed;
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the twelve-syllable mantra and the root mantra.
And having performed praise with the Puruṣasūkta,
the wise one [should do so] with the Viṣṇusūkta, the Mūla-mantra, and with the twelve and eight [verses].
One should devoutly offer flowers with the names beginning with Keśava, using vessels either filled with śāli rice or filled with water. (21.72)
Having first arranged the jars beginning with the east, one should worship Keśava and the others;
having invoked all those deities with the *praṇava* alone, one should install them.

The deities of the forms (mūrtidevīs) are to be worshipped outside, and the mudrās and the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) further out; having praised and obtained permission from that deity, one should practice the first peace (śānti).
Having established the fires in the directional sacrificial pits as before, the bearers of the forms should commence the preliminary oblations (ādhivāsana-homas) as previously performed.
Having performed the oblation and obtained the permission of the deity, the preceptor should perform a rite of pacification;
then, having touched [the site] with mantras and recited them, he should wash it with the five products of the cow.
One should bathe [the image] first with decoctions of astringent herbs mixed with turbid water, both individually and collectively; then with water mixed with gold, and finally with pure water.
Having praised the deity with hymns, one should worship him in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
thereafter, one should place water-pots at all the entrances on every side.
One should collect materials for worship and for the fire-oblation, and one should appoint many skilled persons with musical instruments and cymbals in their hands. (21.79)
Having brought all this forward and having observed the signs,
he arranged the stations of the deities in their proper order.
When bad dreams and such occur, one should perform expiatory rites;
one should offer clarified butter into the fire a thousand or even a hundred times with the root mantra.
Amidst the proclamations of "Auspicious Day" and "Victory," at an auspicious moment, the preceptor circumambulated the deity; having received permission, he stood with palms joined in reverence.
Having worshipped the deity according to the prescribed rite with auspicious recitations for merit, victory, and well-being,
the preceptor should raise him up with the syllable Om and the Śākuna hymn.
Having brought [the image] with the Svastisūkta, he should enter while circumambulating it to the right;
having entered, he should inform Viṣṇu of the time appointed by them.
One should place the image there and utter this mantra:
"O Blessed One, O Hari! Even dwelling in this small house is a hardship for you. (21.85)
"O Blessed One, you should stay for as long as it takes to complete the house, while we witness the supreme and magnificent prosperity of the builder. (21.86)
"You ought to remain here for the sake of compassion toward your devotees.
Having said this, bowing slightly, one should sprinkle that water upon his head. (21.87)
Having meditated upon the mantras of the five Upaniṣads with his whole being,
the preceptor should then perform the Sṛṣṭinyāsa and recite the Puruṣasūkta.
Then, having joined [the deity] with the form (mūrti), one should worship according to the ritual procedure;
one should arrange the retinue and perform the fire-oblations for the directions.
Then one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and provide food and other offerings there;
furthermore, the wise man should perform whatever has not been mentioned here according to the ritual for consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
The agent would be fixed from the exit until the entry.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.

Now I shall explain, in brief and in due order, the ritual of the bali offering, which is prescribed for the three junctions of the day as a daily duty, and especially on festive occasions and the like. 22.1.
Having propitiated the deity in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings according to the prescribed rite,
one should present food to the deity in the consecrated fire that has been duly prepared.
With the very remnants of that [offering], one should prepare the vessel for the ritual worship of the deity's seat;
and even for the sake of the bali offering, one should cook it in the worldly fire without the use of mantras.
Having poured pure rice grains into a vessel with the root-mantra,
having sprinkled them and washed them three times, he then kindled the fire with splendor.
One should fan it with the wind of a fan so that the sacrificial oblation does not spill;
then, having sprinkled it with clarified butter and brought it down, one should place it upon the vessel.
Having spread a base of ghee in another vessel, having placed [the portion] therein and sprinkled ghee over it,
one should offer that portion with ghee to the deity and sacrifice the other portion in the fire.
Having smeared the ground with cow dung, one should place the vessel upon *darbha* grass;
it should be made of gold, silver, or copper, and its circular base should be one *ratni* in measure.

Having sprinkled [the vessel] thoroughly with water using the eight-syllable mantra and having properly turned it face upwards, one should pour the remainder of the oblation over it while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra). || 22.8 ||
With that [mud], one should fashion a pedestal where ritual worship is not intended;
otherwise, having smoothed it out and moistened it with curd and clarified butter, it becomes auspicious.
One should have a *śivaka* made by him, four fingers wide,
twelve or eight fingers high, or even six fingers.
Having placed gold upon the head and invoked Śakti,
one should worship her in the center as the essence of Parameṣṭhin, surrounded by Puruṣa and the others.
One should establish the image in that [liṅga], having invoked it with all [mantras] and the five [limbs];
or, having invoked Hari into gold, one should place Him there, surrounded by the forms of the [divine] colors, using the root mantra.
Having worshipped him with perfumes and flowers and meditated upon him as differentiated by the three times,
one should place that vessel upon the head of the twice-born initiate.
Adorned with the uṣṇīṣa and other ornaments, remaining silent, and having taken up the vyāhṛtis, he should mutter them;
then, standing before the deity and bowing down, he should go outside.
Resounding with the blasts of conchs and drums and with abundant shouts of victory,
it was endowed with the eight auspicious symbols and adorned with canopies and other ornaments.
The gods, nāgas, apsarases, yakṣas, sages, gandharvas, and kinnaras—
all these shall follow him, who is to be meditated upon as being enveloped by his own virtues.
There, those who have been consecrated should take up perfumes, flowers, water, incense, lamps, parasols, and fly-whisks, as well as auspicious items, sacrificial offerings, and bells.
Having gone out with the sounds of the lutes stilled, and with the permission of the Brahmins,
the Guru should recite auspicious verses, and the other twice-born ones should respond, "So be it."
May the gods, who are the lords of the gods and the causes of the creation, destruction, maintenance, and grace of the world, bestow auspiciousness upon us.
May Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Rudra, Pracaṇḍa, Caṇḍa, Garuḍa, and Ṛṣabha—may these grant us auspiciousness. 22.20.
May Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Vaiśravaṇa, and Īśāna grant us auspiciousness. 22.21.
May Varāha, Narasiṃha, Rāma, Śrīdhara, Vāmana, Hayāsya, and Vāsudeva bestow auspiciousness upon us.
May Pūru and Nirṛti, Siṃha and Nārāyaṇa-Acyuta, Aniruddha, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa, bestow auspiciousness upon us. 22.23.
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita.
May these gatekeepers of the gods grant us auspiciousness,
as well as those who are the one thousand and eight attendants of Viṣṇu.
And may the others who are not part of the retinue grant us auspiciousness.
The seven worlds, beginning with Bhūrloka and Bhuvarloka, have been proclaimed.
And may all the oceans likewise grant us auspiciousness,
as well as the worlds of the nether regions and the worlds of the Rudras where one dwells in happiness.
May they who abide in all directions grant us auspiciousness—
the Vedas and the auxiliary Vedas, along with the histories and the sacred narratives.
May the six-limbed sciences and the sacred texts grant us auspiciousness;
and may the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, as well as the Godāvarī and the Sarasvatī, do the same.
May the Narmadā and the Kāverī likewise grant us auspiciousness;
as well as the planets beginning with the Sun, and the zodiac signs beginning with Aries.
May the months, beginning with Vaiśākha and headed by Viṣṇu, grant us auspiciousness;
and may all the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), both those who are divine and those who are human, likewise grant it.
May those dwelling in heaven, the intermediate space, and on earth bestow auspiciousness upon us:
Dharā, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anala, and Anila. (22.32)
May Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa grant us auspiciousness;
likewise may the sacrifices, the five great sacrifices, and the domestic (pākayajña) rites do so as well.
May all sacrifices and great sacrifices grant us auspiciousness;
and may the maidens, the youths, the Gaṇeśas, and the Vināyakas likewise do so.
May the serpents and the kinnaras also grant us auspiciousness;
may Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, Nirṛti, and Aja Ekapāt [grant it].
May Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, Bhava, and likewise Īśvara, Sthāṇu, Bhava, and Pāpāri, grant us auspiciousness. 22.36.
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, Bhaga, Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Parjanya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu. (22.37)
May these twelve Ādityas indeed grant us auspiciousness:
Yavakrīta, Krīta, Arvāvasu, and Vibhāvasu.
May Kakṣīvat, Nārada, Kaṇva, Unmuci, Pramuci, Ātreya, and Agastya bestow auspiciousness upon us.
May Dṛḍhāyus, Idhmavāha, Maṅgala,
Dṛṣadguhya, Mahadguhya, and Parivrāja likewise grant us blessings.
May Kaśyapa, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Bhāradvāja, and likewise Aṅgiras—those proclaimed as one, two, and three [in number]—bestow auspiciousness upon us. (22.41)
May Kauśika and the Blessed One grant us auspiciousness;
likewise may Āvaha, Vivaha, Udvaha, and Suvaha [grant it].
May Parīvaha and Vivaha bestow auspiciousness upon us;
as well as Śvetaketu, Vyāsa, Vālmīki, and Suyaśas.
Aurvaśeya, Śakti, and likewise Parāśara—may these seven divine sages grant us auspiciousness. 22.44.
Thus, through the utterance of auspicious words, those deities grant success;
therefore, at the commencement of every undertaking, one should perform what is highly auspicious.
Having reached the door of the pavilion with the sounding of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments,
one should offer a sacrificial oblation (bali) consisting of scents, flowers, and other items to the gatekeepers and others.
Having worshipped them with these mantras and honored them with their own respective mantras,
one should offer the bali-oblation there, looking upon it with the vision of the gods.
Salutations to you, the gatekeeper Caṇḍa of immeasurable splendor,
who was born from the body of Narasiṃha and whose crown is marked with a discus.
Salutations to you, the gatekeeper Pracaṇḍa of immeasurable power,
born from the body of Narasiṃha, whose crown is marked with a conch shell.
Salutations to you, Garuḍa, the vehicle of Mahāviṣṇu, possessed of immeasurable splendor, the death of all the lords of serpents.
Salutations to you, O wise Śatakratu, destroyer of the pride of the Daityas, thousand-eyed one, whose hand is grasping the thunderbolt! May there be homage to you! 22.51.
Salutations to that consumer of oblations, who is the mouth of all the gods, by whom the sacrificial offering is conveyed,
and through whom everything proceeds.
O Lord of the Departed! Homage be to you, by whom all is withdrawn, by whom the Dharma is protected, and from whom this world stands in awe.
Salutations to that lord of the Rakshasas, who has the form of Nirṛti, and whom Rākṣasas, Yātudhānas, and Piśācas take as their refuge. 22.54.
Salutation to that Lord of Creatures, by whom everything is protected, in whom everything is established, and who holds the unfailing noose in his hand.
Salutations eternally to that Lord of Beings, O Lord of Maruts, by whom the vital breaths and the rest are filled and carried away in succession! 22.56
O Lord of Wealth, salutations to you, the master of Yakṣas and Guhyakas, by whose grace the entire world is filled with riches! 22.57
O son of Brahmā, Virūpākṣa, salutations be to you, that Kālāgni by whom the world is seized at the ends of the ages! 22.58
O Vīrabhadra, salutations be unto you; salutations also to Vighneśvara, and repeated salutations indeed to the seven Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī.
Salutations to you, O Śrīdhara; salutations to you who have the horse as your face.
Salutations again and again to all the Mothers, beginning with Vāgīśvarī.
O Viṣvaksena! Salutations be to you, the wearer of the divine remains of offerings;
O wielder of the conch, discus, and mace; O Lord of the great attendants!
May all the attendants of Viṣṇu, who abide pervading the entire world and desire offerings, accept this supreme oblation.
Having thus proclaimed in the directions outside with the eightfold hosts,
and having offered the *kumuda* and other oblations, one should present the offering upon the sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*).

With the mantra "ye bhūtā," one should satisfy all the attendants of Viṣṇu by making offerings with the fist at each of the cardinal directions, above, and in the center, for the sake of the Lord of Beings.
May those who dwell outside, with faces like birds, who are cruel and of little strength— the bhūtas, pretas, and night-stalkers— accept this offering.
And as for the Vetālas, the Mātaṅgas, and those hosts who are lowly or not lowly—
for all of them, I offer this most excellent oblation.
"Salutations again and again to all beings together with their hosts!
Having circumambulated three times to the right, one should gratify the hosts with offerings. (22.67)
At each and every libation, having offered incense, flowers, and so forth, accompanied by dance, song, and the like, one should finally pour the remainder of the bali offering into water.
Reciting "Oṃ, obeisance to the attendants of Viṣṇu," he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana); being pure, mindful of Viṣṇu, and composed, he should enter.
Having placed that entire image back [in its place], one should again join it to the base;
one should cause all that, along with the garland and the oblation, to be offered to Viṣvaksena.
But if the food-ball (piṇḍa) or the vessel for the offering (balipātra) has fallen or become defiled,
one should wash that [spot], bathe there, and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in the proper order.
Having quickly enclosed that ground, one should smear it with cow dung;
then, having cooked there very beautiful milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with ghee.
Having drawn a svastika there with powders made of rice and turmeric,
and having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with grains of rice, he spread a cloth over it.
Having sprinkled [the vessel] with rice, kuśa grass, and flowers while reciting the Astra mantra,
the concentrated practitioner should place the vessel with the Mūla mantra and then touch it with the Pravaṇa mantra.
Having again sprinkled [the site] with the Astra-mantra, one should worship Śānti on the right;
having performed the rites beginning with the drawing of lines (ullekhana), one should consecrate the fire according to the prescribed rule.
Having offered the food with the root mantra and the clarified butter with the Praṇava,
one hundred and eight or even a thousand times, according to the sequence.
Thereafter, one should place the remnants of the oblation into the vessel for the bali offering;
having done that and sprinkled it as before, the invocation (āvāhana) should be performed with the root mantra.

Then, having offered the lotus for worship, one should honor it with perfumes and flowers; having prostrated and praised it with hymns, one should make this offering: 78. Having offered the lotus for worship, one should then honor it with perfumes and flowers; having prostrated and praised it with hymns, one should thus present this [offering].
O Blessed One! By your grace, this rite of expiation for the offering of the bali has been performed by me; may it be complete and grant us peace. (22.79)
Having caused the Brahmins to pronounce "an auspicious day," he should have them recite blessings;
then, having paid homage and offered praise, he should remain composed, wearing his upper garment.
Having extracted the *vyāhṛtis* and recited them, one should place [the water] upon the head with the *tāra*.
Then, accompanied by conchs, trumpets, and other instruments, one should proceed slowly in circumambulation.
Afterwards, the wise one should cause it to enter within and place it in the northeast;
having removed the food and cast it outside, he should offer it to Viṣvaksena.
Having washed the vessel with water and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) himself according to the rule,
he should place the vessel in the temple and then perform a rite for peace (śāntika).

The wise one, following the procedure for the zodiacal wheel (rāśicakra), should worship Keśava and the others in their proper order within the lotus of the wheel, accompanied by the fire-ritual (agnikārya).

One should also satisfy the lord of the direction where the offering falls, the presiding deity of that month, and likewise the deities of the lunar day, the asterism, the day of the week, and the zodiac sign.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for Offering the Bali Oblation," in the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
Now, for the benefit of all the worlds, I shall briefly describe the worship of Viśva, which bestows all prosperity and is accompanied by the division of the directions. 23.1.
When the deity has been installed according to the rules, one should worship him in the prescribed manner;
the worship of the Viśvedevas should also be performed for the sake of prosperity, or at all times.
In the center, one should worship Viṣṇu along with his limbs (the retinue), and then the deities in the cardinal and intermediate directions:
Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, and Aniruddha, starting from the east.
Viśvarūpa, Vaikuṇṭha, and Sarvabhāvana—
these lords of knowledge bear the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Those who possess the form of Viṣṇu, together with their attendants, should always be worshipped individually;
likewise, the eight Śaktis beginning with Bhṛśā, who are beautiful and grant all desires. || 23.5 ||
Wisdom, intellect, memory, fame, sacred learning, intelligence, fortitude, and forgiveness;
the conch, the Sudarśana discus, the plow, the mace, the club, and the sword.
Outside of that, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, are a bow, eight excellent garlands,
vajras, staffs, tridents, nooses, and likewise other weapons.
Then one should worship Śakti, the weapons, the Vaiṣṇava missile, the Bhṛśadīṣu, as well as the armor for the missiles, the trident, and the battle-axe.
Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Soma, Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśāna— these eight guardians of the world (lokapālas) are situated outside of that.
The Ādityas, the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, the Vighnanāyakas, Skanda, the Rudras, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins [are present] in the Bhṛśa and other [wind-courses]. || 23.10 ||
The hosts of outer planets are to be worshipped, as well as the hosts of ancestors and yakṣas,
the gandharvas, all elemental beings, Ambikā, and likewise the rākṣasas.
The Vidyādharas and Siddhas are all to be worshipped by their respective names;
then the Apsarases, the world-mothers (Mātṛs), the Kūṣmāṇḍas, and the Piśācas.
Nāgas, kinnaras, serpents, and diseases were present in great numbers;
furthermore, Nandana and Kumuda stood as gatekeepers on the right and left.
In the middle of the house-gateway, the banner and the horse are to be worshipped;
within that [space], the chariot; and in the center of the lord of houses (the hall), Parjanya, Indra, and the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) should be present.
Suvarcā, the lord of the jar, is to be worshipped within the Puṃśaṅkha;
Balākhya, the lord of the pavilion, is to be honored in the middle of the city palace.
In a treasury, he is inexhaustible; likewise, in a water reservoir, he is worthy of worship;
in an assembly hall, he is marvelous; and in the kitchen, he brings about great prosperity.
Unmāda was in the kitchen, Tarpaṇa in the dining hall,
Kundara in the flower garden, and likewise Vikṣara at the gateway.
Both Bala and Atibala, the guardians of Bali, are to be worshipped on the throne;
Vikaṭa and Virūpākṣa are the protectors of the eastern gate.
The two gatekeepers stationed at the right and left, bearing maces and of terrifying form—
Sanātana and Sanaka— are the guardians of the southern gate.
Those bearing swords and mallets should be worshipped with diligence;
and those in the west, holding staffs and nooses, should be worshipped as both peaceful and joyful.
In the north are Sarvada and Sarvadamana, both carrying bows and quivers;
Caraka is outside in the northeast, while Pūtana is in the southeast.
In the southwest, outside the wind-god's region, is the Rākṣasa Pāpacāraka;
in the east is the lord of the sacrificial pedestal (Balipīṭha), and the god Nandikara is in the south.
Behind them were Vibhīṣaṇa, Saumya, the guardians of the easily accessible sites (sulabhasthānapālakas),
those Mothers who have not been mentioned, Ananta, and Viṣvaksena, the commanders of the banners.
Revanta and the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas) are indeed to be worshipped here and there;
they number sixty-four when standing or sitting, and eighty-one when lying down.

The common [measurement] is threefold, consisting of a hundred [units]; one should arrange the internal division of the enclosure wall, the inner quadrangle, and the palace, each being double [the size of the preceding]. (23.25)
On the right, one should depict Nandana as a gatekeeper with four arms holding a mace;
likewise, on the left, one should depict Kumuda holding a sword and a noose.
One should construct the temple on the seat to the left, measuring half of a half-finger-breadth;
the temples for the retinue should each be one hundred [units] deep, with their bases entering the main structure.
Just as the sixty-four deities associated with the *saṃgama* are distinct,
so too is the conceptualization of the womb and other stages described in the *Śatapada*.

At the fourth conjunction of Āryaman, one should construct the abode of Puruṣa and others; at the first conjunction of Vivasvat, Mitra, and the Mountains, one should construct the abode of Sāvitrī and others.
One should thus assign the locations for Viśva and the others in their respective order:
Aryaman at the third confluence, and Vivasvat at the fifth.
In the third [generation] from that friend, in the fifth from him,
in the third from that mountain-king, and in the fifth from him, in the third from Aryaman— (23.31)
Thus, the ālayas of Prajñā and the others have been proclaimed in their respective order;
those beginning with Śaṅkha are the [ālayas] of the four beginning with Aryaman at the first conjunction.
Likewise, the abodes of Musala and the others are at the junction of Sāvitra and the rest;
and at each junction, there are twelve [deities] beginning with Aryaman and Sāvitra, two by two.
Then, setting aside a certain sūtra, one should fashion the weapons such as the vajra;
the Vajradaṇḍa and others, along with their respective weapons, should be established together with the hosts of bhūtas.
From the conjunction with the Sun and Indra, the world-protectors beginning with Indra reside in the eight positions;
likewise in the conjunction of Bhṛśa and Khaya, and similarly in Gṛha, Kṣata, and Vaitatha.
And likewise of Gandharva and Bhṛṅgin, as well as of the gatekeepers Sugrīva and Sumantra, and of the two chief Nāgas named Śvāsa and Śoṣaṇa, and of the two called Diti and Ṛka.
Furthermore, other hosts of deities belonging to Jaya and Parjanya are to be worshipped;
outside, however, are the planets and others belonging to Arka, Yama, Varuṇa, Īśa, and Soma.
Outside the northeast [of Agni] and outside the [direction of] the Pitṛs [the northeast], Caṇḍikā and others should be placed;
outside the sky [the zenith], the Apsarases; and in the southeast (Pūṣan), the Pitṛs, Bhadra, and Vināyaka.
The Kūṣmāṇḍas are in Mṛga, the Piśācas when [Mṛga] is in Dvāra, the Ahi snakes in Śoṣaṇa, the Kinnaras in Mukhya, the Sarpas in Argala, and the Vyādhis in Śiva. (23.39)
A wise man should cause a red-colored reservoir of water to be made for Satya,
as well as for the Rākṣasas Caraka, Vidāra, and Pūtana.
The houses of Īśa, Agni, Pitṛ, and Roga are said to be in the outer corners;
outside of those, however, is the boundary wall with its lofty gate-towers.
The sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) should be constructed according to the scriptures outside the gopura;
however, the location for the flagstaff (dhvaja) is prescribed within the Śakra-gopura. 23.42.
There, the abodes of the horse, the chariot, and Tārkṣya should be arranged in order around [the central shrine];
the Lord of the Vessel (Kalaśādhipa) is to be placed in the middle of the conch-shaped gateway.
Likewise, the superintendent of the pavilion should remain stationed within the city temple;
and at the junction with Bhallāṭa, one should establish the treasury.
In Mahendra, however, there is the assembly hall; in Satya, the dining hall;
in Pūṣan, the kitchen; in Mṛga, the flower garden; and in Puṣpadanta, the water outlet.
Or that well may be situated in the region of Satya; it should be made in the domain of Aditi.
In the Asura region, however, is the location of Bali; scent is proclaimed to be in the region of Roga.
Īśa, Agni, the Pitṛs, and Roga are the deities residing in the corners;
the abode of Kṣetrapāla is at the bolt (argala), and that of the Teacher (Śāstṛ) is indeed at the threshold (bhṛṅga).
This procedure for the worship of Viṣṇu has been described for one facing east;
however, for one facing west, the positions of the banner and the other emblems shall be reversed.
Then the arena should be in the Asura quarter and the sacrificial pavilion (balimaṇḍapa) in the Satya quarter;
the water-channel should be in the Mahendra quarter—this is the rule for the hundred squares.
The other four located at the confluence are the Saṅgameśvaras;
this much is proclaimed here as the distinction among the sixty-four.
Kumuda and Karavīra are the two four-armed doorkeepers;
at the fourth confluence in front of Aryaman is the abode of Garuḍa.
The palaces of Subhadra, Subāhu, Vijaya, Bala,
Kumuda, Muni, and Viṣvaksena were likewise there.
The forms of the Gaṇeśas are proclaimed to be fashioned in the directions beginning with the southeast (Āgneya);
all of them should be made four-armed, bearing a mace, a discus, and a sword. 23.53.
Golden, conch-white, blue-cloud-colored, black, tawny, pale-yellow, and dark-blue—
these are proclaimed as the world-protectors stationed at the directions beginning with the southeast (Aryaman).
The deities of the field's perimeter should be placed upon the rampart;
then, in front of the Sun, the discus should be placed upon the pedestal of the gate-tower.
Then, in the four corners, the place of the Rākṣasas is described;
and around the eighty-one [squares], there are three squares each in a count of three.
The lords of the Gaṇas and the masters of the quarters should be depicted established in their own positions;
one should perform the remaining sequence of Viṣṇu’s enclosures as previously specified.
The dwellings of the Rākṣasas should be constructed at the corners of the outer wall;
likewise, the gate-towers and other structures should be made provided with sacrificial pedestals (balipīṭha).
Having thus constructed a temple for Viṣṇu according to this injunction,
one attains all desires and shall go again to the abode of Viṣṇu.
The conch, discus, mace, sword, pestle,
plow, bow, goad, and garland— these are proclaimed here as their respective abodes.
The weapons of Hari should be depicted with the luster of milk, gold, sapphire, blood, a lotus, a cloud, fire, and lightning,
joined at their tips to his own body.
The eastern [directions] should be immovable, while the others should be stable yet flexible;
they should be made facing one another, as well as others oriented north and south.
In front of the temple of the god Sthāneśvara, which was established in former times, a new sanctuary should be built by those free from enemies; no other site should be chosen.
Whoever acts here out of ignorance shall lose his station along with his prosperity;
furthermore, both [the door and the window] should not be made facing each other in the temple of a deity.
When two [kings] stand back-to-back, it leads to the destruction of both the king and his kingdom;
one should not act in such a way as to have their backs turned, for if that is done, another will be installed in their place.

One must never, under any circumstances, place [the image] with its head inverted upon a single pedestal; for whichever direction the principal [deity] faces, all the other deities shall face that same direction.
The attendants must always be positioned facing the principal deity;
they should be arranged along a single line in proper sequence and not placed in reverse order. (23.67)
The mutual gazing of two people with their right eyes is to be known as auspicious; likewise, the gazing with the left eyes is to be understood as inauspicious.
Furthermore, one should not perform even the ritual of the retinue by transgressing the prescribed measurement;
rather, one should have it made while leaving aside at least one finger-breadth or a golaka.
The seat in the middle of the village is desired to face the east;
likewise, the location should be facing the village, either in the east or in the west.
The bed should be placed in the southern direction facing west;
however, in the northern direction, the bed should indeed face east.
The orientation must be determined solely according to the division of the site;
otherwise, reservoirs should be constructed to the south of the front of the temple, or facing all directions.
One should not direct [the image] toward Rudra, nor toward a village or even a city;
nor should it be placed in a high location, for such places as fortresses are not desired.
Where Viṣṇu is situated in a low position and other deities are in high positions,
that place or indeed the entire kingdom shall perish before long.
In the forest, on a mountain, at a sacred ford, on a riverbank, or at a confluence, one should,
with faith and through proper means, acquire land and other resources in a sacred field.
One who is established in his own portion should diligently worship the deity established in that deity’s portion,
avoiding the Paiśāca and Āsura rites.
Or one should worship the God of gods who has reached the station of Brahmā,
remaining in his divine portion with materials situated in that same portion.
Leaving the diagonal thread and resorting to the right side,
he who desires success should worship him with diligence.
One should place the recitation, arranged as an enclosure, at the side of the deity;
or else, one should always offer it to the Blessed One as a mere recitation.
One should wear the Brahmasūtra during times of worship and recitation;
for in this way, the ritual of recitation and worship is always free from obstacles.
Thus, he who worships Viṣṇu in this sequence, endowed with devotion,
shall enjoy his desired pleasures and attain the same world as Viṣṇu.
Having thus made offerings according to the rule, accompanied by all the hosts of gods,
one should then perform the ritual bath for Viṣṇu according to the application of one's own capacity.
Worship of all the gods and the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with their respective names,
using fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked food, or sacrificial offerings, or separately with clarified butter alone for each.
One should offer an oblation to the spirits and feed the Brahmins according to one's ability.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Universal Worship," in the Viṣṇu-saṃhitā.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.

Now I shall briefly describe the supreme rite for the restoration of a dilapidated [image], which must by all means be performed after the initial installation; in this regard, the ritual procedure is tenfold. (24.1)

If the image of Hari, who is the soul of all, becomes broken, decayed, or unstable, there will be the destruction of the village, the kingdom, and so forth; therefore, its restoration must be performed. (24.2)
Just as an embodied being, having abandoned a worn-out body, goes to another body, so too the Lord, having abandoned a worn-out image, resorts to a new one. (24.3)
The Lord of Gods abandons the image like a withered garland;
thinking, "Lest the Yātudhānas see it," one should remove it without delay.
Having immediately summoned a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or even more Brahmins who are experts in the Tantras and have mastered the Vedas, according to his capacity.

Having honored them according to his ability with devotion and having circumambulated them, he prostrated himself with a concentrated mind, reciting the mantra "Obeisance to those who are devoted to Brahman. (24.6)
The preceptor, together with those who attend to the images, should cause many benedictions to be recited;
having bowed to them with the words "Victory to you," he should rise again, remaining restrained in speech.
Having meditated upon the deity with the mind and with palms joined in reverence, one should say this:
"This image of Viṣṇu for worship has been established by former sages. (24.8)
If it should be found that [the image] has been defiled today by this defect, the instruction is that the removal of the defiled image must be performed. (24.9)
We apply ourselves to the task of composing a scripture;
for if this [work] should be composed as having the status of a scriptural authority, it would serve that purpose. (24.10)
"May you grant us your permission; we shall be your obedient servants.
Thus was he permitted without hesitation by those best of the twice-born, who said, "Let it be done."
If one should offer this again to them out of a desire for the welfare of the world,
it is just like that which is prescribed as blameless for the worship of the gods.
Just as a substance such as a flower is later censured as "nirmālya" (remnant), so too is an image that was not defective when it was employed in worship [later held in contempt]. (24.13)
That very [image], once defiled, is later censured as "nirmālya" (used-up offering);
therefore, this image is defective, and you should abandon it without doubt.
"It must be discarded with the thought that it is like a faded flower offering (nirmālya); such is the instruction of the scripture.
Then those Brahmins, freed from doubt, should proclaim this.
For the peace of the sacrificer, the preceptor, and the officiating priests;
and for the king, this realm, this village, and this city.
Then, having emerged and either assimilated the Lord of Gods into himself or having invoked him into the water-pot, the Guru should perform the rite for the extraction of the image.
In front of the palace, one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) according to the prescribed rule,
using either dūrvā grass smeared with the three sweets or fuel-sticks from trees that produce milky sap.
There, oblations mixed with clarified butter should be offered eight thousand times to Sāvitrī;
thereafter, one should cause the recitation of peace-mantras from the Bāhṛta and Upaniṣads.
May there be peace, may there be auspiciousness, may there be nourishment, and may there be well-being;
may there be prosperity, and may all possess abundant wealth.
To the cows and brahmins, to the kṣatriyas, and likewise to the vaiśyas and śūdras;
to the worlds, to all beings, to the king, and to the realm.
For this kingdom, and especially for this village and city;
and for this sacrificer, together with his servants and kinsmen.
Thinking, "May there be completeness in the ritual procedure for extracting the image," the patron, having prostrated before and propitiated the preceptor here, [should say]: 24.23.
One should satisfy him completely with a great gift of gold, jewels, and other such things;
one should offer all of one's own wealth as well as oneself.
Gold, cows, land, horses, jewels, clothing, and elephants;
ornaments, women, slaves, as well as seats and beds—[he gave all these]. (24.25)
Whatever else is dear and possible, that one should give; such is the established rule.
And to those who serve as the images, a gift should be given that is either equal to or greater than his own share.
Then, having performed the ritual placement of the body (dehanyāsa) together with the dissolution and emergence [of the mantras],
the preceptor, accompanied by his retinue, should diligently adorn the image.
Then, having performed the *puṇyāha* rite, with turbans bound, composed in mind,
restrained in speech, and having established their protection, they should remain there with their auspicious threads tied.
The preceptor should bind a golden bracelet upon the hand of the sacrificer with the Cakra-mantra; if that is unavailable, he should bind a yellow garland.
Having performed the recitation, the preceptor should offer white mustard seeds even to the master builder;
thereafter, he should cause it to be proclaimed in all directions with the sounds of musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas.
One should place a bull or an elephant, well-adorned, at the front;
having bound it with calf-ropes and the like, one should employ mechanical devices.
"Burst forth! O Father, may your hymn be such that it is not false;
may it be an infinite hymn, most sweet, and likewise other auspicious ones. (24.32)
The Yaudhājaya, the Raurava, the Bṛhat-sāman, the Rathantara,
the Kayāśubhīya, the Jyeṣṭhasāman, and the beautiful Vairāja.
The entire Sudarśana-pavitram, which is most excellent and has Viṣṇu as its deity,
as well as the Puruṣasūkta, the Pāvamāna hymns, and likewise the five Upaniṣads.
The discus, the bow Śārṅga, the sword, the sciences, the forms of beauty, the three qualities, the ego, the elements beginning with the gross elements, and others as well.
Accompanied by the officiating priests who were turning the soil, the Teacher himself,
having released the binding of the pedestal, [plowed] with auspicious golden ploughs.
"By means of the eight-syllable mantra, I, Viṣvaksena, shall take up the remains of the offering (nirmālya).
Having thus formed a firm resolve, [he should say] "bhūrbhuvaḥ suvar om. || 24.37 ||
The practitioner should raise the image from the pit by means of mechanical contrivances,
accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and hymns, musical instruments, and abundant shouts of victory.
Then, accompanied by dancing, singing, and loud laughter, one should carry the image outside,
having wrapped it all around with smooth, unwashed garments.
Having performed the ritual service with the Gāyatrī mantra preceded and followed by the Praṇava,
one should prepare a square sand mound on the south.
Having scattered sesame seeds and darbha grass, one should lay the image there;
one should wash it with water and worship it with perfumes and flowers. (24.41)
Having circumambulated [the funeral pyre] three times in a counter-clockwise direction, he should scatter sesame seeds mixed with rice;
then, having covered [the body] with other smooth garments and placed it upon a vehicle, [he should proceed].
Adorned with umbrellas, banners, flags, and yak-tail fans,
and accompanied by the shouts of a great multitude, one should lead it to the river that flows to the ocean.
Then, having meditated upon the four-armed Viṣvaksena in that unfathomable [water],
one should cast the image into the waters with his mantra ending in "namaḥ."
One should consider the pedestal and the Brahma-stone as the remains of offerings (nirmālya);
having bathed there, they all then proceeded to the temple.
Having purified many Brahmins and fed them according to his ability,
he should diligently keep cows for four nights or even three nights.
And one should give them abundant fodder and water during the nights;
having thus performed this for three days, one should have the ritual for the recitation of benedictions (svastivācana) performed with food and other offerings.

Having first performed the *rākṣoghna* sacrifice for the site, the recitation of Vedic hymns and so forth, and the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), he then [proceeded] with various distinct mantras.

One should sprinkle [the site] both outside and inside with water, products of the cow, and unbroken grains; one should then perform oblations with the five Durgā mantras, the Mūlamantra, the Upaniṣads, and so forth.
One should cause the area to resound with Rakshasa-destroying mantras and the sounds of musical instruments;
then, having brought forth the image that has been consecrated in water, together with the presiding priests (mūrtipas), [one should proceed].
Having performed the purification according to the rule, the Guru should have [the image] laid down in the pavilion;
the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) should offer oblations in the directions, and the mantra-reciters should perform recitation.
Having placed the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning, one should recite the Vedic and Tantric mantras, as well as the names [of the Lord] by the thousands, and indeed the Vaiṣṇava mantras.
Having touched [the heart] with the syllable *praṇava* and meditated upon Mādhava within the heart,
one should [worship] the heart of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, by means of his stride (*vikramaṇa*).
Having touched the mouth, the eyes, and the nose with this mantra,
one should again touch all the limbs with the Hiraṇyagarbha mantra.

Having taken that [image] which had been consecrated with the *Puruṣasūkta* hymn, and having performed three circumambulations as before while it was joined with the depositing of jewels and other offerings; 24.55.
Having gone there preceded by the Vedas, the Jaya-hymns, praises, dances, and songs, and having established [the image] with the mantra "dhruvā dyauḥ," he should proclaim "vaṣaṭ te. (24.56)
One should place each [syllable] individually after meditating upon it as consisting of the five Upaniṣads, conjoined with the Praṇava and the Parameṣṭhi-vidyā and others. (24.57)
With the syllable "Om," he should touch his feet, knees, thighs, navel, heart, mouth, and head in sequence;
and with the Nārāyaṇa-sūkta and the Pauruṣa-sūkta, he should likewise touch them all.
Then, one should meditate upon the entire [deity] as "the one with eyes on all sides";
having thus transferred [the deity] from the pitcher into the new image, one should perform the ritual in this manner.
One should perform everything up to the conclusion of the festival according to the ritual for consecration;
here, one should arrange the propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma) with the Sāvitrī and the Pañca-kṣara mantra.
If the arm is severed, the image should be abandoned at the hand; likewise, if any limb is broken such that there is deformity, one should abandon it at that very part.
If a single finger or two fingers are broken here, one should not abandon [the vow];
beyond that, some maintain that abandonment occurs upon the breaking of three.
One should apply this same principle elsewhere even in the case of a cut in the toe or a branch; likewise, abandonment [of the limb] is prescribed when it has burst open or split asunder. (24.63)
The finger that is broken should be made of gold, and those two [other fingers] likewise;
if it is on an image of stone or made of metal such as copper or silver.
But in all cases where there is a break in the thread, one should fashion it out of gold;
this is recommended for the crown, the earrings, and likewise for the garments and other items.
In the case of abandoning an image, it is said that one should proceed as with the removal of a spy;
here, neither the installation nor the worship is to be accepted, and the pedestal remains intact.
In the subsequent sacrifice (anuyāga), nine substances indeed bestow auspiciousness;
these include the pedestal, the stone slab, and so forth. However, a single seat for both [deities] is censured.
One may wish to bury a mountain in the depths, burn a wooden object with fire, give away jewels and metal, or even cause them to vanish. (24.68)
One should cast the earthen image into the waters, or even all earthen materials;
even when the deity's image is broken, it is the temple where the grace [of the deity] is perceived that matters.
There too, one should have another image made— either of gold, or of metal, or of jewels— and, having placed it before oneself, one should worship it according to the prescribed rite.
The wise have declared that even those images from the Purāṇas, though established by gods and others, are to be worshipped without mantras. (24.71)
This very [method] should be understood as the way to act when one is born with doubts oneself, or when such doubts arise together with many Vaiṣṇavas who have mastered the Vedas. (24.72)
Having performed a grand worship of the deity with devotion,
accompanied by the sounding of divine musical instruments and the like, on the twelfth lunar day or even under the Śravaṇa asterism.
Having observed the fast, they should sleep upon beds of darbha grass in the presence of the deity:
"Speak, O God, Lord of Gods! I have come for refuge unto you. (24.74)
"Whatever tasks we have in our hearts, let them all be accomplished in a dream for those who sleep"—having made this request, may a favorable dream appear to them here. (24.75)
Having performed it thus two or three times, the wise man should determine the task;
he should construct a new temple, either circular or square.
As before, it may be either square or circular, but in the case of a circle, it must not be otherwise;
indeed, in that case, there should be no reduction of ground nor any reduction of the constituent parts.
The denizens of hell indeed resort to a place devoid of deities;
therefore, for the sake of avoiding that, one should especially perform protection.
One should not neglect cow-dung, incense for the city, a consecrated lamp and fire, the five products of the cow, the twice-born, darbha grass, and mustard seeds.
One should recite the Rākṣoghna Sūkta, the Nārasiṃha Sūkta, and the Sudarśana Sūkta;
and during the evening watches, one should perform hymns of praise and the Svastivācana rite.
May Viṣṇu be for our well-being always; may the four-faced Brahmā be for our well-being;
may Rudra be for our well-being always; may Śatakratu be for our well-being. (24.81)
May Agni ever be for our well-being; may Yama ever be for our well-being;
may Nirṛti, the renowned one, be for our well-being; and may Varuṇa ever be for our well-being.
May Vāyu ever be for our well-being; may Dhaneśvara be for our well-being;
may Īśāna ever be for our well-being; may the host of Maruts be for our well-being.
May the Vasus be for our well-being, and may the Rudras always be for our well-being;
may the Ādityas be for our well-being, and may the sages always be for our well-being.
May the Gandharvas be for our well-being; may the Vidyādharas be for our well-being;
may the Nāgas be for our well-being; and may the Pannagas be for our well-being.
May the lords of knowledge be for our well-being; may the apsarases always be for our well-being;
may the rivers be for our well-being, and may the streams always be for our well-being.
May the oceans be for our well-being, and may the mountains always be for our well-being;
may the brothers be for our well-being, and may the ancestors always be for our well-being.
May all the attendants of the gods be ever for our well-being;
may there be welfare for the devotees of the Lord, and may there be welfare for the twice-born.
May there be well-being for the worshippers, and may there be well-being for the cows as well;
may there be well-being for the stationary beings and likewise for the moving ones.
May there be well-being for the mantras, and may there be well-being for the ritual acts as well;
this offering is indeed for the god Viṣṇu—salutations, salutations to him!
Whatever specific ritual action is performed, having specifically stated it, the preceptor should perform the recitation of the benediction (svastivācana); in this way, it shall become auspicious.

Then, having installed the new image, one should cause the ritual bathing and the festival to be performed, and likewise offer the bali-oblation to the eight classes of beings in the various directions.
One should worship as before constantly; thus, success will surely come to pass.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
Now I shall briefly describe the expiation for portents,
as well as the sequence of purification for both the site and the image, in their proper order.
Those portents which fly up in front, foreboding fear, are known as celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial; they are proclaimed in the Tantras. || 25.2 ||
The sanctum, the pedestal, and the image within the temple are conceived as the very body of the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
they must always be protected by Brahmins out of fear of portents.
When portents have arisen, worship of Hari must not be performed;
the images, their pedestals, and the temples, along with the presiding deities, become untouchable. 25.4.
But if the expiation is not performed, the deities become clearly angry;
therefore, having honored them with effort, one should quickly cause the expiation to be made. 25.5.
The discus of Viṣṇu, resembling a canopy of fire, when defiled by portents, must under no circumstances be worshipped by the wise until the expiation has been performed. (25.6)
If there is delay, however, the presence of the deity may perish due to the lack of expiation;
the pretas residing there would then cause fear for men through diseases, grief, and other such afflictions. (25.7)
Falling, trembling, perspiring, laughing, and weeping;
being uprooted, carried off by thieves, burning, and violent destruction. (25.8)

The collapse of pedestals, temples, banners, weapons, and archways, as well as the destruction of attendants, and the emergence of mushrooms, anthills, worms, insects, and the like [are signs of impending ruin]. (25.9)
The entry of dogs, thieves, outcastes, heretics, temple-priests, and the like;
and worship by those ignorant of the mantras, by those devoted to other [deities], and by the uninitiated. || 25.10 ||
The employment of minor mantras, digestion at the wrong time, taking recourse to the [wrong] directions, and worship with stale, sapless, corrupted, or forbidden offerings. (25.11)
There is lack of propitiation and freedom from fault; at the proper time, there is indifference due to negligence;
there is quarreling, death, and birth; and the shedding of blood, phlegm, and tears.
These and other such portents should be recognized as bestowing many evils;
therefore, with every effort, one must act without delay. 25.13.
The expiation should be performed according to one's capacity; otherwise, there is total ruin—especially in the case of many great and terrible calamities. (25.14)
Wherever there is an immediate expiation for even the slightest of infractions regarding the ritual signs—
whether on the image, the pedestal, the house, the porch, or the courtyard— it should be performed exactly as prescribed.
One should perform the procedure for excavation and so forth according to the relative strength or weakness of the defects:
excavation, removal, burning, filling, and the settling of cattle.
The remains of what has been vomited, and products of the cow—these seven are the purifications of the site.
Having dug with a wooden sword made of khadira wood and using the weapon-mantra, measuring from the hand downwards.
Having removed all the contaminated soil with vessels, one should cast it outside;
then, having burned it with kuśa grass, darbha grass, and so forth, one should again remove the ashes and other residue.
Having filled the pit dug with excellent earth by the sacrificial elephant-keepers, and having sprinkled it with cow's urine and pounded it with the water from the feet of Brahmins; 25.19.
Having settled the cow, he should feed many Vaiṣṇava brahmins milk-rice;
once their remnants have been removed, he should sprinkle [the ground] with products of the cow and scatter it with offerings.
This is declared to be the purification of the locus; now the purification of the image is described, consisting of washing, immersion, bathing, and wiping, in their proper order.
Afterwards comes immersion in a stream, and here the seventh is the ritual ablution;
then follows cleansing with *darbha* grass, clay, and cow-hides, as well as purification with silent waters.
Sprinkling with water mixed with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and parched rice, performed without mantras;
and bathing with those same substances along with a bunch of kuśa grass, performed with mantras. (25.23)

Having filled the vessel with water as prescribed and having worshipped it with mantras, one should sprinkle the image with the tips of the *kūrca* grass while reciting mantras; this is what is meant here by "cleansing" (*mārjana*).
Having placed a vessel made of iron, containing a bundle of grain, in the northeast,
he should fill that vessel dedicated to Varuṇa with auspicious waters and a bundle of grass.
One should place therein two golden fish and two silver tortoises, as well as a lotus plant washed clean, together with its stalks and flowers. (25.26)
Having worshipped Varuṇa there and invoked the Vaiṣṇava Tīrtha, one should place a vessel made of wood such as Palāśa, or one made of iron, upon three feet. || 25.27 ||
Having filled the golden perforation along with the ritual tuft (kūrca) over the image,
an unbroken stream [of water] should be maintained day after day for the duration of one watch (yāma).
Having taken water from a vessel dedicated to Varuṇa with the appropriate mantra, one should fill [the vessel] here;
the five Upaniṣads should be recited by those who are silent and hold darbha grass in their hands.
With steady hands, they touched the vessel while meditating upon the imperishable Viṣṇu,
reciting the Puruṣasūkta, the Pāvamāna hymn, and other Vaiṣṇava hymns.
Or else, one may recite the entire Saṃhitā of the other [Veda]; here, the recitation should be performed at the beginning and the end.
At the conclusion of the stream, one should worship the deity, and having dismissed Varuṇa again, [proceed]. || 25.31 ||
The water-vessel belonging to Varuṇa must not be moved for three nights while the recitation is being performed;
having taken out the water and refilled it, one should perform everything as before. (25.32)
The supreme [consecration] should be performed with scented water, or with milk, or even with a stream of clarified butter;
and here too, the worship of the sacrificial post (varuṇa) must likewise be carried out.
Having covered the image all around with fine cloths and darbha grass, and having established it within a vessel of prescribed dimensions constructed by experts in sacrificial rites; 25.34.
Every day, according to the rule, one should perform the ritual immersion with cow products— either used individually or all together— with perfumed water, in their proper sequence.
Having established five jars, together with blades of kusha grass and wrapped with threads,
filled with scents, flowers, unbroken grains, and water, according to the sequence of the Upanishads.
Having placed small bowls with their openings covered by sprouts and containing rice grains,
and having honored them by wrapping them in cloth, one should consecrate them with those very same mantras.
One should thus bathe [the deity] with five [substances]; this is remembered as the ritual of consecration (abhiṣeka).
Sixteen, twelve, or eight initiated Vaiṣṇava twice-born men [should perform it]. (25.38)
Clad in new garments and having sipped water for purification, the four or eight reciters of the Veda, acting as the attendants of the Guru’s image, should cause [the sound] to resound day and night.

Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made there according to the rules, those who are composed should sprinkle [the area] with mantras that destroy demons and are conducive to peace and prosperity.
Both the followers of the Vedas and those of the Tantras, all with darbha grass tips in their hands,
sprinkled water used for that purpose throughout the house— both outside and inside, on every side.
One should scatter mustard seeds and unbroken rice grains mixed with the five products of the cow while reciting the five mantras;
then, once the pavilion has been purified, one should consecrate the fire according to the prescribed rite.
All the image-keepers (mūrtipās), together with the preceptor (ācārya), should perform oblations in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas),
having completed the primary homa at the end of the fire-mouth rite (agnimukha) in due order for all of them.
Meditating with undistracted minds upon Viṣṇu, who resides within the fire along with his limbs and is free from decay,
they should offer clarified butter three thousand times with each of the five [mantras] into all the fires.
Then, all of them together should offer a thousand oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, rice, sesame seeds, and parched grain, using the eight-syllable mantra in due order.
Thereafter, they should all offer one hundred and twelve fuel-sticks of palāśa wood smeared with clarified butter, accompanied by the vyāhṛtis.
With milk, curd, honey, and clarified butter, they should all perform oblations one hundred and eight times respectively, using the Sāvitrī mantra alone for the sake of universal peace.

At the conclusion of the oblation, the sacrificer should give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to these [brahmins] according to his capacity; thereafter, he should have them recite the benediction (svasti).
One should perform the ceremonial bath (snapana) according to one's enthusiasm, excluding the lowest [grade];
having washed the feet and performed worship, one should give the teacher’s sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
According to his capacity, while meditating upon Viṣṇu, he should give gold, land,
and a cow to one hundred and eight Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas who have been properly honored.
Having prostrated, one should cause Śiva to be recited for the sake of pacifying defects such as deficiency or excess;
there should be four image-protectors (mūrtipās) in a minor [rite], eight in a middling one, and twelve in a superior one.
They should be provided with garments and ornaments according to the strength or weakness of their respective defects,
as well as the officiating priests, the reciters of the homa, the members of the assembly, and the Vaiṣṇava brahmins.
One should worship all [the deities] according to one's capacity with auspicious food, drink, and other offerings.
Having duly consecrated the fire in the southeast corner during the extraordinary rites, the Guru—

Having completed the conclusion of the principal oblations, one should again perform offerings of clarified butter with the five [mantras] consisting of twelve and eight syllables, the Gāyatrī, and the Puruṣasūkta.
Having offered oblations twenty-four times, or perhaps a hundred or a thousand times,
with fuel-sticks of *apāmārga* wood, together with *indrī* and the auspicious *añjali* gesture.

Having offered into the fire *dūrvā* grass, white mustard seeds, rice, barley, sesame, clarified butter, and oblation— along with the "falling-off" (*sampāta*) and the products of the cow (*gavya*), consecrated five times with mantras— 56.25.
One should sprinkle the remaining water with the heart-mantra where the honey and other substances have been applied;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual bathing (snapana) one hundred and eight times or more.
Having purified the image touched by oneself— which has been extensively cleansed with cow-products—
one should purify it with pure water, excellent fragrances, and waters from sacred fords (tīrtha).
One should arrange for the cows to stay for five nights or three nights;
afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins and have them pronounce an auspicious day.
Having performed the sacrifice, he should cause the Vedas to be sounded and, having offered the food, present the bali-oblation;
he should cause it to be sounded with the noise of musical instruments, and thereafter have the fire-offerings (homa) and other rites performed.
With wood from the aśvattha, khadira, plakṣa, palāśa, pāṭala, and vaṭa trees,
[one should perform the rite] with the Nārāyaṇīya Sūkta and likewise with the Śrīsūkta.
Then, with the hymn beginning "ato devā," as well as with "nāsad," "aṃhomucaḥ," "saṃsamit," "drapso," and likewise with the verse "arāyi. (25.62)
Here, one should offer oblations with the Gāyatrī mantra five times according to the prescribed rule;
when the ritual bath is completed, one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as before.
Having caused him who had departed by means of the signless [rite] to re-enter quickly,
one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering, a ceremonial bath, and the recitation of benedictions.
Having rendered it empty for three nights by dogs, jackals, and other such creatures, he shall perform a festival, a pilgrimage to sacred sites, and a feast for Brahmins.
One should perform the previously mentioned pacification rite and an extensive purification of the site;
in the event of burning, one should invoke a milch cow by the name "Pacification."
Having offered dūrvā grass and other items to her, one should milk a cow into a lotus leaf;
having heated the milk, curdled it, churned it, and consecrated it, one should take the clarified butter (ājya). || 25.67 ||
Having milked in the same manner on the following day, one should prepare curd;
on the third day, one should likewise collect dung, urine, and milk.
Having worshipped the fivefold [substances] beginning with urine in order upon lotus petals,
and having combined them upon five petals, one should churn them while reciting the *praṇava*.
Having performed worship, one should recite the five Upaniṣads eight thousand times;
having sprinkled [the image] everywhere with that, one should then bathe the image.
Having removed the ashes and other remains and having flooded the area on all sides with water,
one should perform the expiation (prāyaścitta) in due order, beginning with the establishment of a cow-pen and so forth.

The wise one, having invoked [the deity] into the jar, should render it either mobile or immobile; having performed the preliminary consecration according to the rule, he should then perform the rite of rejuvenation.
Having removed a broken image, the wise man should install another;
once the image has been removed, he should again join the transferred [deity] to the new one.
Having performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsya), one should make the image well-established along with the clay mold;
however, in the event of contact by wicked persons or similar incidents, one must perform a further purification for it.
One should perform all the rites beginning with the fire-oblation (homa) and ending with the festival, especially so;
for the theft of [the image] by thieves is proclaimed to be the foremost among faults. (25.75)
In that case, the ritual procedure must be performed with great effort in its full detail, provided that the image stolen by thieves is recovered with diligence. (25.76)
Having purified it according to the prescribed rite, that very same [liṅga] should be installed there;
however, if it is not obtained, or if it has been stolen, broken, or worn out, a new one should be installed again.
However, even a deficiency in the specific form of the womb (yoni) is not accepted here;
once the temple exists, one should meditate upon it as complete, joined with the image.
The wise one, having withdrawn [the deity], should invoke [it] into the water-jar preceded by mantras;
likewise, having invoked [it] into the womb-chamber or its pedestal, he should do so in that same manner.
When neither a pedestal nor even a sanctum is available,
one should invoke [the deity] from the place where the image resides and perform the ritual according to the prescribed injunctions.
Even when that which has been transferred is destroyed, the rite must be performed as if it were the destruction of the original;
likewise, it is proclaimed that the same applies to the destruction of its constituent deities.
Since all deities are proclaimed to have the nature of mantra, it is established that their emission occurs in this very same manner at the time of their dissolution. 25.82
A pacification rite (śānti) should be performed with five [mantras], but if there has been no worship, it should be more extensive:
a hundred oblations with eight [mantras], followed by the feeding of Vaiṣṇavas.
Here, milk-rice (pāyasa) should be offered for ten [deities], and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to one's capacity;
this ritual procedure should be multiplied by the number of days up to the twelfth.

The ritual bathing (*snapana*) lasts for four months; after that, it is the Great Bathing (*mahāsnāna*), which throughout the year is accompanied by peaceful fire-offerings (*śāntihoma*) and the worship of Brahmins.
Having consecrated the spilled oblation with the right hand,
one should offer it with clarified butter using the eight-syllable mantra five hundred times.
Having cast dūrvā grass and other items into the water and likewise offered them as oblations, one should cook the food;
once it has cooled, it should be purified by adding cow products mixed with water, fragrant substances, and so forth.
One should perform the rite for an auspicious day, the fire-oblation for peace, and the offering of food and other oblations.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
Now I shall briefly describe the supreme procedure for the ritual bathing (snapana), which should be performed by the wise according to the divisions of the highest and other grades. 26.1.

On the fourth day after the installation, at the conclusion of the procession, during eclipses and the like, during calamities, upon contact with the end [of life], or when the principal person has perished— 26.2.
At the conclusion of initiation, consecration, and sacrifice; during auspicious mantra-practice;
when other minor mantras have been deployed; and when worship has long been neglected—(3) || 26.3 ||
In the absence [of the deity], at the time of consecration, for the sake of the prosperity of kings, for the pacification of unknown defects, and every year according to the prescribed rule. (26.4)
The ceremonial bath (snapana) should be performed with devotion according to the specific occasion,
on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), under the auspicious asterism of Śravaṇa, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, at the solstices (ayana), and so forth.
One should perform [the rite] on the birth-star of the patron or on the full moon day;
having constructed the pavilion as before, adorned with arches and banners. (26.6)
In the center, a sacrificial altar (vedikā) should be constructed, thirty-two barley-corns in height, strewn with pearl necklaces and other ornaments, and adorned with heaps of flowers.
The extent of the sacrificial altar (vedi) should indeed be equal to the number of jars to be taken;
one should cause sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to be made in the cardinal directions and place auspicious objects within them.
In a vessel placed in the northeast, containing grain and covered with a new cloth,
the initiated one should pour in water originating from a river, a sacred ford, or similar source, which has been purified.
Having worshipped with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī using his hand adorned with a pavitra,
the learned man should consecrate the kūrca one hundred and eight times.
May these waters be auspicious, beautiful, pure, and stainless;
may they be purifying, cool, and sanctified by the rays of the sun.
Having spoken thus, he should sprinkle the purified altar with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and then scatter fragrant unbroken rice grains and products of the cow all around it.
Then, one should lay down twelve threads starting from the eastern and northern corners,
and arrange square compartments measuring one tāla each.
One should fill all the lines, one finger high, with white powder, making them even;
then, one should scatter a small amount of that same powder in the center.
Alternatively, for the sake of completing the meter, one may use five colors by transposition;
four paths should be made, oriented toward the east and likewise toward the other directions. 26.15.
In the fortnight associated with pure water, there are no pathways for the ritual bathing with substances;
the middle position belongs to Brahmā, and immediately after that is the divine one.
One should arrange sixteen spokes for the human [wheel] on all sides, eight for the divine,
and an eight-petaled lotus with a radiant pericarp for the Brahma [wheel].
Altars should be constructed everywhere, four finger-breadths in height;
in their centers, they should be filled with rice grains mixed with kusha grass and sesame seeds and rice.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the Gāyatrī mantra into the consecrated fire as before,
he should then ritually prepare (adhivāsaya) the jars of the prescribed characteristics with faith.
Having placed all of them, measured finger by finger with a thread, facing downward with the syllable *TĀRE*, upon the western layer of *darbha* grass; 26.20.
The wise one, having arranged them in rows from Agni to Īśāna and having placed darbha grass over them, should display the darbha mudrā.
Having sprinkled all [the vessels] with scented water, one should scatter auspicious unbroken grains (akṣata) over them;
then, having lifted them up and turned them face upwards, one should do so according to the sequence of the five [fingers].
One should establish [the deity] in the Brahma, human, and divine stations;
then, with the eight-syllable mantra, one should place the *kūrca* grass-bundles upon the jars.
In rites for peace (śāntika), they should face downward; in rites for prosperity (pauṣṭika), however, they should face upward.
Having sprinkled them again with the root mantra using the hand holding a pavitra-grass ring, [one should proceed].
Being self-restrained and facing the east, he should first set out the water for bathing in the Brahma-vessel,
while recollecting Hari along with his root-mantra, all his forms, limbs, and retinue.
Having worshipped him with perfumes and flowers, one should again envelop him with two garments;
