then the initiated ones, having invoked [the deity], should offer the ritual substances such as water for the feet (pādya) and so forth in their proper order.
Being composed, one should fill [the vessel] both outside and inside in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
one should place the water for washing the feet (pādya) in the east (Aindra), the water for honoring (arghya) in the south (Yama), and the water for sipping (ācamana) in the west (Vāruṇa).
Likewise, one should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the north, clarified butter in the southeast,
curd in the southwest, and milk in the northwest.
Honey is in the direction of the Lord (Īśāna) with the twelve-syllable mantra;
hot water is in Bhṛśa, and likewise a decoction is in Vitatha.
In the case of Bhṛṅgarāja, cleansing with water is prescribed; in Puṣpadanta, with fruit-water;
in Śoṣa, with barley-water; in Mukhya, with gems; and likewise in Āditi, with iron.
One should duly place the water with *kuśa* grass under the Parjanya [pitcher];
the remaining pitchers, however, one should fill with pure water while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra.
Then, in the region of Aryaman, there is fragrant water; in Vivasvat, water with flowers;
likewise, in Mitra, water with Upamānīka; and on Dhara, fragrant Āmalaka fruit.
In the Sāvitra [vessel] there is water with unhusked grain; in the Indraka, coconut water;
in the Rudradāsa, sugarcane juice; and likewise in the Āpa [vessel], rice-water.
One should fill all those divine vessels in sequence with the eight-syllable mantra;
as each is filled, it is immediately adorned with sprouts.
Having arranged the small discs along with rice grains using the Cakra-mantra,
one should wrap them all in new cloths that are free from hair and other defects.

Having placed darbha grass and unbroken grains (akṣata), the Guru should scatter them in sequence with the root mantra; having sprinkled them with the eight-syllable mantra, he should worship them with his own mantras.
Having sprinkled [the image] again with the syllable Om and with scented water,
and having caused those initiated [into the rite] to perform oblations in all directions, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsana).
Having offered oblations with the five [mantras], he should perform the recitation for well-being (svastivācana) for the presence of the gods, for auspiciousness, and for the pacification of evil.
The learned man should cause the benediction to be recited: "May the rite be complete without flaw.
Then, having brought water for peace (śāntitoya) mixed with the remnants of the clarified butter, || 26.39 ||
The Guru should again sprinkle all the jars with the tip of the *kūrca* grass-bundle, [saying]:
"May these jars, together with the *kuśa* grass and their lids, become pure. (26.40)
Overwhelmed by wind and heat, yet endowed with auspicious marks,
they abide as twenty-fivefold manifestations of Viṣṇu according to the divisions of the principles (tattva).
May all these manifestations, which depend upon the measure of substances, come together;
and let this bathing, as ordained by the scriptures and fashioned by the gods, take place.
"By this ablution, may the Blessed Lord Hari be pleased.
Having spoken thus, the preceptor, permitted by the other image-keepers, accompanied them.
Wearing a turban and an upper garment, having performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa), well-adorned,
and accompanied by the lustration rite (nīrājana) and other ceremonies, he should then proceed to the inner sanctum.
Having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times while standing before it,
and having opened the door with air, he— pure and restrained in speech— should offer the arghya water.
Having removed the covering with the *viśve* mantra and washed it with the *praṇava*,
one should meditate upon the Lord of the Gods as endowed with the *tattvas* in the order of emanation.
Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa rite and having again offered water for the feet (pādya) and the respectful offering (arghya) with the *jitā* mantra and others,
one should cut the marriage-thread (kautuka) with the Gāyatrī mantra and again offer water for sipping (ācamana).
One should cast unbroken grains together with the tips of dūrvā grass upon the head and at the feet with the syllable "Om";
one should perform the lustration three times with the Astra-mantra and dedicate auspicious objects with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
In an auspicious vessel made of metal, filled with rice grains of the *śāli* variety,
[one should perform the rite] with weapons placed upon leaves of the *aśvattha* tree and prepared with fresh cow dung.

One should perform this lustration ceremony (nīrājana) in the center, joined with brightly blazing lamps made of ghee that increase in size and are radiant with color, arranged according to their beauty.
Beautiful materials for worship should be prepared here by those who have been initiated:
rice mixed with turmeric powder, and unbroken grains of gold and gems. (26.51)
In brief, the following ingredients should be combined with the bathing water:
dūrvā grass, amāka grain, lotuses, and viṣṇuparṇī; these constitute the water for washing the feet (pādya).
One should briefly prepare the eightfold *arghya* offering consisting of siddhārtha, fragrant flowers, fruit, barley, sesame, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and the tips of *kuśa* grass. (26.53)
There, the practitioner should prepare the fourfold *ācāma* offering, provided with *takola*, nutmeg, camphor, and clove blossoms.
One should prepare a decoction from the barks of the aśvattha, udumbara, brahmavaṭa, bilva, vikaṅkata, śamī, and khadira trees.
Sahā, niśā, sadābhadra, śirīṣa, sūryavartinī,
and the tips of kuśa grass— these six ingredients are prescribed for cleansing.
One should prepare the eight-ingredient fruit-water (phalatoya) with plantains, coconuts, mangoes, emblic myrobalans, breadfruit, pomegranates, bhavya fruits, and bilva fruits.
With diamond, pearl, lapis lazuli, ruby, and coral, there shall be the "five-limbed water of jewels"; the metals are the five beginning with gold.
One should apply sulphur with the juices of the sevya, arka, ambuja, tāla, āyu, mura, and śīta plants,
along with jasmine (jāti), mallikā, kunda, nandyāvarta, lotus (abja), and campaka flowers.
One should prepare water with flowers from *yūthikā* and *bakula*;
and one that is "comparative" (*aupamānika*) [in efficacy] by means of conch shells, *ariṭa*, *arkṣya*, tortoises, and iron products.
If the others are not available, the first limb [of the offering] is recommended for the water for the feet (pādya) and so forth.
The ancestors, Śrī, Sarasvatī, Dakṣa, Viṣṇu, Uśanas, and the Moon [are the recipients]. (26.61)
Indra, Arka, Yama, Viśva, Kubera, Vāyu, Aja, and the Vasus, as well as Sāvitrī, are the deities for the substances beginning with the water for the feet (pādya). || 26.62 ||
Gandharva, Varuṇa, Tārkṣya, Bhūmi, Nirṛti, Śrīdhara, Nṛsiṃha, and Aśvamukha; and in the center is the Supreme Person.
"idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," "āpo hi ṣṭhā," "prajāpate," "tejo 'si," "dadhikrāvṇaḥ," "āpyāyasva," and likewise "madhu. (26.64)
Then [he recites] "akṛṣṇena," "aśvatthe," "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ," "vāyavāyāhi," and "brahmajajñānam. (26.65)
"Upatvāgne," "devasya tvā," "barhirmantrāḥ," "viṣṇorarāṭam," "tattvā yāmi," "suvarṣmāsi," and "syonā pṛthivī"—these are proclaimed as the mantras. (26.66)
In rites for the gods, one should recite "śanno yā divyā" and "yāsāṃ ca paromātā";
in the middle, the hymn "ato devā"; and everywhere at the end, the completion of the self.

From the water for the feet (pādya) at the beginning to the final bath (snāna) at the end, it is proclaimed that one should worship each substance, fumigate it with incense, and then present it. 26.68.
Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa with the root mantra and the limb-mantras, and having properly displayed the mudrās,
one should worship [the deity] together with the limbs according to the rule, using the nīrājana, arghya, and other offerings.
With these very same materials, one should bathe the deities of the limbs;
and one should offer the fourfold food, accompanied by side dishes and saturated with ghee.
And one should offer an oblation to all beings from every side, providing for all their desires;
one should also provide food of every kind, unrestrictedly, to those of all castes.

The performer should honor the preceptor, along with those who attend to the images, those who perform the fire-offerings and recitations, the members of the assembly, and likewise the Vaiṣṇavas, with sacrificial fees.
Having honored twelve or more peaceful Brāhmaṇas who are devotees of Viṣṇu,
one should give them sacrificial fees according to one's ability and have them perform the recitation of auspicious blessings (svastivācana).
From that, there shall be the pacification of defects such as the transposition,
deficiency, or excess [of syllables], by means of substances numbering fifty-one, eighty-one, or one hundred and eight.
With six hundred and fifty, or with two hundred and seventeen,
or with that [number] plus fifty-two, or with three, or with five hundred.
One should thus perform the bath up to one thousand plus one hundred pitchers;
thus has the supreme bathing ritual of Viṣṇu been correctly explained.
Having thoroughly renounced the desires of this world and those of the next, that which he may obtain—|| 26.77 ||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the Viṣṇusaṃhitā.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
Now I shall briefly explain the sequence of rites beginning with the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), intended for the purpose of renewal; everything should be performed according to the proper order. 27.1
Having thoroughly cleansed the house on all sides with the dung of a tawny cow, one should sprinkle it with her urine while uttering "śam. (27.2)
Having performed this likewise in the four directions, beginning with the inner sanctum,
he silently sprinkles it with pure water consecrated by mantras.

One should scatter these auspicious waters, along with mustard seeds and unbroken grains (akṣata), in every direction, having consecrated them with the "Go" mantra and the five Upaniṣads while joined with the Cakra-mantra.
Having first purified the pavilion, adorned with arches and banners,
he should prepare a bed facing south, strewn with a profusion of flowers.
Then, having ensured it is well-protected, one should have the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) recited there;
and having established the Karmāryā with water and the five kinds of jewels, [one should proceed].
One should perform the ceremonial bathing with water from sacred fords and with hymns that are the essence of the three Vedas;
then, having wrapped [the image] in two new white garments, one should do so with the syllable Om.
Then, with the first [syllable], he should offer the sacred thread; with the middle one, the crown;
with the third, the upper garment; and with the seed-syllable of the Puruṣa, the ornaments.

Having worshipped with all kinds of perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should perform the rite for an auspicious day (puṇyāha), reciting: "Oṃ! O Blessed One, you who pervade all and are the ground of all. (27.9)
"Lord of the elements"—thus is every word of the Vedas; furthermore, "consisting of essence," and from that, "Lord of all the gods. (27.10)
"Come, come, O Puruṣa!"— thus [he spoke] with the title "Great Puruṣa," as one who exists at the end, the beginning, and the middle, and who transcends even that which is beyond the supreme.
Afterwards, he should address him with the words "O Yogin! Namaḥ! ending with the word "Svāhā," using the terms "Manifest and Unmanifest" and "Gross, Subtle, and Great."

Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa with the root mantra and the heart-mantra and others, and having uttered "oṃ," one should offer water for the feet (pādya), as well as water for sipping (ācamana), fragrance, and unguents.
One should offer these flowers, the *sumanas*, as well as incense from the forest tree,
auspicious light in the form of a lamp, and the *arghya* offering consisting of ten ingredients.
Water, white mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, unbroken grains, sesame, rice, milk, barley, black gram, and tips of kuśa grass—this, they know, is [the offering]. (27.15)
First, the word "Oṃ namaḥ," then "to Puruṣottama," and thereafter "to the Lord of all worlds," followed immediately by the arghya offering.
Combined with the offering of food, the mantra "namaḥ svāhā" is the jewel;
furthermore, one should offer water for sipping and bathe [the deity] again with the five [mantras]. 27.17.

As before, [he should perform] the offering of garments, ornaments, and so forth, as well as the washing of the feet, the sipping of water, and worship; then, having tied the protective thread (kautuka), he should perform the gift of a cow and the recitation of the Svasti prayer.
Having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), one should cause the fire-oblations (homas) to be offered as before in the various directions;
those initiated and learned in the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas should offer oblations in the cardinal directions.

Gradually, those learned in grammar, etymology, prosody, and phonetics, as well as those who know astronomy, ritual manuals, and history, and those who know the Purāṇas, were appointed as members of the assembly.
Those who know the logic of Mīmāṃsā, Sāṅkhya, and Yoga, as well as those who know Vedānta, act as witnesses;
having churned the fire with the Gāyatrī and sprinkled it with the eight syllables. (27.21)
Having performed the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* using those [mantras] joined with that [deity], and having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*),
they all, having distributed the fire and made it their mouth, should offer oblations.

Then, eight thousand fuel-sticks each— either from milky trees, from the *brāhmī* tree, or indeed from the *pālāśa* tree— should be separately offered, smeared with clarified butter and consecrated by mantras.
Then, having sprinkled the image with water, one should present it to the members of the assembly, saying:
"The sacrificial fuel-sticks have already been well-offered by us, who follow the vision of the scriptures. (27.24)
"May you say 'śam' here, and may Janārdana be pleased.
Then, according to the ritual rule, [the officiant] says, "O sirs, say 'oṃ svasti'."
"Oṃ! May there be well-being and peace!"—thus the eight members of the assembly should say with reverence.
"Oṃ! May there be well-being and peace; may the oblation be well-offered," the Guru should reply. (27.26)

Then, with the consent of the members, they should likewise offer oblations of clarified butter (ājya), saying, "The portions of clarified butter have been offered," and then, "May they pronounce 'śam'. || 27.27 ||
Those eight should announce [the oblation] and say, "May there be peace.
Then the teacher should say, "Oṃ! May it be well-offered. || 27.28 ||

Having offered the *caru* and presented the oblation, saying, "The *caru*-homage has been performed," they should conclude by saying, "Oṃ, may there be auspiciousness! and [the host replies], "May there be auspiciousness! (27.29).
"Oṃ! May there be auspiciousness and a well-offered oblation," the preceptor should say.
Having again offered clarified butter in that same manner, he should present the sacrificial fee (nivedya) just as before.
In this matter, the members of the assembly and likewise the preceptor must speak;
they should perform the oblations with all the vyāhṛtis according to their knowledge. (27.31)
Sprinkling should be performed at the beginning and the end, as well as a full oblation at the conclusion;
having offered in this manner, all should likewise offer the final oblation.
To Indra, Viṣṇu, and the Maruts, and likewise to Agni, Dharmarāja, and Netṛ, to the Sādhyas, and together with the guardians of the quarters and all the hosts of gods; 27.33.
With the Vyāhṛtis; with Agni, Vāyu, Śakra, Varuṇa, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu;
with the two Aśvins, Gopati, Yama, Agni, Viṣṇu, the Vasus, and Bāskara.
To Viśvabhūta, Diśāpāla, Nirṛti, and those of fierce form;
and again to Viṣṇu, to the wielder of the trident (Śūlapāṇi), and to Yama.
Sakāladharma, Daṇḍin, Tryambaka, Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, Mitra, Parameṣṭhin, Ādityabhūta, and Samudravat. (27.36)
To Āpaga, Vāyu, Viṣṇu, the Maruts, Jātavedas, Indra, all the worlds, Brahmā, and Viśvakarman. (27.37)
One should offer oblations to Soma, together with his retinue of Somas, joined by the planets and constellations,
the hosts of stars, the spirits, the terrestrial beings, and the divine nāgas.
And all the deities— the Rudras, those called Viṣṇus of universal form,
Brahmā, the Rudras, and all the gods, together with the obstacles and the lords of the Gaṇas.
At the beginning and at the end, the vyāhṛtis should be joined separately;
then, one should fill the pitcher with the waters of pacification along with the concluding verses.
To the north of the god, the learned one, having placed [the image] together with a water-pot, [filled it] with waters brought from all sacred fords and even those brought from all the oceans.
And now I fill the water-jar with waters drawn from the north-flowing ponds, together with jewels and sacred purifiers.
"Then [the mantra] 'sarvadvayaṃ tato vyāpin sarvalokādhisamyuta pataye namaḥ svāhā' begins with the syllable TĀRĀ and is used for the filling [of the vessel]. (27.43)
Having filled the water-pot with this mantra-form,
one should wrap it with a linen cloth, provided with a lid and adorned.
Having first filled another vessel with the remaining waters of pacification,
he should adorn it with a lid, wrap it in two linen cloths, and cover it.
Then, having worshipped the water-pot and the ascetic's bowl with perfumes and other offerings,
the pure sprinkler, taking up the vessel that brings all auspiciousness, [proceeds].
Endowed with all auspiciousness and wearing new garments, Hari himself, having become [the image], should slowly perform circumambulation while reciting the mantra. (27.47)
Having placed his right hand over the left hand, which held kuśa grass, and likewise holding a water-pot in the other hand, he stood before him. (27.48)
One should cause the stream of water to fall with kuśa grass, uninterrupted and not too forceful;
one should recite the two mantras beginning with "śanno devīḥ" and "aṇoraṇīyān. (27.49)
Having thoroughly cleansed the interior of the temple and prepared it accordingly,
the wise preceptor should, by means of the proper method, cause the purification of the image to be performed by the guardians of the form (mūrtipāḥ).
Having performed the rite of pacification (śānti) before it, one should perform the auspicious bath (kautuka-snāna);
having placed it upon a throne, one should have it carried to the bed by attendants.
Having washed it with pure water, one should bathe it with waters consecrated by mantras;
furthermore, one should bathe it with the remaining waters of pacification while reciting the *praṇava*.
Water for the feet, water for sipping, clothing, ornaments, a sacred thread,
and a turban should be offered again as before, ending with the lamp.
Having honored Brahmā, Īśvara, and the Brahmins according to the prescribed rule,
and having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) with their permission, he should perform the rite of pronouncing blessings (svastivācana).
The rite of raising [the image] from the pedestal should be performed with the Rudrasūkta while it is on its bed;
with the Puruṣasūkta when it is in its place; and with the Brāhma-sūkta during the act of seating.

One should perform the rite of raising [the mantra] according to the appropriate application and method: the king of syllables (akṣararāja) in the Puruṣa, the middle one in the Śāṅkara, and the final one in the Brāhma, as is fitting.
Placing the peace-vessel (śāntikumbha) at the forefront, as well as the stream from his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu),
the wise man, restrained in speech and inwardly remembering Hari, should bring the ritual image (karmārcā).
One who knows the truth should properly carry the jar forward, accompanied by the Śākuna and Svasti Sūktas and joined with shouts of "Victory! and other such sounds. (27.58)
Having circumambulated the fire from left to right, he should enter the temple again;
having offered the arghya water, he should place the image upon the pedestal while reciting the Brahma-mantra.
One should place [the mantras] on the crest, the head, the face, the neck, the two arms, the heart, as well as on the navel, the generative organ, the two thighs, the two hands, and the two feet.
But the placement [of the mantra] upon Indra should be performed from behind; such is the prescribed rule for the ritual assignment (nyāsa).
Then the wise one should thoroughly sprinkle him with the sixteen-syllable [mantra]. 27.61.
Having invoked [the deity] residing in the ritual image, one should bathe the primary image with scents, flowers, and water,
and then with the water of pacification (śāntyudaka).
One should fashion the body with all the [mantras] located in the heart, the secret parts, and the feet;
and one should place the limbs, beginning with the heart, in their respective locations.

The rites beginning with the offering of water for the feet (pādya) should be performed as before; then one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) to be recited, and having worshipped properly and with devotion using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should offer here milk-rice, barley-gruel, or rice with cow's milk;
that [offering] should be accompanied by edible foods mixed with milk, clarified butter, and delicious side-dishes.
In this rite where no specific mantra is prescribed, one should recite the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī;
then, with what remains of that, one should offer the bali-oblation to the attendants in due order.
Having sipped water and offered water for rinsing the mouth, and having set aside that food,
he should then give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and provide food and drink without restriction.
The mantras for the wheel and the other [emblems] should be designated by their own names;
thereafter, one should perform all the rites prescribed for the installation.
Then, according to the procedure prescribed for the installation, one should have the ceremonial bathing performed,
as well as the festival and the procession for seven days with devotion.
One should perform it for three days, or even for a single day in times of distress;
likewise, the festive rite must certainly be performed for the sake of pacification.
Sprinkling with water is desired immediately, especially as an expiation;
and touching [the object] while reciting the Viṣṇu-sūkta accompanied by the thousandfold eight-syllabled mantra.
When purification has been performed, this desired rite involving five oblations of clarified butter is prescribed;
there is no requirement for a specific lunar day, nor a constellation, nor an examination of the time.
In matters of expiation, atonement must be performed immediately;
those who know the Tantras and have mastered four, three, two, or one Veda are the qualified authorities.
If [the teacher] knows even a single Veda immediately, or many Vedas after some delay,
and is a knower of all the Tantras, then he shall be the most excellent according to the rule.
Even an inferior method must be performed immediately by those who are incapable;
this is the established rule for those learned in the words, sentences, and means of valid knowledge, and who remain steadfast in the Vedic sacrifices and vows.
Accompanied by capable, self-controlled, and tranquil image-keepers,
the preceptor should thus perform the ritual sprinkling of water upon Hari according to the prescribed injunctions.
A beautiful, flawless jar, filled to the brim with three āḍhakas,
provided with a tuft of grass, wrapped in a pair of cloths, and endowed with gems.
One should worship [the deity] seated in a full vessel of rice-stalks with the Puruṣasūkta,
and with the root mantra, the ancillary mantras, and the ritual for the four forms, in due order, using the arghya and other offerings.
Therein, one should install Viṣṇu, Mahāviṣṇu, and Sadāviṣṇu;
having performed the rites of delineation and so forth, and having consecrated the fire, one should offer oblations.
The Pauruṣa hymn, the Viṣṇusūkta, the Cittisruk, the Saptahotṛ, the Caturhotṛ, the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ, and the five Upaniṣads—victory! 27.80.
One who is well-composed should offer oblations with the Sāvitrī, the Vyāhṛtis, the verse "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat," and the three root-mantras, as well as the Gāyatrī. 27.81.
Having offered oblation after oblation, one should touch the image, the flask, and likewise the temple;
at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, one should touch [the deity] with the three roots using the *prasṛti* mudrā.

Having caused water to fall from the vessel by sprinkling it from all sides, and having performed a circumambulation while maintaining a continuous stream before him, one should sprinkle [the area] with *kuśa* grass.
When the Vāstu-homa has been performed,
one should finally offer eight thousand oblations of either Palāśa or Khadira wood with the ten Vāstoṣpati mantras.
Likewise, one may perform five hundred or even eight hundred [recitations];
for that duration, one should offer oblations of clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, sesame seeds, and śāli rice.
In this very manner, one should offer oblations for each individual mantra;
however, one should offer according to what is available, following the path prescribed by the scriptures.
For those following the Vedic tradition, one should offer clarified butter with the root mantra;
having performed this according to the prescribed rule, one should then bind the protective thread (kautuka).
Indeed, with the twelve-syllable mantra and with lotus threads,
one should perform a great festival at night to the auspicious sounds of conchs and trumpets.
A great festival should be held at night, and the sprinkling with water during the day;
then, at an auspicious hour in the morning, one should begin the ritual sprinkling.
Having invoked the God, who is characterized by the conch, the discus, and other [emblems], one should worship Him together with His limbs (aṅgas) and with the twelve forms (mūrtis).
It was surrounded by the Ādityas, Rudras, Vasus, and others, as well as the Kinnaras and other beings;
it was the supreme mantra, beginning with Vāṅgīya and the bindu, and ending with the word of salutation.
With a mantra beginning with the *praṇava*, one who is well-composed should bathe [the deity];
the knower of mantras should then bathe Bhuvaneśvara with the remaining water. (27.92)
By means of two hymns. Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
Now I shall briefly explain to you the remainder of the ritual acts, through the application of which every supreme rite becomes complete and flawless. 28.1
Having performed the purification as prescribed for an image defiled by plaster and the like, other purifications should also be carried out with due propriety prior to the consecration. (28.2)
Having thoroughly stirred together water from sacred bathing places mixed with the ashes of the Brahman-skin burnt by the Vaiṣṇava fire, as well as the juice of the five leaves; 28.3.
Having consecrated the image with cow-horn [water], one should again smear it with its powders,
combined with dūrvā grass, sadābhadrā, white mustard, and turmeric.
Rubbing with the bark of milky trees destroys the humors (doṣas), as does an ointment;
likewise, an application of a paste made from dūrvā grass and white mustard mixed with cow's milk [is effective]. (28.5)
There was incense made from powdered sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, along with frankincense;
and a garland of lamps made of cow's ghee and lotus fibers surrounded it on all sides.
Likewise, an ointment made from five ingredients— pippala bark, sahā, lakṣmī, gandhanāga, and lotus filaments— ground together with the juice of milk-exuding tree bark, should be applied.
One should perform bathing, anointing, and especially fumigation;
this removes all defects and is supremely conducive to the increase of one's position.
The filling is said to be threefold, performed with auspicious food, flowers, and water;
it bestows nourishment, grants victory, is meritorious, and likewise wards off untimely death.
The filling with milk-rice (pāyasa) is the most excellent for removing all defects;
it should be combined with bulbs, ghee, sugar, cakes, and plantain fruit.
It is declared to be for the sake of purification, for bestowing nourishment, and indeed for the purpose of expiation;
it should also be performed during festivals by those who desire their own spiritual prosperity.
He placed jars filled with five kinds of water, containing grains, rice, and cloth,
joined with gold, gems, and other precious things, provided with tufts of kusha grass, and adorned with sprouts.
Having covered them with lotuses and other flowers, they were adorned with kuśa grass, blossoms, and the like; they were draped in unwashed garments and honored with perfumes and flowers.
Having anointed [the image] with the entire [set of substances], one should bathe it in sequence with the five [products of the cow],
as well as with perfumes and the products of the cow such as milk, curd, clarified butter, and so forth.
Having worshipped according to the rules, having smeared [the image] with perfumes and covered it with a garment—
specifically a fragrant, unwashed one— and having likewise covered the pedestal with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
With pure milk-rice, turmeric, and sesame seeds prepared with purity,
along with drinks, linctuses, chews, and such things as bulbs, roots, and fruits.
One should fill [the vessel] on all sides with many divine delicacies accompanied by side dishes,
as well as with curd, milk, molasses, clarified butter, and seasonally ripe fruits.
The vessel should be filled with cold food accompanied by auspicious recitations such as the *Annasūkta*;
one should set it for seven *ghaṭikās* and cause it to be sounded with the resonance of musical instruments.
One should offer milk-rice and other oblations in the four directions in due order,
and with the five Brahma-sūktas, one should offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge in sequence.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, he should present the bali-offering to the spirits in the various directions;
then, having obtained permission, he should dismiss all of that and cast it into the water. (28.20)
Then one should properly propitiate [the deity], perform the festival with food and other offerings, and likewise have the ritual bathing performed; in this way, all prosperity shall come to pass.
If [the corpse] is touched by Brahmins of mixed caste (varṇasaṅkara), one should prescribe one hundred and eight [repetitions];
likewise for those who approach a woman of their own caste, but for the slayer of a Brahmin, eight thousand.
In this case,
as well as for one who has violated the teacher’s bed or for one associated with the theft of gold, there is likewise sprinkling with water.
In this case, one should arrange for the feeding of the twice-born and perform their ritual bathing;
even when [the site] has been touched by those who drink liquor, one should perform the sprinkling with water and other such rites.
If Janārdana is touched by those defiled by such acts as the killing of a Brahmin, the gift of cows to many Brahmins, the offering of food, or likewise the ritual bathing [must be performed]. (28.25)

By means of sprinkling with water, ritual bathing, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and eating [only at prescribed times], as well as by the gift of land, gold, and Kapila cows, and likewise by a hundred recitations of the entire Veda; 28.26.
If, through negligence, one enters a house or approaches a divine image that has been defiled by contact with a single outcaste, it should likewise be sprinkled with water.
If it is touched by many people who are free from defects, it likewise possesses great merit;
even when a temple or a sacred image is touched by Caṇḍālas or Śvapacas, [it remains pure].
If the materials for worship are touched [by an impure person], one should perform sprinkling with water and other rites;
for five, six, or seven days, one should perform the great ablution (mahāsnāna) and the worship of the twice-born.
When the image or the temple itself has been touched by the seven types of outcasts,
there shall be a sprinkling with water, a ritual bath, the gift of a cow, and an extensive distribution of food and other provisions.
When images are touched by Śūdras in the guise of thieves, purification is desired through sprinkling with water, fumigation, and bathing. (28.31)
The Vaiśyas, assuming the form of thieves, should, being well-composed, perform the ritual sprinkling with water, the bathing, and the feeding in due order.

If, out of delusion or for the sake of wealth and desire, one acts in the guise of a thief, purification shall come through sprinkling with water alone by the kings; there is no doubt in this matter. (28.33)
If Keśava is clearly seen even in the form of a thief, one should have him bathed there; sixteen jars are prescribed for that occasion.

If a superior twice-born man, out of devotion, should touch [an impure object] without having bathed and being devoid of the consecration of mantras, he should purify himself with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If the Lord Janārdana is touched with devotion by the king,
he is purified simply by the bathing ceremony using the nine jars as prescribed.
If he has been touched by a Vaiśya who is devoid of mantras but acts with devotion, he becomes purified by bathing with exactly fifty jars [of water]. || 28.37 ||
If one who is devoid of mantra-consecration is touched by a Śūdra out of devotion,
the bathing must be performed again with exactly one hundred and eight [repetitions].
When Janārdana has been touched with devotion even by the people of the seven [lower] castes,
one becomes pure here through the sprinkling of water and through bathing.
If he should be touched by these women through delusion or out of desire, the previously mentioned expiation must be performed; the remainder consists of the worship of Brahmins.
Furthermore, one should perform the gift of a cow and the ritual bathing with cow-products according to the prescribed method,
when Madhusūdana has been touched by a Brāhmaṇī on the path to the city.
One should perform a ceremonial bath according to one's ability and provide a meal for Brahmins, even if there has been contact with a Kshatriya or a Vaishya due to delusion or through theft. (28.42)
If a Śūdra should touch [the image] through theft or enter the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), there must be a sprinkling with water, a ritual bath, and a feeding of Brahmins. (28.43)
One should perform a sprinkling with water accompanied by a great ablution for those born of the lowest castes,
for dogs, or even for the fetus of a woman artisan.
Upon giving birth, one should perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) for twelve days or ten;
and the Great Bath (mahāsnāna) should be performed, accompanied by festivals and the distribution of food.
If a woman of the [lower] castes should give birth in a temple of the gods through negligence, she becomes pure by sprinkling water and performing the great ablution (mahāsnāna). || 28.46 ||
If a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya gives birth through ignorance [of the rules],
one should perform a sprinkling with water for three or four days.

The wise man should perform the sprinkling with water according to this sequence: it is doubled for a blacksmith, a dog, a woman who has recently given birth, and one who has performed a cremation, respectively. 28.48.

The recitation of the Pārāyaṇa, the study of the Vedas, the gift of a cow, as well as a meal, the performance of offerings, and even a vehicle at the time of the [daily] rounds—[all these should be done with that vessel]. 28.49.
In whichever direction it fell, one should perform a fire-oblation there with ghee, sacrificial offerings, and eight hundred palāśa leaves while reciting that mantra.
Likewise, when the constant offering of bali has been defiled by dogs, crows, and the like,
one should purify it with the two root mantras as well as the five upaniṣads.
And here, with a concentrated mind, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the Viṣṇu-sūkta;
it is recommended for all expiations as well as for recitations and oblations. 28.52.
Having washed the vessel, bathed, and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the rules— whether it be an eight-syllabled or a twelve-syllabled self-recitation— 53.53.
Having properly covered that ground and smeared it with cow dung,
the practitioner of mantra should cause very beautiful milk-rice mixed with ghee to be offered.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound with rice grains, he— being composed— placed upon it a cloth, then rice,
and *kuśa* grass and flowers, and sprinkled them while reciting the Astra-mantra.
One should place the vessel with the root mantra and touch it again with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Then, having sprinkled it with water while reciting the Astra mantra, one should worship Śānti on the right side.
Having offered the food with the root mantra and the clarified butter with the *praṇava*,
one hundred and eight times or even a thousand times, according to the sequence.
Thereafter, one should place the remnants of the oblation into the vessel for the bali offering;
having done that, and having sprinkled it as if it were the Linga, one should invoke [the deity] with the root mantra as before.
Alternatively, having purified the ritual image (karmārcā), one should invoke [the deity] into it and worship;
having offered water for the feet, the arghya-offering, and water for sipping, one should then honor [the deity] with perfumes and flowers.
Then, having paid homage and offered praise, with his upper garment on and composed in mind,
he should utter the vyāhṛtis, perform the recitation, and place [the syllable] Tāra upon his head.
Accompanied by conch shells, trumpets, and other instruments, having proceeded slowly clockwise around it,
the wise man should enter within and place that vessel in the northeast.
Having performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsya) and discarded the washed vessel, one should bring forth another;
for the subsequent sacrifice (anuyāga), having purified a new image, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsaya).
The preceptor, being well-composed, should specifically offer the expiatory oblation into the Vaiṣṇava fire with the mantras of the five Upaniṣads. (28.63)
Then one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the twelve-syllable vidyā;
one should sacrifice sacrificial wood, clarified butter, and cooked rice in sequence with the eight-syllable mantra.
Having taken a thousand, or even a hundred, or indeed twenty-five iron jars, well-fastened and wrapped with thread.
Having filled it according to the rules with gems, gold,
and all kinds of seeds, one should place it there in a stable position.
Having invoked Hari there, one should thereafter worship him according to the prescribed rule;
one should perform the remaining rites by the very same path previously described.
Having worshipped Janārdana with devotion for a year, a man should perform the ceremonial bath (snapana) and a festival according to the rites prescribed by the rules. (28.68)
Whatever fruit one obtains by performing the Pavitrārohaṇa rite,
that same fruit he does not obtain who performs the Pavitrārohaṇa without following the prescribed injunctions.
The wise have declared that his annual worship is fruitless;
therefore, the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) to Hari should be performed year after year. 28.70
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, according to the prescribed rite,
it should be performed when the sun is situated in Leo or in Virgo.
One should have a thread spun by a maiden—whether made of cotton, lotus fiber, or linen;
but in its absence, one may use a thread made of *darbha* grass. (28.72)

That which has been used in a ritual, or defiled by other food and so forth, should not be employed; it must be purified with the three-fold [mantra]. Thus, the best [food] is of three kinds, distinguished by its lack of alcohol.
One should make it twenty-seven-fold, or likewise fifty-four-fold;
it may also be one hundred and eight-fold, or a thousand-fold forest garland.

The fruit—whether human or divine, residence in the same world as the deity (sālokya), or even liberation itself—does not depend on the image being merely the size of the navel, thighs, or knees; rather, it depends on the supreme measure of the original form.
Twelve knots are prescribed, as well as twice that and thrice that;
one hundred and eight knots should always be made in the forest garland (vanamālā).
In the Adhivāsana-sūtra, however, there are exactly twelve knots;
for the twice-born, the mantra is "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," while for others, it is the twelve-syllable mantra.
One should recite the mantra as many times as there are knots made upon the purifying thread (pavitraka),
whether once, twice, or even thrice.
Then, having smeared the interior of the knot with ointments such as saffron, uśīra, camphor, and sandalwood, one should perform the ritual placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa).
Having accepted the purificatory materials and fasted on the eleventh day,
he should worship with perfumes and flowers and place them before the deity at night.
Those devoted to the knowledge of reality should perform the rite of ascending the sacred thread for Hari on the eleventh day, having worshipped him with devotion using the root mantra.
Having worshipped the one whose banner is Garuḍa with ornaments, necklaces, and offerings,
one should perform a vigil there accompanied by dance, song, and other such arts.
Having fasted, become pure, performed his prayers, and subdued his senses, he should give gifts to the foremost of the twice-born with devotion, having worshipped them while remembering Hari. 28.83.
Having consecrated it there, one should take that purifying thread in the morning and place it upon the head of Viṣṇu with the hymn beginning "Atodevā".
A Śūdra, however, should worship Hari with the root mantra or whatever [mantra] he may have,
accompanied by the resonance of the Vedas, shouts of victory, hymns of praise, songs, and auspicious sounds.
One should perform the rite of ascending the purifier (pavitrārohaṇa) and then address the deity with garlands of gems and coral, mandāra flowers, and other such offerings.
O Garuḍadhvaja! May this annual worship be yours;
O Janārdana, [may it be accepted] even if it is deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in devotion.
O Lord! May that which has been worshipped by me be fulfilled for you, just as you always bear the forest garland and the Kaustubha gem upon your heart.
"Likewise, bear these purifying threads and this worship with your heart.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should bow with devotion and ask for forgiveness.
Then one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins, dedicating it to Hari;
thereafter, one should worship the preceptor with devotion and others as well with devotion. (28.90)
One should offer oblations of barley mixed with ghee into the fire while reciting the root mantra;
thereafter, one should worship the Brahmins with devotion and bestow sacrificial fees upon them.
One should honor all supplicants according to one's ability with food such as boiled rice;
for as many tens of thousands of principles (tattvas) as there are in that honor, so many fingers are there in this [act].
One should consecrate as many knots as have been mentioned with those very principles.
Sāṃvat.
Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter.
Now I shall briefly explain the characteristics of the conduct of the pledges (samayācāra), by the practice of which all perfections (siddhis) are attained by all those who have been initiated. 29.1
The four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas—among these, those who are initiated, devoted, self-controlled, and tranquil—are all remembered as Samayins. (29.2)
First is the initiate (samayī), then the consecrated one (dīkṣita), followed by the one who has received the cakravartin consecration;
likewise, the guru, the ācārya, and the venerable one (bhagavat) is remembered as the seventh. || 29.3 ||
Yāga, stoma, mahāyāga, adhvara, sava, kratu, and hari-stoma—these are to be known as the seven sacrifices in brief. (29.4)

The initiation of those belonging to the [four] orders is prescribed for spring, summer, autumn, and the rainy season respectively; or, for all of them, it may take place during the northern course of the sun.
For those belonging to the [four] social orders (varṇa), the initiation (dīkṣā) should be performed once, twice, thrice, four times, or seven times;
likewise, it may be performed twelve times or even every year.
A name is first taken according to the season of the flowers;
for the members of the social orders (varṇas) here, it ends in -śarman, -varman, or -gupta, or ends in -dāsa.
One should understand that [the names] beginning with *samayin* are like those beginning with *keśava*;
however, for women, the names beginning with *keśavā* and ending with *devī* are proclaimed in the three genders. (29.8)
From the Śūdras down to the male and female slaves, all were duly initiated according to their various sacrifices;
they were all constantly devoted to their gurus. (29.9)
They should protect the duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life, as well as their respective observances,
through constant service rendered to gurus, gods, the twice-born, and the sacred fires.
If they should desire prosperity through vows, fasts, and observances with devotion,
one should not eat without having sacrificed to the gods, nor in the house of one who has not been initiated.
One should not touch the remains of offerings (nirmālya), nor should one give them away, step over them, or eat them;
for the nirmālya of all the gods is traditionally held to be impure.
Others accept as pure flowers and other offerings already enjoyed by Viṣṇu;
one must not eat from a bell-metal vessel, nor should another deity be worshipped [therein]. (29.13)
One should not reveal the Siddhānta to those who are unfit, such as the uninitiated; one should not converse with a woman in her courses, nor with Caṇḍālas, nor with those of the lowest castes.
One should never dwell in an improper place, nor with heretics;
one should not apply the horizontal sectarian mark (tiryakpuṇḍra), nor utter the syllable "dviṭ," nor engage in impure mixing.
One should always avoid the hornless goat, garlic, drumstick tree, fermented grain-water, sheep's milk, oil-cake, millet, and mushrooms.
One should not occupy a seat, a bed, or a vehicle that bears the form of a wheel [or the marks of a Tathāgata] in the presence of a [Buddha] image;
nor should one perform the praise of another image in the presence of [a Buddha] image.
One should not listen to slander, nor should one spend time in vain;
marked with the discus and bearing the name of Viṣṇu, one should have sons, servants, and cattle.
One should sleep placing one's head in that very direction where the sun has set;
one should not stretch out one's feet toward the fire, a cow, a teacher, a Brahmin, or other objects of veneration.
One should not eat the flesh of fish, tortoises, or boars;
one should perform circumambulation of Brahmins, fire, Vaiṣṇavas, the Aśvattha tree, and cows.
Having seen all the temples of Viṣṇu, one should salute them with devotion;
one should not cross a river by means of one's arms, nor on a cow, nor in another's garment.
One should not enter the water naked, nor should one run when rain falls;
moreover, one should honor all those mortals who bear the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* marks according to their capacity.
One should always give the first alms-food, as well as a handful of fodder to the cows;
one should not eat food that has been kept overnight, nor wait for food that has not arrived from another's house.
One should not touch any part of the body with oil that has been applied to the head;
one should not remain seated without wearing undergarments, nor should one honor another who eats different food.
One should not eat salt that is visibly impure, nor substances produced from excrement;
one should not engage in dispute with Vaiṣṇavas or with Brahmins who have been initiated.
One should not despise even an outcaste or a dog-cooker who is a devotee of Viṣṇu;
one should mentally remember that all actions are indeed for the sake of Viṣṇu. (29.26)
One should even give up one's life for the sake of Viṣṇu, by performing whatever action through which the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of the World, [is attained]. (29.27)
For that task is indeed accomplished by the Vaiṣṇavas at all times;
when the mind is fixed on the path of the righteous, speech likewise abides on the path of the righteous.
Therefore, one should train first in all the sense faculties;
it is the firm conviction that the supreme duty for all is to be of service to others.
Therefore, with every effort, one should act for the benefit of all;
among the fruits [of action], gifts that bring great renown are thus considered middling.
The secret gift should be performed according to the suitability of the recipient, the time, and other factors;
all things should be given to a worthy recipient by one who is wise.
Aiming solely for the god, with fame as a secondary consequence, the mental dharma of one who has conquered the senses and is devoted is supreme. (29.32)
It is said that for the ordinary person, dharma consists of physical action; for the middling person, however, it is verbal.
Dharma is traditionally held to have the form of ritual action, whereas the supreme [dharma] has the form of knowledge.
Through knowledge one attains liberation, and action is intended for the sake of knowledge;
however, in this world, pure discernment exists only through the favor of dharma.
A mind possessed by worldly existence is not capable of being easily purified;
therefore, having worshipped Him for the sake of removing obstacles, one attains knowledge through His grace.
Then liberation shall be attainable by those alone who are devoted to Him, and not by others.
One should never reveal the deity installed within the temple. (29.36)
Except during the time of worship and at the conclusion of the ritual, one should not expose contact with impure substances nor even a crowd of people. (29.37)
In the palace, one should always avoid worldly implements,
as well as Vedic and Vaiṣṇava mantras intended for pacification and nourishment.
Within that interval, the tantras and mantras should be applied as appropriate—
those purifying mantras found among the Ṛg, the Yajur, and the Sāma Vedas.

Furthermore, those mantras from the Atharvaṇa texts which are directly based upon the Supreme God, whether by means of a lakṣa or a lakṣya, are to be employed in rites such as the worship of the gods. (29.40)
The Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs, are to be acquired separately; having investigated them, one should apply them here.
Indeed, there exists nothing superior to these among the literary works on earth. (29.41)
Born once again into a lineage purified by those very Vedic mantras which are remembered as the granters of desires, he himself was consecrated with all the sacraments.
Disregarding those [other doctrines], he ought not to follow other mantras;
for the Vedic injunctions are established as being primarily concerned with the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa). || 29.43 ||
Those who desire worldly pleasures must be separated from whatever deity they have resorted to;
those Vedic mantras, whether performed collectively or individually, have been mastered.
Those who, for the most part, engage in the accomplishment of ritual acts based on various fruits, should be examined again and again and accepted by the Vaiṣṇavas who uphold the Vedic word. 29.45.
This tantra indeed serves as the basis for its worship;
having understood that, one should extract other Vedic mantras oneself. (29.46)
And relying upon this tantra, one should worship Puruṣottama;
having performed recitation, praise, and attendance with these, one should remain mindful of Hari.
He who recites the mantras according to the prescribed rule is the principal sacrificer to Viṣṇu;
those who especially perform the sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña) with Vedic hymns [are likewise so].
They perform worship at the proper time, and Hari is well-pleased with them;
having meditated upon Viṣṇu within the orb of the sun, he is praised with Vedic mantras.
While that [mantra] is being held, one should offer oblations into the fire for the sake of accomplishing the task;
therein, that which is mere meditation, as described in the Vedānta, is without support.

In that case, there is no entitlement for one engaged in ritual action due to the weakness of the senses, just as [there is none] for one who desires the fruit of a tree standing on a mountain precipice. (29.51)
He should apply himself tirelessly to the means; thus he should exert effort.
Effort must be applied methodically in all things; mere desire alone is not sufficient.
Therefore, one should desire the supreme goal through the application of body, speech, and mind in due order;
however, in the formless [state], worship or meditation performed with devotion is desired.
That which appears delightful is indeed the cause of misfortune,
for his senses, by virtue of birth, are prone to the perception of gross objects.
They do not comprehend the subtle reality, whether after a long time or even sooner;
moreover, no one is able to meditate upon the God without his form.
For when the intellect has ceased from all forms, where does it abide?
When the intellect has ceased, it either languishes or is overcome by sleep. (29.56)
Therefore, the wise man should worship Him with his intellect as having form; he should reflect that "He exists" in a manner that is beyond direct perception. 29.57
In every way, a wise person, without abandoning the prescribed forms,
should worship the Supreme God for the sake of liberation or for the sake of rewards.
By means of the mantras that take refuge at the feet of Viṣṇu as they are being repeated,
one's true nature is perceived within the intellect through His grace, and not otherwise.
All mantras, hymns, meditations, and acts of worship exist for the sake of devotion;
he in whose heart that devotion is intense is considered a true devotee, and no other.
He who constantly perceives with his intellect that pleasant things are gifts from the gods and unpleasant things are born of one's own karma— he is a devotee, and no other person.
One should know his form to be composed of yoga and pervading all things;
he, consisting of mantra, is to be meditated upon eternally for the sake of compassion toward his devotees. (29.62)
When that wise one, having desisted from action, delights in nirvāṇa,
then the subtle body should worship him as the Supreme Person.
His powers are to be known as having the form of weapons; his arms are the directions.
The sky is his head, the earth his feet, the sun his sight, and the moon his mind. (29.64)
This [Self] is indeed uncuttable, unburnable, undissoluble, and likewise undryable;
it is eternal, omnipresent, immovable, and always worthy of worship by the wise.
Whenever the mind is serene, one should then meditate upon the subtle;
even ascetics, becoming distressed by doubt, falter in this regard.

One who possesses self-mastery should make the meaning of the scriptures firm through all branches of knowledge; and by means of pure discernment, one should not engage in a mere superficial flooding over of the scripture.
One should always practice that which is declared in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra and Dharma-śāstra,
as well as that which is taught in the Tantras provided it is not contradictory and conforms to one's family, caste, and stage of life.
For all Śrīs and Śūdras, however, there is no rite of initiation (upanāyanika);
their initiation consists of the *dīkṣā* and a brief ritual according to the Tantric system.
The Tantras, the mantras of the Tantras, and the ritual injunctions based upon them exist;
and the threefold performance is carried out with the root mantras, the Gāyatrī, and the Vedic mantras.
In the case of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, [the initiation] should take place before the king or a Brāhmaṇa; or rather, everything may be performed by a Brāhmaṇa.
In rites such as the fire-oblation (homa), they should use their own mantras, or those of the anuloma [caste]. || 29.71 ||
All those born from the four castes, whether born in the natural order (anuloma) or the inverse order (pratiloma), exist therein;
among them, those born in the natural order are superior, while those born in the inverse order are to be avoided.
Among all those born of inverse unions, only the Sūta is accepted;
the others, being excluded from the system of castes and stages of life, are not entitled to initiation at all. (29.73)
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—
thus are the four stages of life divided, and further subdivided according to their specific distinctions.
Among them, the first is the celibate student (brahmacārī), the bearer of the sectarian mark (liṅgin), the disciple, and the lay follower (upāsaka);
he eats food free from pungent spices and salt, subsists on alms, and is moderate in his diet. (29.75)
He who sleeps on the bare ground or upon a deerskin and observes celibacy is called a *brahmacārī*.
He who performs such rites and bears the marks made by the discus and other symbols [is likewise so called]. (29.76)
He who is devoted to the worship of the deity is proclaimed as a *liṅgin*;
he who lives on alms alone, being intent on service, is a reciter and a worshipper. (29.77)
He who is never intent on other tasks is proclaimed a disciple;
he who worships the God at the three junctions of the day and is not devoted to other affairs.
Having bathed three times, he should constantly attend upon his guru; such a person is an upāsaka.
Even while remaining a householder, he is observant of vows and is wealthy; these indeed are the householders who act as teachers.
Four types of practitioners are proclaimed here according to their differences in conduct:
one who observes vows and fasts, one who eats only at night, one who performs regular worship, and one who has conquered the senses. (29.80)

Approaching his wife only during the proper season, moderate in diet, always observant of vows and devoted to roots, he is intent upon sacrifice, Vedic study, worship of the gods, and the maintenance of his disciples and others. (29.81)
A man who is devoted to his own wife should be known as one who belongs to the householder stage;
he should always be intent on hospitality toward all guests, enjoying pleasures while remaining endowed with happiness.
A devotee intent on the festivals of the deity is said to be rich in sacrificial offerings on the holy days;
he is engaged in officiating at sacrifices and teaching, whether they be Vedic or Tantric.

One who performs daily sacrifices, one who has conquered anger, a teacher intent on bestowing grace, as well as a forest-dweller, a knower of the Tantras, and a Guru who is indeed partless (niṣkala). 29.84.
In this system, the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) is proclaimed to be of four kinds: he who eats food free from pungent and salty flavors, and who is accompanied by his wife and sons. 29.85.
Sleeping on the bare ground or upon a deerskin, the Vaikhānasa should always meditate,
subsisting on forest fare, worshipping at the three junctions of the day, and being devoted to silent recitation and burnt offerings.

Wearing bark garments, skins, and grass mats, sleeping on darbha grass, constantly reciting prayers, bathing three times a day, dwelling in a fixed abode, clad in rags, and subsisting on roots and fruits. (29.87)

Having bathed at sacred fords, worshipping and meditating, the Guru—performing twelve-fold recitation, content with whatever comes by chance, eating only at night, and firm in his vows—[should proceed]. (29.88)
Cīrin, Vimatsara, Maunin, Niṣkala, Arcayannahnas-triḥ, Haṃsa, Paramahaṃsa, Bhagavān, and Prabhu—these are his names. (29.89)
In this Tantra, the initiated ascetic is declared to be of four kinds:
he constantly bears the conch and the discus, carries a single staff, and subsists on alms from a single house. (29.90)

Always radiant, skilled in ritual action, and meditative, he is a *haṃsa* ever devoted to the recitation of mantras; intent upon non-duality, he is a staff-bearer (*daṇḍin*) dedicated to wisdom and meditation. (29.91)
Peaceful, devoid of the topknot and the sacred thread, subsisting on alms and established in his vows,
the ascetic shall be a Paramahaṃsa, dedicated to the practice of the Tantra.
Carrying a conch, a discus, a grass mat, a carrying-net, a water-pot, and a purifier;
possessing a triple staff and a bowl, the Blessed One was a mendicant wearing a yogic belt.
Constantly carrying these very items— the umbrella and the image—
as well as worshipping the Lord of Gods through the ritual of the wheel, he remained self-restrained.
Engaged in the worship of the three junctions of the day, established in goodness, and devoted to recitation,
the lord [should perform this] during the equinoxes, the solstices, on one's birthday, on the twelfth lunar day, and under the Śravaṇa asterism.
On the eighth, the ninth, and the fifth lunar days, one should not approach a woman;
likewise, after sprinkling food with water under the Mūla asterism, one should not touch it, nor drink water.
Having meditated within upon the Puruṣa and likewise upon the blazing Vaiśvānara,
the silent sage should then offer five oblations with the Praṇava to the Fivefold Self.
One should swallow the morsel so that it barely enters the mouth; one should neither laugh nor show agitation.
One should abandon all fickleness everywhere and eat without making a sound.
If he then sees a menstruating woman, an outcaste, a heretic, a temple-priest, a cock, or artisans, he should abandon the food and drink immediately and bathe.
Having recited the five Upaniṣads, one should sprinkle [the materials] with the Praṇava.
Viṣṇu, Mahāviṣṇu, and Sadāviṣṇu—these three [are to be invoked]. (29.100)
At the three libations, they should always be worshipped in sequence through recitation, meditation, and other means:
at dawn, the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī; at midday, the twelve-syllable mantra.
In the evening, one should constantly recite the eight-syllable mantra, or always recite the root mantra;
having risen and bathed, one should meditate upon the Guru and worship the God.
He should go out with his right foot and enter his dwelling again;
by the permission of his guru, he should go for alms, speaking "Śam" while holding the bowl.
Having shown it to the guru, he should deposit it with his permission;
then, having sipped water and offered fuel-sticks into the fire with the root mantra, he becomes pure.
Seated comfortably on a seat with his feet placed upon the ground,
and touching the vessel with his left hand, he should perform the oblations to the vital breaths (prāṇāhuti).
If a twice-born man, having eaten, should rise from his seat without having sipped water for purification, he must immediately perform a bath; therefore, he should sip water right there.
Having again performed the twilight worship and likewise offered oblations of fuel-sticks,
and having worshipped Hari, he should go for alms just as before.
Thus, abiding by the word of his guru both morning and evening,
he later entered the stage of a householder with the permission of his guru.
Having bathed, one should worship him daily and thereafter perform one's ritual duties.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter of the Viṣṇu-saṃhitā.
Now begins the thirtieth chapter.
Now I shall briefly describe the supreme Bhāgavata Yoga, which was never heard before by others, and which is the highest benefit for those seeking welfare. 30.1.
Restraining his diet and conduct, disciplined in his actions, composed, and self-controlled, he should constantly practice the Bhāgavata yoga. (30.2)

Knowing the division of the five periods of the day, speaking measuredly, eating moderately, conquering desire, anger, and the rest, he was devoted [to his practice], regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal.
Endowed with the conduct of the observances, devoted to recitation and meditation,
he should stay in a solitary, secluded place, free from wind and devoid of noise.
Having assumed a yogic posture and observing silence, the knower of yoga should practice yoga;
having worshipped Hari, he should offer that very worship there. (30.5)
With palms joined in reverence and face cast downward, one should not beg for any reward as a servant; if [the Lord] is pleased, he will grant it of his own accord.
For he indeed knows the proper time, as well as the merits and defects of devotion and worship;
being pleased, he bestows grace, but never with haste.
But one should certainly not fail to show favor [to others], even across hundreds of future births, when other karmas that are ripening have reached their exhaustion. (30.8)
Hari reveals himself to his devotees, bestowing his grace upon them;
consequently, prosperity itself appears before him.
His enemies perish constantly, his prosperity increases of its own accord;
fruit shall arise in abundance without effort, and diseases vanish by themselves.
Nowhere does his affliction increase, nor do his livestock and progeny;
his lifespan shall be long, and his offspring will be fortunate.
People praise him, and neither thieves nor robbers would steal from him;
his sovereignty remains untroubled for a long time, requiring no effort to maintain.
The intellect shall be directed toward dharma and the like, and turned away from adharma and the like;
and at the time of merit, it shall continue thus until the very end with ease.
Being born again into an excellent family and possessing devotion toward Acyuta once more—
this shall be most excellent, and so too in birth after birth.
Through its grace, the eightfold sovereignty will become undefiled;
one may dwell for a long time according to one's wish, or likewise attain nirvāṇa.
By his grace, there must certainly be favor toward his devotees in every way;
even one who has fallen may obtain various desires and shall not be abandoned.
But through the persistence of karma, suffering arises in saṃsāra;
therefore, devotion to Him alone shall be the cause of his prosperity. (30.17)
Through that knowledge, men’s devotion should be diligently increased;
for when it has been especially increased, it leads them onto the true path. 30.18
Therefore, one should make a distinction here regarding the merits and defects as they truly exist;
with a pure mind, one should contemplate all the defects in solitude.
The mind, freed from desire, anger, and the like, will become pure;
through practice on the path of yoga, the purification of the mind shall come to pass.
When the mind is purified, devotion to Him arises and becomes unwavering;
once that devotion has been produced, the consciousness remains fixed upon the Reality.
For one who is overwhelmed by passion and hatred, the vision of reality is fruitless;
therefore, those two must first be dispelled by one who desires to see reality correctly. (30.22)
When holy places are seen, and when fears and deaths [are encountered], as well as diseases and insults, dispassion arises. (30.23)
When death and other such states are perceived, one should remain composed by oneself and constantly maintain discernment through the intellect as the cause of dispassion.
From discernment, devotion and detachment will always arise for him;
from that, an intellect directed toward reality will become unswerving.
The wise devotee of the Lord should not be attached to enjoyments, nor should he set his mind on what is difficult to obtain; he should always be content with even a little. (30.26)
Seeing only the ripening of karmas when perceiving the pleasant and the unpleasant, one should never lament, thinking, "This is right; this is not. (30.27)
One possessed of discernment should see that there is no sovereignty whatsoever belonging to the self;
one should not proclaim one's duties, nor should one ever display agitation.
One should not desire any fame from the worship of the God of gods;
rather, one should cultivate a mind that is as attached to the God as it is to its own dear objects. (30.29)
When devotion has become constant, the vision of reality arises.
One who knows reality, being free from attachment, should wander as a mendicant wherever he may be.
Furthermore, one should always frequent a single sacred ford and a single holy field;
with devotion, one should meditate upon the God, being established in Him and having Him as one's supreme goal.
And by remembering Him at the time of death, one shall attain union with Him;
being dispassionate, one dissolves all principles into the Supreme Self.
Having rendered the mind free from objective domains and remaining equanimous, one is liberated;
even while established in sovereign power, the yogi shall never forget the Divine.
For otherwise, there would certainly be an impairment over the course of time;
however, those devotees of pure mind who have attained union (sāyujya) [are exempt]. || 30.34 ||
They always become servants of Viṣṇu, free from all affliction;
yet, by the power of their attachment, saṃsāra may arise for them once again.
Otherwise, there would be either continued existence or liberation through dispassion;
however, those who have desisted and perceive reality as it is are distinguished above all others.
For them there shall be no further existence nor any negligence whatsoever here;
rather, liberation alone is to be known as the supreme goal among all goals.
All other states of existence, however, are unstable and subject to negligence;
nevertheless, due to the diversity of human intellects, both views are accepted by men.
Whether it be sovereign power or liberation, each belongs to someone to a certain extent;
yet devotion directed toward that [object] alone is the means for achieving both of them.
As his concentration increases, through the discernment that distinguishes [the self from the mind],
he diligently practices the limbs of yoga with a mind established in sattva.
Abiding in those [stages], one should remember Viṣṇu with a one-pointed mind; by that, the darkness (tamas) of this self-controlled person gradually dissolves, as does the passion (rajas). 30.41.
Then, through successive births, he attains perfection itself;
when, however, he abides in *sattva*, untouched by *rajas* at any time. (30.42)
Then liberation alone shall come to this great-souled one, or else union with Him;
therefore, one should always seek devotion, which is the cause of all this.
When devotion is cultivated, there will be welfare for him, and not otherwise;
for those obstacles which constantly corrupt the practice of yoga [must be overcome]. (30.44)
While those [sensual objects] are being pursued, one should resort to the vision of reality;
one should not practice them excessively at all times, nor should one cause the body to suffer.
One should also withdraw gradually and with effort from sense objects,
as well as from the sight of new things and from reliance on worldly rumors.
A wise man should desire application to the pursuit of useless thoughts;
for when all these have ceased, devotion increases in a person.
Sense objects are difficult to abandon; one should enjoy them provided they do not conflict with the treatises on Dharma.
Yet, because they are associated with many dangers, one should strive to turn away from the desire for them.
From those things, by turning away from which the mind would always become pure;
and the means for that turning away is indeed the purity of the supreme self. (30.49)
Since he is being honored by the Śuddhāvāsa deities, this Bibhatsu will not be born among impure things; his association shall be with the pure. (30.50)
Through non-association with impurities, his mind becomes serene;
for one who is serene and free from longing, devotion arises, and from that, liberation is certain.
Having conquered the objects of the senses, such as sound, and having closed the doors [of perception] in every way,
one should dissolve the senses within and contemplate the supreme state.
Having restrained the five vital airs through the practice of yoga, the knower of yoga,
with a mind made steady, should constantly meditate upon that supreme state.
One should contemplate the colors of the five winds;
they are to be meditated upon in succession, one after another, in the midst of the preceding ones.
The prāṇa is the color of kāśa flowers; the apāna, situated in its midst, is red;
the vyāna has the brilliance of a flashing lightning bolt; and the udāna is like a jasmine flower.
But then, the *samāna* breath should be meditated upon as resembling pure crystal;
having thus meditated, one should gradually restrain the five vital airs within.
Having understood the six limbs, one should employ them according to the rule:
first breath control (prāṇāyāma), then withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and then concentration (dhāraṇā). (30.57)
Then, reasoning (tarka), meditative absorption (samādhi), and meditation (dhyāna) are the six limbs in sequence,
which were previously described by the yogis as pūra, recaka, and kumbhaka.
The breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) are to be understood according to their respective measures in sequence;
having circumambulated the knee, neither too quickly nor too slowly. (30.59)
The snapping of the fingers that is performed here is proclaimed as one *mātrā*;
when the inhalation (*pūraka*) is performed with twelve *mātrās*, then—
Recaka (exhalation) should be performed with two counts, and kumbhaka (retention) with three;
thus is the regulation of the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma) proclaimed here in its proper sequence.
In all the scriptures, that which is known by the experts of the treatises is called prāṇāyāma;
however, that which is known as dhāraṇā is said to consist of three prāṇāyāmas.
The concentrations (dhāraṇā) are to be known as dark, yellow, reddish, and white in sequence;
first, by means of the seed-syllable of the nature of the Puruṣa situated in the center of the navel.
The Vāyavyā concentration should be performed; it is dark-blue in color and consists of inhalation (pūraka).
Then, that which was established in the heart by means of the red seed-syllable of the Universal Self (viśvātman) [is to be contemplated]. (30.64)
That is designated as Āgneyī; the second is considered to be Recakā, which is performed at the throat by means of the yellow seed-syllable Nivṛtti.
That is designated as the Māhendrī dhāraṇā, consisting of the kumbhaka breath-retention;
it is performed at the crown of the head with the white seed-syllable of the Universal Self (sarvātman) by means of these three [breaths] repeated three times each.
The concentration (dhāraṇā) performed while departing [from the body] is proclaimed as Vāruṇī;
when consciousness is held within those seeds while they remain steady, [that is Vāruṇī]. (30.67)
At that time, one should contemplate the entire world as endowed with those qualities,
with the seed-syllables situated in the navel and other locations as previously described, consisting of the qualities of the elements.
Those activities by which something is maintained are considered "maintaining activities" (dhāraṇākriyā);
for whatever is perceived through positive and negative concomitance [is established as such]. 30.69.
That [state] is proclaimed as *tarka* during the stages of *dhāraṇā* and so forth;
it consists of the effort of application (*āvaprayāsa*), characterized by the qualities (*guṇa*) according to one's karma.
And here, samādhi is to be understood as consisting of three successive stages of dhāraṇā;
therein, one should effect the cessation of the manifestation of the nature of both the meditator and the object of meditation.
The characteristic of meditative absorption (dhyāna) is thus characterized by the three qualities of concentration;
likewise, for one who in every respect is in some way equal to the objects of knowledge, [this state prevails].
This is declared by yogins to be yoga, through the sequential application of discernment:
it is the gathering together of the qualities (guṇas) along with the mind as its companion. (30.73)
That yoga is proclaimed here as being through the intellect by means of the state of true existence;
and that yoga is to be known by the wise as twofold, according to the division of knowledge and action. 30.74.
The realization of their identity with the Self through the modification of the internal organ is designated as Jñānayoga; Karmayoga, on the other hand, consists of action. (30.75)
Having first performed worship through the yoga of action, one should then worship Him through the yoga of knowledge,
and again sequentially with physical, vocal, and mental acts.
When the mind, having been established in the gross, is again established in the subtle,
and when it is joined with the supreme form, then that person is said to be liberated.
He who perceives with his intellect that light which is higher than the highest, whose nature is consciousness, immovable and eternal, is not born again upon this earth.
Therefore, with every effort, a devotee should always become a yogi;
being disciplined, he should worship the God, and in this way, perfection will surely come to pass.
Thus, this entire Viṣṇu-saṃhitā has been briefly recounted by me to you;
it was obtained by me directly from the mouth of Viṣṇu himself in another age.
This is the supreme knowledge among all knowledges, the highest secret among all secrets, and the greatest benefit among all benefits; therefore, this must be guarded by you as nothing else.
Just as I previously heard it directly from the mouth of the Blessed One, so has this entire tantra been related by me to you. (30.82)
It must not be given to one who has not been initiated, nor to one who has not resided [as a student] for a year;
nor to one who is not a devotee, nor to one who is undisciplined, nor ever to one who is devoted to another [deity]. (30.83)
"It must be taught in every way by teachers to one who is grateful, humble, pure, and a celibate student; such is the ordinance of Viṣṇu. (30.84)
For a man should keep everything secret; that which is not kept secret he shall destroy.
Therefore, this must always be guarded with every effort by the wise. (30.85)
Whoever should constantly read, listen to, or cause others to hear this with a concentrated mind, being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. 30.86.
Therefore, this should be studied and recited constantly by devotees;
it should always be written in a book and worshipped with great effort. (30.87)
Wherever this [text], established in a book, is constantly worshipped by those who are self-restrained,
there no fear whatsoever arises from disease, thieves, or other such perils.
Therefore, with every effort, one should constantly worship [it] at home;
one should install it there and protect it, for thus prosperity increases and becomes unshakable.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the Viṣṇu-saṃhitā.
